articles.title: Mirror Particle is building a ‘world model’ of human behavior | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Startups that promise to predict how humans will behave are having a moment. Over the past year, Simile raised $200 million at a $2 billion valuation; Aaru raised $88 million at a $1 billion valuation; and Humans&, an AI startup that announced a massive $480 million seed round in January at a $4.48 billion valuation, launched Persimmon to model human behavior.
The status quo for human behavior prediction today relies heavily on large language models (LLMs) that are prompted or fine-tuned to role-play as a target demographic. But two-year-old, San Francisco-based Mirror Particle thinks that approach is fundamentally broken.
“It’s like bringing a super soaker to Niagara Falls,” says Abhivyakti Ahuja, co-founder and CEO of Mirror Particle, which provides brands with an AI engine that predicts consumer behavior and the reasons behind it. “LLMs have been trained on hundreds of billions of data points. How much can you influence its behavior by [fine-tuning] with such a small amount of data? It’s still stuck in the past.”
Ahuja doesn’t think LLMs see the world the way a human does. “LLMs are modeling written language, but humans are made of visual perception, spatial reasoning, social intelligence.” Relying on them, she says, means getting insights based on what humans don’t notice, which is beside the point when trying to predict human behavior.
Mirror Particle is taking another approach: building a foundation model, or as Ahuja describes it, a world model built from scratch that simulates why humans do what they do and how human behavior changes over time.
“We don’t want to capture the static person,” Ahuja said. “We want to capture the changing person. That means capturing the longitudinal data on how people are changing, what triggers are changing them and to what degree.” If they aren’t changing, she added, “that’s also a signal.”
Mirror Particle has already raised an angel round and says it’s close to closing its first venture round. The company is also competing next week in Startup Battlefield 200, TechCrunch’s renowned startup competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on October 13-15.
The startup relies on a proprietary combination of data that includes its clients’ customer data, current events, pop culture, social media, and more to model a demographic segment, thinking of it as a system that evolves over time and tracking how motivations shift as it moves through experiences. Much of the focus is on “revealed behavior” — what people actually do rather than self-reported survey answers.
Like its rivals, Mirror Particle’s initial go-to-market strategy focuses on where budgets already exist for these kinds of insights: market research and brand and product strategy. Mirror might, for instance, help a beauty brand not just write better ad copy for makeup that would appeal to Gen Z, but also determine if that demographic even wants that product.
“What if [the target demographic] doesn’t want eyeshadow palettes?” Ahuja said. “Maybe blush is a better option to go for if you want to sell a product to this market.”
Mirror Particle’s prediction engine also provides customers with the “why” behind current or future behavior — the motivations, constraints, and additional context that justify its recommendation, helping brands make smarter decisions.
In one early pilot, a well-known pet food brand wanted to know what imagery to put on the packaging to boost sales. Chicken? Beef? Vegetables? Mirror’s technology found that the brand was asking the wrong question. The imagery didn’t matter. The problem was that the brand was so recognizable that it was considered mass market and cheap, and sales would plateau until it addressed that perception issue.
“The way we see our model evolving is like how a baby learns about the world,” Ahuja said, noting that babies move from vision to language to body awareness to social intelligence.
That fundamental interest in modeling the human brain comes from Ahuja’s background studying neuroscience and computer science. Originally from India, she ended up studying at the University of Toronto, where she became inspired by AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton’s contributions to neural networks.
After school, Ahuja ended up at Amazon Robotics building robots that build other robots. That’s where she met her co-founders, Will Song and Thomson Yen. Song has spent a chunk of his career building sales personalization engines, and Yen focused on using deep learning to learn about how AI agents understand human behavior.
The startup’s long-term vision is to be the “general layer for anticipating human behavior” and moving from broader population-level analyses to individual-level insights.
“We just need a better model of humans if we’re going to work alongside AI and with each other,” Ahuja said.
Check out Mirror Particle and many other innovative startups that have been vetted by TechCrunch’s editorial team next week at Disrupt in downtown San Francisco. The winner of this year’s Startup Battlefield will be decided by our slate of VC judges on the afternoon of Thursday, October 15.

articles.title: Googlebook "Better Together" phone features don't work with Samsung at launch
articles.text:
Googlebooks are Google’s latest attempt to carve out a piece of the premium laptop market, and tight integration with Android phones is a key part of that effort. Now that Googlebooks are available, we’re learning of some frustrating limitations of that plan. For now, Googlebooks will only play nicely with your phone if you have a Pixel.
When Google announced the launch window for Googlebooks, it said the laptops were “engineered to work with your Android phone right out of the box.” But as with many things Google, the truth is more convoluted. We have since learned that you need Android 17 for any of the nifty integrations to work. With a compatible Android 17 phone, you can seamlessly stream apps to your laptop, access files on your phone, mirror notifications, and continue where you left off in certain apps when switching from phone to laptop.
You might think that the latest Samsung phones, which shipped with Android 17, would be ready for this experience. You’d be wrong, though. Some early Googlebook adopters have complained that phones like the Z Fold 8 won’t work with the laptops. While the devices appear to see each other, the phone doesn’t stay connected. Google representatives have since confirmed that these “Better Together” features are not currently supported on even the latest Samsung phones. An update that brings support to Samsung phones will roll out in “the coming weeks.”

articles.title: Generar imágenes en ChatGPT tendrá una nueva condición: aparecerán anuncios
articles.text:
OpenAI comenzó a desplegar un nuevo formato publicitario en ChatGPT que mostrará anuncios junto a las imágenes generadas por el chatbot. La compañía busca que las marcas puedan presentar productos y servicios relacionados con las solicitudes visuales de los usuarios, aunque asegura que estas piezas estarán claramente identificadas y separadas de las imágenes creadas por inteligencia artificial.
El nuevo formato comenzó a probarse con un grupo reducido de usuarios y anunciantes en Estados Unidos. Está dirigido exclusivamente a personas mayores de 18 años y forma parte de la expansión del sistema de publicidad que OpenAI comenzó a introducir dentro de las conversaciones de ChatGPT.
Los anuncios aparecerán junto a las imágenes generadas
Según OpenAI, los nuevos anuncios visuales estarán diseñados para complementar determinadas solicitudes realizadas en ChatGPT. La compañía plantea que puedan servir como inspiración, mostrar cómo funciona un producto o presentar la experiencia asociada a un servicio.
Por ejemplo, una persona que utilice ChatGPT para generar ideas para decorar una habitación podría encontrarse con publicidad relacionada con muebles u objetos para el hogar. Del mismo modo, una conversación sobre un viaje podría incluir anuncios de ropa, hoteles u otros servicios relacionados con el destino mencionado.
La publicidad no formará parte de la imagen generada por ChatGPT. Los anuncios aparecerán como elementos independientes y tendrán una identificación específica para que el usuario pueda distinguirlos del contenido creado por la inteligencia artificial.
Esta separación busca evitar que una persona interprete una recomendación comercial como una respuesta generada de manera independiente por el chatbot.
OpenAI asegura que los anuncios no modificarán las respuestas
La compañía también mantiene la misma separación que aplica al formato publicitario dentro de las conversaciones de texto. OpenAI sostiene que los anuncios no influyen en las respuestas que ofrece ChatGPT ni determinan el contenido que genera el modelo.
En los formatos de publicidad que ya se habían incorporado al servicio, los anuncios aparecen identificados como contenido patrocinado y separados visualmente de la respuesta principal. El nuevo sistema llevará esa misma lógica al contenido visual.
Esto significa que una imagen generada a partir de una solicitud continuará respondiendo a las instrucciones del usuario, mientras que el anuncio se mostrará como un elemento independiente asociado al contexto de la conversación.
Los anuncios tendrán restricciones para proteger a los usuarios
OpenAI también estableció límites sobre los contextos en los que podrá aparecer publicidad. Los anuncios visuales estarán disponibles únicamente para usuarios mayores de 18 años y contarán con filtros destinados a evitar su aparición en conversaciones consideradas sensibles.
La compañía señala que estas medidas buscan impedir que las marcas aparezcan en situaciones en las que una persona pueda encontrarse en una situación de vulnerabilidad emocional o frente a temas delicados.
Además de los sistemas automáticos, OpenAI utilizará supervisión humana y mecanismos de seguimiento para detectar posibles incumplimientos de sus políticas publicitarias.
Estados Unidos será el primer mercado
La prueba de los anuncios junto a imágenes comenzará en Estados Unidos con un grupo reducido de anunciantes. OpenAI prevé ampliar progresivamente el formato a otros mercados durante los próximos meses, incluido México.
La situación será diferente en España y otros países de la Unión Europea, donde la compañía deberá adaptar el funcionamiento de la publicidad a las normas locales de protección de datos y privacidad.
De este modo, la publicidad en ChatGPT continúa extendiéndose a nuevos espacios del servicio. Ahora, además de aparecer dentro de determinadas conversaciones, también podrá acompañar las imágenes que los usuarios soliciten generar mediante inteligencia artificial.

articles.title: Le dernier grand iPhone standard d'Apple baisse pour les Prime Day d'Amazon
articles.text:
L’iPhone 16 Plus est le dernier représentant des modèles Plus chez Apple. Apple a décliné ce format sur trois générations (iPhone 14 Plus, 15 Plus et 16 Plus), puis a retiré le 16 Plus de son catalogue en septembre 2026. On ne le trouve plus neuf que chez les revendeurs. Il profite actuellement d’une baisse de prix chez Amazon.
Si vous voulez un grand écran sans passer par un modèle Pro, la version 128 Go chute à 849 € au lieu de 969 € chez Amazon. Soit 120 € de moins que le dernier prix pratiqué par Apple, et 170 € de moins que l’iPhone 16 (6,1 pouces), vendu 1 019 € sur l’Apple Store depuis septembre.
Que vaut l’iPhone 16 Plus deux ans après sa sortie ?
À sa sortie, nous lui avions donné 9/10 dans notre test des iPhone 16 et iPhone 16 Plus. Avec cette génération, Apple avait rapproché ses iPhone standards des modèles Pro. Le 16 Plus a ainsi hérité de la puce A18, une vraie montée en gamme par rapport à la génération précédente. Il a aussi reçu le bouton Action, programmable pour lancer une application ou un raccourci, ainsi que le bouton Commande de l’appareil photo, une touche située sur la tranche qui permet de piloter l’appareil photo.
Côté photo, son double module associe un capteur principal de 48 mégapixels à un ultra grand-angle de 12 mégapixels, qui permet notamment de réaliser des clichés en macro. Le smartphone est également compatible avec Apple Intelligence et prend en charge le Wi-Fi 7.
L’écran OLED Super Retina XDR de 6,7 pouces est toutefois limité à 60 Hz. Cela signifie que l’image se rafraîchit 60 fois par seconde, soit deux fois moins qu’une dalle à 120 Hz. Le défilement d’une page ou d’un fil d’actualité paraît donc moins fluide, un défaut que nous regrettions déjà en 2024. Sur une surface aussi grande, cette différence se remarque d’autant plus.
À ce prix, l’iPhone 16 Plus est-il une bonne affaire ?
À 849 €, l’iPhone 16 Plus reste intéressant surtout parce qu’il est le dernier iPhone au format Plus. Apple a depuis remplacé ce modèle par l’iPhone Air (6,5 pouces, 1 329 € chez Apple) dans sa gamme, tandis que l’iPhone 17 standard coûte désormais 1 119 € chez Apple, après une hausse de 150 € en septembre. Cette année, Apple n’a présenté que les iPhone 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max et l’iPhone Duo pliant. L’iPhone 18 standard ne devrait arriver qu’au printemps 2027. Le 16 Plus conserve donc un positionnement assez unique : celui d’un grand iPhone de 6,7 pouces, sans basculer dans les tarifs des modèles Pro Max.
Ses deux ans d’ancienneté se voient surtout face à l’iPhone 17. L’écran du 16 Plus reste limité à 60 Hz, quand celui de l’iPhone 17 monte à 120 Hz. L’iPhone 17 démarre aussi à 256 Go de stockage, le double du modèle en promotion. La puce A18 reste toutefois parfaitement capable pour un usage quotidien et compatible avec Apple Intelligence. À 849 €, l’iPhone 16 Plus s’adresse à ceux qui veulent un grand écran chez Apple sans payer les 1 329 € de l’iPhone Air ou les 1 629 € de l’iPhone 18 Pro Max.
Quelles sont les dates des Jours Flash Prime ?
Les Jours Flash Prime 2026 se déroulent les mardi 6 et mercredi 7 octobre, avec un lancement à 00h01 le 6 octobre. L’événement dure donc deux jours. Certaines promotions sont proposées en avance, notamment depuis le 29 septembre sur une sélection d’appareils Amazon, dont les Echo, Fire TV Stick, Kindle, Ring et Blink.
C’est quoi les Jours Flash Prime ?
C’est le rendez-vous promotionnel d’automne d’Amazon. Le principe est le même que pour Prime Day : des réductions réservées aux abonnés Prime sur des milliers de produits, mais concentrées ici sur 48 heures. La high-tech n’est pas la seule concernée : les offres couvrent aussi l’électroménager, la maison, les jouets, la mode ou encore les produits du quotidien.
Qui peut participer aux Jours Flash Prime ?
Les offres de l’événement sont réservées aux membres Amazon Prime : un simple compte Amazon ne suffit pas. Il faut disposer de l’abonnement Prime, facturé 6,99 €/mois ou 69,90 €/an.
L’abonnement comprend aussi la livraison rapide gratuite sur les articles éligibles, l’accès aux films et séries inclus dans Prime Video, à Amazon Music Prime et au stockage illimité de photos avec Amazon Photos
Les comptes éligibles peuvent bénéficier d’un essai gratuit de 30 jours, qui permet également de profiter des promotions. Attention toutefois : à la fin de l’essai, l’abonnement devient automatiquement payant. Pensez à annuler son renouvellement avant cette échéance si vous ne souhaitez pas le conserver.
Qui peut participer aux Jours Flash Prime ?
Les offres sont exclusives aux membres Amazon Prime. Un simple compte Amazon ne suffit pas. Il faut souscrire à l’abonnement Prime (6,99 €/mois ou 69,90 €/an).
Celui-ci ne sert pas seulement à profiter des ventes flash, il donne aussi droit à la livraison rapide gratuite, au catalogue de films et séries de Prime Video, à Prime Music et au stockage de photos dans le cloud.
Pour ceux qui ne veulent pas s’engager tout de suite, il existe une période d’essai gratuite de 30 jours qui permet d’accéder aux promotions sans frais immédiats.

articles.title: Cloudflare Introduces CLI for AI Agents, Sunsetting Wrangler
articles.text:
Cloudflare recently launched the open beta of cf, a new open-source, agent-focused command-line interface for interacting with Cloudflare services through a unified CLI. Written in TypeScript, it provides structured output and command discovery to make Cloudflare’s APIs easier for both developers and AI agents.
The hyperscaler argues that introducing a new CLI avoids conflicts with LLMs’ learned behavior around Wrangler, allowing cf to adopt agent-focused design changes without the compatibility constraints of an established tool. Matt Taylor, senior product manager at Cloudflare, and Samuel Macleod, senior systems engineer at Cloudflare, explain why a new CLI was needed:
Wrangler was hand-built with each product team contributing and taking their own approach to their command developer experience. Enforcing patterns across teams was virtually impossible, even across our ~280 command paths. We had inconsistent terminology across d1 info, hyperdrive get, workflows describe as each team came up with their own practices at different times.
Released under either the Apache License 2.0 or MIT license, the cf CLI is designed for agent-driven development, with command discovery, JSON output optimized for both humans and agents, and a new TypeScript-based cloudflare.config.ts configuration format. It also makes Vite the default development environment, providing a consistent local development experience and plugin support.
Using Cloudflare’s OpenAPI schemas as the source, cf can cover more than 3000 API operations, compared with roughly 280 functions built into Wrangler. Taylor and Macleod add:
We wanted to both standardize what we had and make a massive expansion, all at once. Forge — Cloudflare’s new unified API generation pipeline — enabled us to do this, building on the idea of generating our CLI commands directly from the API schema that powers our API documentation and SDK generation.
In a popular Hacker News thread, community reaction has focused in particular on the choice of TypeScript for a CLI, with discussion around startup time, portability, and dependency management. User slowin comments:
I don't understand why this is written in TypeScript. This is a great example of how agents can write code (I'm sure they wrote `cf`), yet having fundamental computer science knowledge is still critical. Do not force your users to manage the dependencies of your CLI. Do write your CLI in a compiled language.
Cloudflare argues instead that TypeScript makes configuration easier for both humans and agents by providing type safety and LSP support, enabling agents to understand and modify configurations more accurately. The authors contrast this with TOML and JSONC, where schema information is less accessible to agents, and say programmatic configuration can also reduce configuration duplication. Ashish Ganda notes on LinkedIn:
Cloudflare's new cf CLI outputs JSON by default. Not a table. You have to ask for the table (...) Tables are for eyes. JSON is for parsers.
Cloudflare makes JSON the default output format, allowing agents to filter and transform the output into the format required by human users while avoiding the table output used by default in Wrangler. The company plans to deprecate Wrangler after the cf open beta ends, release a final major Wrangler version directing users to cf, and provide 18 months of maintenance support to allow migration.

articles.title: Exjefe de PlayStation Studios, contra la muerte de los juegos en disco: “Si no eres dueño del juego, ¿qué estás comprando?”
articles.text:
Pasan los meses, pero la decisión de Sony de matar los juegos de PlayStation en disco sigue dando que hablar. Si bien la medida comenzará a regir a partir de 2028, se espera que sus efectos empiecen a verse mucho antes de la fecha límite y que sus consecuencias forjen la estrategia hacia futuras generaciones de la consola. Y si bien se han alzado voces en contra de la decisión, han sido mayormente del público. Pero también hay exejecutivos de la compañía que no están de acuerdo con el camino que se ha elegido.
Tal es el caso de Shawn Layden, exjefe de lo que hoy se conoce como PlayStation Studios. En una reciente entrevista (vía VGC), el ejecutivo no ocultó su disconformidad con el plan de la plataforma de avanzar con un futuro totalmente digital. Incluso lo consideró como una medida de gran riesgo y que trae consigo un fuerte impacto negativo sobre la marca y su reputación.
Según Layden, nadie pone en tela de juicio la practicidad de las descargas digitales desde la PlayStation Store por sobre los juegos en disco. Pero sí enfatizó en que el porcentaje que todavía se inclina por el formato físico suele ser el que representa al fanático más acérrimo de la plataforma.
"A los gamers nos gustan las descargas digitales. La gente dice: «Ah, descargar un juego es más fácil que ir a la tienda». No. Descargar un juego es más fácil que cruzar la sala para meter un disco en la consola. Ni siquiera tengo que hacer eso. Simplemente pulso un botón en el mando y no tengo que moverme. Y esa comodidad es indiscutible", explicó el exlíder de PlayStation Studios; y agregó: "Creo que, especialmente en el mundo de los videojuegos, tal vez el 80 % de la gente descarga los juegos y el 20 % no [...]. Pero ese 20 % es sumamente importante. Se trata en gran medida de los más fieles entre los fieles. A menudo son quienes compran dos copias de cada juego. Una es la que nunca sacan del empaque, y la otra es la que usan para jugar".
Shawn Layden no está de acuerdo con matar los juegos de PlayStation en formato físico
Layden no desconoce que la decisión de eliminar los juegos de PlayStation en disco seguramente se tomó tras analizar una gran cantidad de datos y estadísticas, pero sí esgrime que la medida atenta contra el sentido de la propiedad. Esto último es lo que alimenta la principal queja de los jugadores; después de todo, si toda tu biblioteca de juegos pasa a ser 100 % digital, quedas a merced de que los servidores sigan funcionan ad eternum para acceder a ella. Y hoy por hoy no hay nada que garantice que eso será así por siempre.
"Creo que probablemente el aspecto más insidioso de esto es que cambia la conversación a: ¿Eres dueño de un juego o tienes acceso a un activo digital? Si no puedes vender algo, significa que no eres dueño de ello. Y si no eres el propietario [del juego], ¿qué estás comprando? Si lo que compras es acceso, la verdad es que no suena tan atractivo. Además, la gente tiende a imaginar el peor de los escenarios posibles. [...] Como ya he dicho, desconozco los detalles financieros, pero el impacto en la imagen de marca es considerable, así que espero que para ellos haya tenido sentido", reflexionó.
Desde que PlayStation anunció la muerte de los juegos en disco a partir de 2028, los fanáticos se han expresado con vehemencia. Las quejas han llegado a los oídos de Sony, que ha reconocido la validez de ese enojo. No obstante, la compañía ya ha dejado en claro que no piensa recular. Así las cosas, el futuro del catálogo de PlayStation será completamente digital, por lo que ya se especula con que la PS6 llegará sin lectora de discos.

articles.title: Furientis lands $25M from Benchmark to mass-produce low-cost missile interceptors | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Until recently, venture capitalists largely steered clear of defense startups. Investments in the sector were viewed as morally controversial, and the process of securing government contracts was too lengthy and uncertain to justify venture funding.
But that sentiment changed rapidly after conflicts in Ukraine and Iran began to deplete the U.S. military’s missile supply. Startups that prove they can build equipment fast and affordably now stand a real chance of landing a Pentagon contract on an expedited timeline.
Four years into the defense tech boom that arguably began when Russia invaded Ukraine, the storied Silicon Valley venture firm Benchmark is placing its first bet on a pure defense startup.
Benchmark is leading a $25 million seed round into Furientis, a startup on a mission to mass-produce interceptor missiles. Just one year old, the company—whose name means “of fury” in Latin—has already secured a funded Pentagon contract to build mid-range interceptors. The startup was valued at $125 million, according to a person familiar with the company.
Furientis’ seed round follows a $5 million pre-seed that was announced in May.
“What they accomplished with just a pre-seed round was nothing short of remarkable,” Benchmark general partner Chetan Puttagunta, told TechCrunch. “They manufactured prototypes with just $5 million. They had they had already successfully done [a dozen] launches by the time we invested.”
That efficiency is in stark contrast to the slow-moving, high-cost development models used by traditional defense primes. The startup’s velocity is driven by its co-founders, who bring years of aerospace and defense engineering experience. Brody Franzen served as deputy chief engineer at Virgin Galactic before joining Castelion, a hypersonic missile startup valued at $13 billion, while Aris Simsarian previously led rocket engine testing at Virgin Orbit.
The duo launched Furientis after realizing the U.S. military is facing a severe shortage of “exquisite” missiles, which can cost around $3 million each, to counter inexpensive adversary threats, Franzen told TechCrunch.
According to Franzen, the U.S. Navy receives a mere 300 to 500 interceptor missiles annually, compared to China, which claims a production rate of 3,000 anti-ship cruise missiles a month.
“We’re being outproduced by a factor of 100 plus,” he said. “That is why we started the company.”
Furientis is not aiming to match the performance of best-in-class missile interceptors; instead, it is designing and manufacturing its systems so they can be assembled quickly from readily available components. As a result, each unit costs a fraction of legacy interceptors, a compelling value proposition for a Pentagon desperate to scale inventory within strict budget limits.
Unlike traditional defense primes such as Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, which are bogged down by long design cycles, Furientis has been testing its missiles in the field on a bi-weekly basis. The startup’s ultimate goal is to manufacture 1,000 systems a year in each factory. But for now, the young company is working out of its facility in Los Angeles, and taking its prototypes for trial launches to White Sands, New Mexico.
Given the need, Furientis is not the only company working on helping the government restock its stockpiles. Franzen said that larger defense startups like Anduril, Castelion, and Shield AI are also racing to build mass-produced interceptors, while traditional primes scramble to modernize their own manufacturing cycles.
Benchmark’s Puttagunta is not fazed by the seemingly crowded space. “I think there’s opportunity for lots more companies in this sector,” he said.

articles.title: Why is NASA bringing 7,500 contractors back to work as civil servants?
articles.text:
As a flight director during NASA’s Apollo missions, Gerry Griffin led several lunar landings. He helped bring the crew of Apollo 13 safely back to Earth. Later, he directed Johnson Space Center in Houston.
Through these experiences, Griffin learned the value of teamwork in spaceflight—during the dynamic moments that can make or break a successful launch or landing, you absolutely have to trust your colleagues in the trenches.
“When lightning struck the rocket during Apollo 12, we had to react in a hurry,” Griffin said in an interview. “With people like John Aaron and Jerry Carr, the trust and communications came through. It made the difference.”
This really happened in 1969. Griffin’s “Gold Team” in Mission Control led the launch of the Apollo 12 mission, when the ascending Saturn V rocket triggered lightning as it soared through electrically charged clouds. The lightning strike disrupted the Apollo spacecraft’s electrical systems, which flight controllers and astronaut Alan Bean scrambled to reset. The rocket and spacecraft survived, going on to complete the second lunar landing.
During the Apollo era, Griffin said, contractors were brought in to supplement NASA’s workforce. But the positions in Mission Control remained NASA employees, and that was important because the space agency ultimately had responsibility—success or failure—for what happened during its missions.
After he left NASA, that began to change. “Midway through the space shuttle era, I was surprised to find that a lot of the jobs in Mission Control had gone to contractors,” he said.
Griffin doesn’t want to denigrate contractors. They play a critical role in extending the agency’s expertise for subsystems built for the space agency. But over time, often as a way to increase headcount at the space agency without raising the NASA civil service count, critical jobs were outsourced to contractors.
This year, in a move that has largely gone under the radar, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman sought to reverse this trend. As part of his “workforce initiative,” Isaacman is bringing 7,500 contract positions back into the agency, making them civil servants to rebuild what he calls “core competencies.”
This is a massive shift in how NASA does business, and it’s not without controversy. But Griffin said he welcomes the change and believes it will be better for the agency in the long run. “I applaud Jared’s idea to get back to that kind of in-house capability and responsibility,” he said.
Not without controversy
Not everyone is a fan of Isaacman’s workforce initiative, which they believe has been rolled out too hastily and has been disruptive at the space agency. But because it is largely a fait accompli, almost no one has wanted to speak on record opposing it.
For this article, Ars spoke to half a dozen people on background, including contractors who are now civil servants, industry leaders, and senior NASA officials to understand their concerns about Isaacman’s initiative.
The largest and most directly affected contractors are Amentum, Jacobs Engineering Group, and KBR. Each firm provided a few thousand contractors to NASA for engineering and other services at field centers across the country. These companies say that radically departing from a workforce model that has allowed NASA to be successful for decades introduces uncertainty at a time when the agency is embarking on its most ambitious mission in decades, returning to the Moon and building a base there.
Isaacman has said NASA will benefit not only from rebuilding NASA’s technical workforce but also from saving money. In staff memos, Isaacman has said that early pilots of the workforce initiative had already identified more than $100 million in savings from making employees civil servants and that over time, this could grow to more than $1 billion.
“There are, of course, cost savings from this effort,” Isaacman wrote in May. “There are also operational benefits, as contractor structures often include layered management, third-party tools, contractual barriers, and other inefficiencies that can challenge progress.”
The contracting firms dispute this, saying the overhead they charge is only about 2 or 3 percent of an employee’s compensation.
Prior to this initiative, NASA had about 40,000 contractors and about 14,000 civil servants. The latter number had shrunk by about 4,000 from early 2025, when thousands of employees left through deferred resignation and other programs run by DOGE to slim down the federal workforce.
But this is not really an effort to bring back people who were indiscriminately cut by DOGE. Isaacman’s changes are focused on increasing NASA’s technical acumen, and NASA has a considerably larger civil servant workforce today than before the outset of the second Trump administration—about 21,000 people.
“I thought we were draining the swamp, not growing the number of civil servants,” one industry source said.
This criticism aside, it reflects Isaacman’s political skill that he was able to increase the federal workforce at a time when the White House has been pushing for reductions. Rather than the cutting or even gutting experienced by some federal agencies, Isaacman seems intent on building NASA to be successful.
Is NASA losing some flexibility?
To implement the workforce conversion, NASA’s 10 field center directors were tasked with identifying contract employees—particularly those tied to launch, operations, and mission-critical engineering capabilities—to bring on board.
For some employees, this has been a disruptive process. Most, but not all, have been able to remain at their current location. And to be clear, many employees prefer to be civil servants. But there are some differences in pay and benefits, and contractors are basically told they must give up their existing job for a position at NASA—they cannot keep working for their contract firm. This has created churn and uncertainty, some former contract employees-turned civil servants say. And not all of them want to be government employees under the Trump administration.
Beyond the frustrations of some individual employees, a broader concern among industry groups opposing the transition is that the current contracting system gives NASA flexibility. Under the previous contractor setup, if the agency decided to change directions, it could simply not renew a contract with a contractor. Civil servants have considerably more protections once hired by the government.
“NASA over the last 50 years has built an incredible ecosystem that is specialized to serve NASA and other federal agencies,” an industry source said. “The system allows for flexibility and innovation by the companies. Now, that’s going to go away.”
This contractor ecosystem also supports NASA and its efforts in Congress through lobbying. Some industry officials believe that if this contractor support goes away, NASA’s efforts to secure Congressional funding may be more difficult, and some of its programs will become more vulnerable.
Isaacman and his leadership team have dismissed these concerns. They say they’re focused on the mission and that the current process is not working for the space agency.
A “coherent and necessary vision”
For example, one member of Isaacman’s team who worked on the Artemis II launch described confusion in the firing control room at Kennedy Space Center.
When there was an issue on the launch pad with the rocket’s ground systems, the NASA controllers working the problem did not have direct access to the schematics. These were bound up by intellectual property and other contractor rules. The information, therefore, had to be conveyed to the flight controllers via screen sharing during a Microsoft Teams call rather than NASA being able to call up the schematics directly in the launch center.
“You would be sitting there with some tool that’s livestreaming someone else’s display, trying to see a schematic,” this engineer said. “How effing absurd is that?” The goal of the workforce conversion is to ensure that the core functions in critical facilities at NASA are filled by civil servants to remove some of these barriers.
Critics of the workforce initiative have used various lines of attack this year, including suggesting that its disruptive effects would impair NASA’s chance to return to the Moon, delay Artemis III, or increase safety risk. However, during a meeting at the end of August, NASA’s independent Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel—which is expressly tasked with identifying safety risks at the space agency—lauded the effort.
The panel’s chair, Lieutenant General Susan J. Helms, said the workforce initiative had achieved “substantial progress” during its rollout. She noted that the process faced some challenges due to its “speed and scope” and acknowledged that organizational change can be unsettling. But she added that the panel has not identified any critical concerns.
Moreover, the safety panel, which is often critical of NASA, offered a warm endorsement of Isaacman’s workforce conversion efforts. “From the panel’s perspective,” she said, “the administrator’s directive is a coherent and necessary vision for the future of NASA’s workforce.”
Eric Berger is the senior space editor at Ars Technica, covering everything from astronomy to private space to NASA policy, and author of two books: Liftoff, about the rise of SpaceX; and Reentry, on the development of the Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon. A certified meteorologist, Eric lives in Houston.

articles.title: SpaceX Crew Dragon, traversée à 1 600 °C et records : Sophie Adenot s'apprête à rentrer sur Terre
articles.text:
L’heure est aux adieux à bord de la Station spatiale internationale (ISS). D’ici quelques heures, Sophie Adenot s’installera confortablement à bord de la capsule Crew Dragon de SpaceX, dans sa combinaison spatiale. Puis, la Française et ses trois coéquipiers de la mission Crew-12 se détacheront du laboratoire. Direction : la Terre.
L’Agence spatiale européenne (ESA) a publié le programme de son retour ce mardi 6 octobre. La capsule doit se détacher de l’ISS ce mercredi 7 octobre vers 14h05 (heure de Paris), puis amerrir au large de la Californie ce jeudi 8 octobre à 17h34. Ainsi s’achèvera la mission de huit mois de l’astronaute tricolore.
Des records puis une rentrée à 1 600 °C
Sophie Adenot avait décollé le 13 février 2026 dans le cadre d’εpsilon, nom du volet européen de sa mission spatiale. Le 3 septembre, elle atteignait les 200 jours de suite à bord de l’ISS. Elle détient désormais le record européen du plus long vol spatial, devant Luca Parmitano et Thomas Pesquet. Quand elle amerrira, elle en comptera environ 237.
Entre-temps, elle est devenue la première Française à sortir dans l’espace, et la deuxième Européenne après l’Italienne Samantha Cristoforetti en 2022. Elle l’a fait trois fois en 14 jours, pour un total de 19h42 de travail hors de la station. Le 1er septembre, elle a dirigé une sortie avec l’Américaine Jessica Meir, un binôme entièrement féminin : seules six des 284 sorties menées depuis l’ISS l’ont été par deux femmes.
On savait, peu avant son départ pour l’orbite terrestre, que Sophie Adenot allait battre des records aussi bien en France qu’en Europe.
Pendant la descente dans l’atmosphère, le bouclier thermique protégeant la capsule sera mis à rude épreuve, car il encaissera des températures jusqu’à 1 600 °C. Cette chaleur proviendra du plasma, un gaz qui se forme devant la capsule à très haute température. Une fois récupérée en mer, la Française prendra l’avion pour Cologne, en Allemagne. Le but : se réadapter à la gravité terrestre dans le Centre des astronautes européens de l’ESA.

articles.title: FBI Blames Contractor’s Missed Patch for ShinyHunters Breach
articles.text:
The FBI has removed an Accenture contractor over a data breach that exposed personal information of thousands of bureau employees, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing two people familiar with the matter.
The FBI has not publicly named the contractor or the organization involved. However, a senior bureau official told Reuters that its review so far points to a security patch that had not been applied by the contractor responsible for the affected system.
“To date, our review has determined that the incident occurred as the result of a security failure of a platform managed by a third-party organization — after a contractor failed to implement a security patch explicitly issued to secure the platform,” FBI cyber chief Brett Leatherman said in a statement.
“As such, the FBI has removed the contractor and taken all necessary steps to both mitigate any further risk and protect our workforce,” Leatherman added.
According to Reuters’ sources, the system in question is Oracle’s PeopleSoft human resources platform, and the outside organization is Accenture.
ShinyHunters had previously claimed it exploited PeopleSoft to break into the FBI’s job site, and Google recently warned that the threat actor had been targeting vulnerable PeopleSoft instances to steal data.
Accenture did not answer questions about the contractor or the alleged patching failure. Instead, the company said in a statement that it was “proud to support the mission of the FBI and will continue to do so.”
The ShinyHunters cybercrime group announced on September 22 that it had hacked FBI systems. It targeted the agency’s jobs website and allegedly obtained information on all employees, including sensitive information, some of which it leaked to the media.
The attack allegedly aimed to pressure the FBI to correct or remove a report the agency published in May to warn organizations about ShinyHunters attacks. The hackers claimed the report made false allegations.
Shortly after ShinyHunters announced the breach, law enforcement said it had arrested an alleged leader of the group in the Netherlands on September 15. ShinyHunters seemed defiant and urged victims to continue negotiating, threatening to leak their data unless they paid up.
The arrest of another alleged ShinyHunters leader, Saif al-Din Khader (aka Rey), came to light on October 3. Rey was reportedly arrested in Jordan and has been cooperating with authorities.
At the time of writing, ShinyHunters’ website is still live, but a post urging organizations to pay up has been removed. The most recent victim post is dated September 22.

articles.title: Google officialise Nano Banana 2.1 : meilleures images et édition plus facile — Frandroid
articles.text:
Google confirme enfin un modèle que les curieux avaient déjà vu passer deux fois. Ce mardi 6 octobre, le compte X de Google AI Studio a présenté Nano Banana 2.1, la nouvelle version du modèle de génération d’images de la firme de Mountain View. Il prend la suite de Nano Banana 2, lancé le 26 février.
Google promet des progrès sur quatre points :
- un meilleur rendu visuel ;
- des images plus naturelles ;
- une meilleure cohérence des sujets (le même personnage reste reconnaissable d’une image à l’autre) ;
- la retouche par masque.
La retouche par masque permet de ne modifier qu’une zone précise de l’image, sans toucher au reste de la scène. Google affirme que son modèle fait mieux que les précédents sur tous les points, mais son message ne donne ni chiffre ni comparaison.
Google Cloud a aussi publié ce mardi la fiche technique de Nano Banana 2.1, disponible en version finale sur Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, son offre destinée aux entreprises. On y apprend que Nano Banana 2.1 génère des images en 1K, 2K ou 4K, accepte jusqu’à 14 images de référence dans une même requête et peut aussi partir d’une vidéo. La fiche ne donne en revanche aucun benchmark et se contente de renvoyer vers la grille tarifaire générale de Google Cloud.
Deux fuites avant l’annonce
Le 27 septembre, TestingCatalog, un site qui fouille le code des applications pour repérer les nouveautés à venir, avait trouvé le nom dans Google Flow, l’outil de création vidéo de Google. Il y remplaçait un « Nano Banana 2.5 Flash » repéré quelques jours plus tôt, un nom qui laissait espérer une évolution plus marquée.
Ce lundi 5 octobre, Nano Banana 2.1 est même apparu un court moment dans la liste des modèles de Flow, avant d’être retiré. TestingCatalog notait alors que ses images ressemblaient beaucoup à celles de Nano Banana Pro, sans pouvoir dire si un nouveau modèle se cachait vraiment derrière. Jusqu’à ce mardi matin, Google ne proposait officiellement que Nano Banana 2, 2 Lite et Pro.
Google met surtout en avant Nano Banana 2.1 dans Google AI Studio, sa plateforme destinée aux développeurs. Toutefois, sur le compte X officiel de Nano Banana, on peut lire : « Découvrez Nano Banana 2.1, notre tout dernier modèle de génération et de retouche d’images ! Testez-le dans l’application Gemini ». En dehors de cette bio, aucun message ni communiqué de Google ne précise la disponibilité dans Gemini.

articles.title: Marvel y Webtoon estrenarán app con 35.000 cómics: tendrá historias de Star Wars y funcionará con suscripción
articles.text:
Webtoon y Marvel anunciaron el lanzamiento de una nueva aplicación de cómics digitales, Marvel Comics, que estará disponible desde el 16 de noviembre de 2026. La plataforma reunirá historietas actuales y clásicas de Marvel, Star Wars y 20th Century Studios, con una suscripción que permitirá acceder a un catálogo en expansión.
La nueva app, desarrollada por Webtoon Entertainment para dispositivos móviles y web, ofrecerá más de 35.000 cómics digitales. Incorporará herramientas de recomendación personalizadas, listas de seguimiento y la posibilidad de leer lanzamientos recientes desde 30 días después de su publicación impresa, según el plan elegido.
David Abdo, director general de Marvel Comics y Franchise, señaló que la alianza busca atender a los lectores que prefieren consumir cómics en formato digital. La compañía apostó por Webtoon para construir una plataforma que acompañe nuevas formas de descubrir historias y seguir series en curso.
“Nos entusiasma colaborar con Webtoon, líderes del sector, para crear una nueva aplicación que pueda seguir creciendo y evolucionando al ritmo de cómo los lectores descubren y disfrutan de los cómics”, dijo Abdo.
Cómo será la nueva app
La aplicación combinará el formato tradicional de páginas con la lectura vertical, habitual en los webcómics.
Los usuarios podrán recorrer miles de portadas mediante una interfaz de desplazamiento, consultar páginas dedicadas a personajes y creadores, y recibir sugerencias de acuerdo con su historial de lectura e intereses.
La función Pull List permitirá seguir series, personajes y autores para identificar nuevos números apenas estén disponibles.
Además, la sección Upcoming Releases mostrará los próximos lanzamientos y ofrecerá la posibilidad de incorporarlos a esa lista antes de su salida. La plataforma también actualizará sus paneles inteligentes para mejorar la lectura en pantalla.
Marvel Comics tendrá dos niveles de suscripción. El plan Base costará USD 9,99 al mes o USD 69,99 al año e incluirá el catálogo completo, con nuevos números disponibles tres meses después de su lanzamiento impreso.
El plan Ultimate costará USD 12,49 mensuales o USD 99,99 anuales y habilitará el acceso a las novedades 30 días después de su publicación física.
Los lectores podrán registrarse de manera anticipada y obtener un precio de USD 59,99 para el primer año del plan Ultimate anual.
La aplicación permitirá importar la biblioteca, el historial de lectura, los cómics canjeados y los números guardados en Marvel Unlimited, servicio que dejará de incorporar contenido nuevo el 7 de diciembre de 2026 y será retirado el 28 de diciembre.
Marvel confirmó que usó IA generativa en la producción de la última película de Spider-Man
Marvel Studios confirmó que utilizó inteligencia artificial generativa durante las primeras etapas de producción de Spider-Man: Brand New Day, para crear algunos bocetos y artes conceptuales.
La información figura en el libro de arte oficial de la película, al que tuvo acceso The Direct.
Los materiales corresponden a una fase inicial de exploración visual y no prueban que la tecnología haya generado escenas completas ni reemplazado a los artistas de la producción final.
Esas imágenes se emplean para definir posibles diseños, escenarios, personajes y situaciones antes de avanzar a otras etapas. Algunas presentan errores de proporción, composición y otros rasgos asociados con contenidos producidos mediante IA.
El caso reabrió el debate sobre el uso de estas herramientas en Hollywood, especialmente por su impacto en los artistas conceptuales, los derechos de autor y el entrenamiento de los modelos.
Aunque los estudios pueden generar numerosas propuestas visuales en poco tiempo, actores y guionistas ya reclamaron límites y garantías frente al uso de inteligencia artificial.
Marvel no es el único estudio relacionado con superhéroes que habría recurrido a estas herramientas: materiales de Supergirl también revelaron su empleo para elaborar conceptos sobre Lobo. Por ahora, el caso de Marvel muestra el ingreso de IA generativa.

articles.title: Egyptian fintech unicorn MNT-Halan secures $76.5m securitisation deals - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Egyptian fintech unicorn MNT-Halan has successfully completed three securitisation issuances with a combined value exceeding EGP4 billion (US$76.5 million) for its two subsidiaries, Halan Consumer Finance and Tasaheel for Finance.
Founded in 2018, MNT-Halan was created to digitally bank the unbanked and substitute cash with electronic solutions. The MNT-Halan digital ecosystem includes small and micro business lending, payments, consumer finance, and e-commerce.
Since inception, MNT-Halan has disbursed over US$15.5 billion in loans and served more than 8 million customers globally. Serving over 2.3 million active customers quarterly globally across its ecosystem, MNT-Halan’s app alone has reached 10 million downloads.
In the meantime, the company has also become a unicorn, raising several significant funding rounds, including a EGP3.4 billion (US$71.4 million) securitised bond issuance in October of last year and some undisclosed equity funding in June, in a deal that values the company at US$1.4 billion.
The latest transactions include an issuance of EGP528.5 million (US$10.1 million) for Halan Consumer Finance, and two issuances for Tasaheel for Finance, valued at EGP1.2 billion (US$23 million) and EGP2.28 billion (US$43.6 million). These issuances further strengthen MNT-Halan’s access to diversified funding sources and support the continued expansion of its financing activities across Egypt.

articles.title: I tested the OM System PEN for weeks and it’s the best value retro camera right now — here’s why
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The much-adored Olympus PEN series is back with a new name, and the OM System PEN is a refreshingly affordable and feature-packed mirrorless camera — cramming a 20.4MP sensor with image stabilization and rangefinder-style EVF into a compact, IPX1-rated retro body. There are no major upgrades here, but nonetheless OM System has made the best beginner camera of the year so far.
Reasons to buy
- + Excellent value
- + In-body image stabilization and neat computational photography modes
- + Classy design
- + Splash-proof, as is the new kit lens
Reasons to avoid
- - Basic video features
- - Some controls are fiddly
- - Design less suitable for long lenses
- - Lower rated weather resistance than the OM-5 II
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
OM System PEN: Two-minute review
Given the ongoing component shortages and price pressures, producing an affordable camera in 2026 is no mean feat — and that's exactly what OM System has achieved with the new PEN.
It has delivered the rangefinder-style mirrorless camera many PEN fans have been crying out for, and equipped it with in-body image stabilization, twin displays, a retro weather-proof design (IPX1-rated), and a range of fun computational photography modes — and kept the price to $1,000 / £850 / $AU1,800. Need a lens? The 14-42mm f/3.5-5.6 III kit (see below) is just $100 / £100 / AU$300 extra.
Beyond that kit lens, the OM PEN is part of the Micro Four Thirds system, with hundreds of lenses to choose, covering just about any situation, though any of these will add to the cost. I found it to be a great pairing with the low-cost Olympus 45mm f/1.8 for portraiture.
There's little that's new here, mind you — we have the same 20.4MP CMOS sensor with 5-axis image stabilization as previous models, including the OM System OM-5 II, and the same 121-point hybrid phase-detection autofocus, with stripped back subject-detection options. The vari-angle touchscreen and 2.36m-dot EVF are borrowed from previous models, too.
However, the OM PEN remains utterly compelling because it's so much fun to shoot the everyday with, so easy on the eye, and kind on the wallet. Sure, the PEN could be better in various areas (some of the controls are particularly fiddly), but all is forgiven when you consider the overall package, and that price tag.
Having used the camera for several weeks (and made direct comparisons with the excellent Lumix 10 premium compact), I think the OM System PEN as an ideal starter camera for smartphone upgraders — and it's the best beginner camera for 2026 so far.
OM System PEN review: Price and release date

- Costs $999.99 / £849 / AU$1,499 (body-only) or $1,099 / £949 / AU$1,799 with new 14-42mm f/3.5-5.6 III kit lens
- Available in two colorways: all black, and black with silver trim
After years of rumors, OM System finally put its name on a successor for the Olympus PEN series of cameras. And like the OM-5 II before it, the OM System PEN is excellent value for money in an industry otherwise feeling the effects of component shortages and price hikes — where else can you find a new interchangeable-lens camera with a viewfinder and in-body image stabilization for less $1,000?

The third-generation kit lens was announced alongside the camera, and gains a splash-proof design, matching the OM PEN camera.
The camera is available for preorder now in two colorways: black, and black with silver trim.

There's no shortage of OM System bodies, but the PEN is the first OM-branded rangefinder proper, with its 2.36m-dot EVF neatly tucked into the top-left corner of the compact, IPX1-rated retro body.
It's the same EVF that you'll find in the slightly pricier OM-5 Mark II — a camera that we awarded a 5-star rating, and which sits in top spot in TechRadar's best travel cameras guide.
The key difference between those two bodies is that the OM-5 Mark II has higher-rated weatherproofing, a pronounced viewfinder bump, and a larger grip — meaning it's better suited to inclement weather, outdoor photography, and use with larger lenses. Why not require just a press of the CP button to open the menu?

If you have moderately large hands like I do, the whole layout might feel a little fiddly. Computational photography modes can close the gap where there are drawbacks; addressing the fewer pixels and lesser dynamic range versus larger-sensor alternatives, though they don't work for every scenario. (I've included some examples, above.)
With 5.5EV image stabilization, the High Res Shot mode can be used handheld to increase resolution from 20MP to 50MP, though it won't work for scenes with movement in them. There's nothing wrong with OM System's 121-point hybrid phase-detection autofocus system, despite its stripped-back selection of subject-detection options that includes humans or animals (cats and dogs).
I've used other systems with a wider range of subject-detection modes, but for the most part you'd struggle to see a major difference in performance — when tracking birds, for example, I found the animal-detection autofocus to be sticky. There's not the same degree of complexity for face and eye detection, though — it's reliable, but you can't manually switch which eye the camera autofocuses on.
Battery life is decent, being rated at 410 shots, but video specs are fairly basic for 2026 — 4K up to 30fps / C4K up to 24fps, with a wide choice of color profiles including OM System's flat OM-Log400 profile, but just 8-bit color depth. The slow and quick mode unleashes up to 120fps slow-motion recording, or down to 1fps quick motion, but in 1080p only. Image stabilization works for video, though, which is a major draw for a camera at this price point.

Should I buy the OM System PEN?
Buy it if...
You're a smartphone upgrader
The experience of using the PEN compared to a smartphone is both wildly different and somehow familiar — its retro design and viewfinder are highly appealing, while its modern features, such as computational photography, eke out the best image quality possible and encourage creativity, much as a good smartphone camera can. 
You want a highly enjoyable everyday/ travel camera
The PEN's compact and classy design features a decent EVF, vari-angle touchscreen and capable image stabilization, making it a highly versatile and enjoyable walkaround snapper.
Don't buy it if...
You're more into outdoors and action photography
Yes the PEN is capable in all photography genres, but its design is less suited to long lenses and inclement weather, for which the slightly pricier OM-5 II is a better bet (or even pricier OM-1 II). 
You're unlikely to buy more lenses
Micro Four Thirds cameras are blessed with a plentiful number of lenses. However, if you're only likely to buy the camera with the kit lens, you might find it doesn't scratch your photography itches — I would budget for a fast aperture prime.  
OM System PEN review: also consider
Panasonic Lumix L10
The Lumix L10's design is strikingly similar to the PEN, and it also uses a Micro Four Thirds sensor. Where the cameras differ is how the Lumix model is a compact camera with no stabilization and a built-in 24-75mm f/1.8-2.8 lens and it costs more, while the PEN has stabilization and a MFT lens mount. I've compared the two cameras directly to find out which is best.
Read our Panasonic Lumix L10 review
OM System OM-5 II
If you like the sound of the PEN's features but you'd prefer a tougher body, chunkier grip for comfortable use with a wider range of lenses, plus pronounced viewfinder design, the OM-5 II is the camera for you — and it doesn't cost too much more than the PEN. The Fujifilm X-T30 III is another option, and it costs the same as the PEN, coming with an 26MP APS-C sensor, but no image stabilization.
See our OM System OM-5 II review
How I tested the OM System PEN
- OM System loaned me the black and silver version of the PEN and the 14-42mm f/3.5-5.6 III kit lens for several weeks
- I also used it with Olympus 45mm f/1.8 / Leica 12-60mm f/2.8-4 lenses
- I took the camera to China for a work trip, and used it in a variety of scenarios, trying out the various computational photography modes
OM System sent me the black and silver version of the PEN with the new 14-42mm f/3.5-5.6 III kit lens, and I used the kit regularly for several weeks, including during a work trip to China. I also paired the camera with an Olympus 45mm f/1.8 lens and a (Panasonic) Leica 12-60mm f/2.8-4 lens.
I've tried the various computational photography modes, used slow shutter speeds, and shot video handheld to test the image stabilization effectiveness, and tried out various autofocus modes.
I've used the camera in light rain and in bright light, testing its splash proof credentials and the brightness of its displays. Along the way, I compared the PEN to the Lumix L10, a similar MFT camera.

articles.title: Hadrian raises $40M for AI agents that find the weaknesses attackers can exploit - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Hadrian raises $40M for AI agents that find the weaknesses attackers can exploit
Dutch offensive security startup Hadrian Security B.V. today announced that it has raised $40 million in new funding to expand its business internationally.
Hadrian’s software points artificial intelligence agents at a company’s internet-facing systems to work out which weaknesses an attacker could actually exploit. No other vendor offers continuous exposure management and agentic penetration testing together on one platform, the company claims.
The platform is split into two products, Atlas and Nova. Atlas maps an organization’s external attack surface around the clock, and agents built for the job check whether each exposure it turns up can really be used in an attack. Nova handles penetration testing on demand. Because the two share context, a team that spots something suspect in Atlas can send Nova in to dig deeper without starting from scratch.
The funding comes less than a month after Anthropic PBC disclosed that criminal and state-linked groups had used its Claude models to automate attack chains and hunt for zero-day vulnerabilities. Hadrian argues that defenders have not caught up. By its count, 87% of organizations still rely on manual penetration tests, and just 0.47% of the findings vulnerability scanners produce turn out to be exploitable.
Co-founder and Chief Executive Rogier Fischer said AI, which is reshaping the threat landscape, may also hold the answer. In his view, “most people are focused on automating the wrong bits.” Hadrian has worked with large language models since before they went mainstream, according to Fischer. He said the platform was built to emulate the attack paths hackers take so that customers can see their biggest risks and decide where to put their security resources.
McKesson Corp., NBCUniversal Media LLC and TotalEnergies SE are among the company’s customers in the U.S. and Europe. Hans Quivooij, chief information security officer at Dutch shipbuilder Damen Shipyards Group N.V., said Damen used to rely on periodic assessments and a known asset inventory. Hadrian now gives the shipbuilder “continuous visibility into what an attacker can actually see and potentially exploit,” he said. Across its customer base, the company says, visibility into critical exposures is up tenfold and issues get resolved 80% faster.
The new money will go toward growth across Europe, the Middle East and Africa and in the U.S. Hadrian’s engineering and research teams are also set to get bigger.
Fischer started Hadrian in 2021 with Olivier Beg and Maurice Clin. He and Beg were ethical hackers in their teens, and Fischer later launched one of Europe’s first cryptocurrency exchanges before working with Beg on Hadrian.
Forgepoint Capital International and Smartfin co-led the round. HV Capital, which led Hadrian’s 2022 seed round, returned alongside Motive Partners, Picus Capital and Oetker Ventures.
Smartfin partner Saumitra Dubey said the firm is backing the company’s plan to “build a nine-figure revenue business.” Investors have now put $65 million into Hadrian.

articles.title: Bell reveals cause behind 87-minute 911 outage across six provinces
articles.text:
Bell has revealed the cause of an 87-minute outage that disrupted 911 services across six provinces on September 17.
PlanHub says the outage affected Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island.
According to the telecom giant’s report to the CRTC, a previously undetected software issue triggered an unexpected condition in its Next-Generation 911 network. Interestingly, Bell noted that it was not a cyberattack and was not caused by a software or network change.
According to the report, the outage first began at 3:13 a.m., with alarms triggered at 3:13 and 3:19. Interestingly, the elements of those alarms that trigger Bell’s “war room” weren’t functioning, and engineers were only alerted roughly 24 minutes after another system detected an unusual drop in traffic for 911 calls.
Bell said that its backup systems handled the vast majority of calls, but noted that some legacy 911 calls did not reach emergency call centres. Bell did not disclose how many calls were missed, but affected 911 centres reported that no critical public safety incidents were connected to the missed calls.
Bell said it installed a permanent fix later that morning and added independent monitoring, along with an end-to-end review of its NG911 infrastructure.
As PlanHub noted, Canada is still transitioning away from its old 911 network to NG911, and the CRTC has ordered the legacy infrastructure to be decommissioned by March 31, 2027.
This outage report also comes as some provinces are starting to charge more for 911 fees, including some of the provinces listed in the outage (Quebec, New Brunswick).
Source: PlanHub

articles.title: Get a rare deal on the shuckable 16TB Seagate Expansion Desktop hard drive at $0.02 per GB — save $100 on this big HDD ahead of Prime Big Deal Days
articles.text:
Get a rare deal on the shuckable 16TB Seagate Expansion Desktop hard drive at $0.02 per GB — save $100 on this big HDD ahead of Prime Big Deal Days
A surprisingly decent value when high-capacity HDDs are into four digits.
The AIpocolypse has consumed everything in its path, including the once-affordable high-capacity HDD. Newegg has a rare deal on a high-capacity 16TB external Seagate drive, knocking $100 off the price to bring it down to $449.99. That comes out to around $0.02 per GB, which is surprisingly sensible given HDD prices right now.
The cheapest 16TB HDD we can find new right now is the IronWolf Pro at $599, which itself is on sale for 6% off. Around this point last year, before HDD prices started soaring, you'd be able to pick up around 28TB for $500. Now, most 16TB drives are around $700, with higher-end Exos drives pushing up above $800.
If you prefer internal storage, you can remove the enclosure, extract the drive, and put it in a case. Note that doing so will void your warranty, so although it's possible, you might want to rethink that move given how expensive HDDs are right now.
The Seagate Expansion Desktop drive is a 16TB HDD that connects via USB 3.0. It's formatted to ExFAT by default, allowing it to work with virtually platform out of the box.
As with most external drives, the actual drive inside of the enclosure varies. Seagate doesn't list the speed of the drive inside, though many external HDDs run at 5,400 RPM. User reports online have shown both Barracuda and IronWolf Pro drives inside the Expansion Desktop, so naturally, your milage will vary.
You shouldn't expect great speeds from this drive. Most 5,400 RPM drives offer sustained sequential reads and writes around 100 MB/s. Thankfully, the USB 3.0 interface offers plenty of bandwidth to keep up with the slower drive. For long-term storage, speed shouldn't be an issue.
If you install the drive internally, you can use it for games, though you should stick to older titles. A lot of modern AAA games require an SSD, and even titles with HDD fallback like Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart struggle on slower 5,400 RPM drives.
Seagate ships the drive formatted to ExFAT, so it'll work with virtually any platform out of the box. Of course, you're free to reformat the drive to any file system you want.
At $449, the 16TB version of this drive is the one to buy. Both the 12TB and 14TB versions are more expensive at $619.99 and $660, respectively, while the 26TB version is $1,179.99.

articles.title: ChatGPT va bientôt signer tous les textes qu'il écrit à votre place
articles.text:
Ce lundi 5 octobre, OpenAI a annoncé l’arrivée d’un filigrane invisible dans les textes générés par ChatGPT et Codex au sein de l’Union européenne. « Dans les semaines à venir », OpenAI va incorporer « un filigrane invisible aux textes éligibles de ChatGPT et Codex dans l’Union européenne », écrit l’entreprise dans un billet de blog.
Cette nouveauté, de taille, concernera tous les abonnements, gratuits comme payants, mais concernera uniquement l’Union européenne. OpenAI précise que le filigrane textuel n’est pas pensé comme « un réglage par défaut mondial » à ce stade. Selon la start-up américaine, cette approche « donne de la marge pour apprendre des usages réels et des retours ». Avant de proposer le « watermark » dans le monde entier, le géant de l’IA veut d’abord voir comment ça se passe en Europe.
 We’re expanding our approach to content provenance to include text in response to EU regulatory requirements, while recognizing the significant limitations of current text watermarking technology.
Our tools already help verify whether an image or audio file was created with our models. This work builds on those efforts to help people better understand when content may have been generated or edited with an OpenAI model.
In the EU, we’ll start watermarking eligible text from ChatGPT and Codex over the coming weeks to comply with the EU AI Act.
Customers using our API can turn on text watermarking for select models worldwide today.
— OpenAI (@OpenAI) October 5, 2026
Une signature cachée dans les textes de l’IA
Baptisée textGrain, la technologie utilisée par OpenAI « ajoute un signal statistique invisible aux choix de mots du modèle », explique le groupe. Un détecteur n’a ensuite qu’à rechercher le signal statistique pour évaluer si un passage porte la signature de ChatGPT, ou s’il vient plutôt d’un esprit humain. Il n’y aura donc pas de code ou de symbole caché dans les textes.
Quand ChatGPT écrit une phrase pour le compte de ses utilisateurs, il ne choisit pas un mot au hasard. À chaque étape, il hésite entre plusieurs mots qui conviennent, et choisit le plus probable. Avec le filigrane, OpenAI ajoute une règle secrète à la manière dont ChatGPT choisit les mots qui vont composer ses phrases. Cette clé secrète, uniquement détenue par OpenAI, pousse l’IA à choisir certains mots plutôt que d’autres, sans changer le sens ni la qualité du texte. Cette règle finit par créer une sorte de signature invisible, qu’un détecteur va pouvoir repérer. La start-up ne constate « aucune différence significative » de qualité sur les textes marqués du filigrane.
Un marquage IA qui est loin d’être infaillible
OpenAI affirme que textGrain a « égalé ou dépassé » les autres approches destinées à labelliser les contenus IA, dont SynthID, la solution de Google. L’entreprise s’empresse d’ajouter que « de bonnes performances en conditions idéales ne garantissent pas une détection fiable au quotidien ».
OpenAI admet d’ailleurs que le système n’est pas infaillible. Plus le texte est court, plus la détection se complique. OpenAI a conçu son détecteur pour qu’il se trompe très rarement, mais, une fois sur cent, il accuse à tort un texte écrit par un humain d’avoir été imaginé par ChatGPT. Sur un passage d’environ 150 mots, le détecteur retrouve le filigrane dans 80% des cas. Sur un passage deux fois plus long, d’environ 300 mots, le taux de détection grimpe à 95 %.
Sans surprise, la moindre retouche réalisée par un humain complique la détection du filigrane. En fait, « remplacer 10 % des mots par des synonymes a réduit la détection d’environ 92 % à 66 % », reconnaît OpenAI. La traduction du texte source complique également la détection de l’intelligence artificielle. Des outils de contournement promettent d’ailleurs déjà d’effacer les filigranes qui fonctionnent de la même façon.
De facto, « l’absence de filigrane détecté ne prouve pas qu’un texte a été écrit par un humain », prévient-elle. Le texte peut en effet être trop court, trop retouché par la main humaine, traduit, ou provenir d’une autre IA. Pour rappel, les détecteurs d’IA accessibles en ligne, comme le controversé Pangram, sont également loin d’être infaillibles. Côté confidentialité, OpenAI assure que le filigrane « n’identifie pas l’utilisateur » et n’associe aucun compte, requête ou conversation au texte généré par ChatGPT.
À lire aussi : Sur LinkedIn, vous allez enfin pouvoir dénoncer tous les posts IA insupportables
Un détecteur réservé aux chercheurs
Dans un premier temps, le détecteur de filigrane sera réservé aux chercheurs et organisations spécialisées. Ceux-ci devront aider OpenAI à évaluer la fiabilité du système, vraisemblablement en vue d’un déploiement grand public. Les développeurs peuvent quant à eux activer le filigrane dès maintenant sur certains modèles d’IA, partout dans le monde. Il reste toutefois désactivé par défaut.
OpenAI n’est pas la première entreprise à franchir le pas. Il y a deux mois, Anthropic annonçait déjà qu’elle allait signer tous les textes générés par Claude. En miroir de son rival, Anthropic précisait que l’outil a ses « limites », et refuse de parler de preuve irréfutable en cas de positif.
Une exigence de l’AI Act
En marquant tous les textes générés par ChatGPT, OpenAI se plie aux exigences de l’AI Act, le règlement européen sur l’IA. Depuis le 2 août, l’article 50 impose aux fournisseurs d’IA générative de rendre tous leurs textes identifiables par une machine. OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Google et Meta, ont jusqu’au 2 décembre 2026 pour se plier à la réglementation et éviter une amende.
L’arrivée de textGrain survient alors que l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle fait des remous dans tous les secteurs de la société, y compris dans le milieu littéraire français. Après avoir reçu plusieurs prix prestigieux pour son roman « C’était ça ou mourir », l’écrivain Thélyson Orélien a été accusé d’avoir eu massivement recours à l’intelligence artificielle. En dépit de ses démentis, l’Académie Goncourt a retiré le livre de sa première sélection « pour préserver l’intégrité du prix ».
