articles.title: Paciente con ELA sueña con el remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time: le queda un año de vida y quiere completarlo
articles.text:
Un jugador identificado como Blake, diagnosticado con esclerosis lateral amiotrófica (ELA), busca terminar por primera vez en su vida un videojuego antes de que la enfermedad se lo impida, y eligió para ese objetivo el remake de The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
Conocido en Reddit bajo el nombre de MadCybertist, el usuario compartió su historia en la plataforma y generó una ola de apoyo entre jugadores de todo el mundo, poco antes de que Nintendo confirmara los detalles finales del lanzamiento del juego.
Cómo es la historia de Blake y su objetivo pendiente
A Blake le diagnosticaron ELA a los 38 años. En ese momento, los médicos le dieron un pronóstico de apenas 12 meses de vida.
La ELA, o esclerosis lateral amiotrófica, es una enfermedad neurodegenerativa que afecta las neuronas motoras y reduce de forma progresiva la capacidad de movimiento. A Blake se la diagnosticaron con un pronóstico inicial de doce meses, un límite que terminó superando por casi cinco años gracias a distintos tratamientos.
Según relató, le queda aproximadamente un año más de vida, y uno de los puntos pendientes en su lista de objetivos es completar un videojuego por primera vez.
Blake jugó la versión original de Ocarina of Time en 1998, pero nunca llegó a terminarla. En diálogo con el medio GamesRadar, explicó por qué el remake representa una oportunidad particular para él.
“Incluso los juegos para un jugador que jugué mientras crecía, nunca llegué a terminar ninguno por completo. Ese era otro de los objetivos de mi lista de cosas pendientes: terminar un videojuego. El momento en que anunciaron el remake de Ocarina of Time fue perfecto para mí. Sabía que quería terminar un juego, sabía que quería darle otra oportunidad a OOT y entonces anunciaron el remake. Para mí todo encajó. Este será el primer videojuego que termine y, probablemente, el único que llegue a completar”.
Cuándo llega el remake y cuánto costará
Nintendo confirmó que el remake de The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time se lanzará el 5 de noviembre de 2026, en el marco de la celebración por los 40 años de la saga.
La fecha queda a pocos días del estreno de GTA 6, previsto para el 19 de noviembre en PlayStation 5 y Xbox Series X|S, por lo que el cierre de año reunirá dos lanzamientos de gran escala.
El precio oficial en formato digital quedó fijado en 59,99 dólares. La primera tirada física incluirá un empaque conmemorativo con arte de portada en lámina texturizada, disponible mientras dure el abastecimiento.
Antes del lanzamiento del juego llegarán una consola temática de Nintendo Switch 2 y un Pro Controller a juego, el 29 de octubre de 2026. También está previsto el lanzamiento de dos nuevos amiibo para 2027.
Qué cambia en el remake del juego de Nintendo
El primer tráiler de gameplay mostró modificaciones respecto al original de Nintendo 64. Link cuenta ahora con un botón dedicado para saltar libremente, una función ausente en la versión de 1998, además de poder nadar y bucear sin las restricciones previas.
La cámara se controla de forma independiente mediante el stick derecho, y el acceso a objetos se reformuló con un esquema similar al utilizado en Breath of the Wild y Tears of the Kingdom. Link también puede esprintar si mantiene pulsado el botón mientras rueda.
El ciclo de día y noche avanza ahora de forma continua incluso dentro de las ciudades, algo que en el original solo ocurría en los exteriores de Hyrule. Los alrededores del castillo se ampliaron con zonas antes inaccesibles, y todo el contenido visual se renderiza en tiempo real, sin secuencias pre-renderizadas.
El remake incorpora una función vinculada al micrófono integrado de Nintendo Switch 2: los jugadores pueden tocar melodías reales, con la voz o con un instrumento, para que la ocarina virtual las reproduzca dentro del juego, aunque también se mantiene el método tradicional de botones.
Las texturas de cada material fueron reconstruidas por completo, los tiempos de carga se redujeron y el juego mantiene un rendimiento más estable durante la exploración. La banda sonora cuenta ahora con arreglos orquestales sinfónicos y los efectos de sonido fueron actualizados en su totalidad.

articles.title: Why Nigeria is missing from Airtel Money’s $7bn IPO
articles.text:
When Airtel Money lists on the London Stock Exchange later this month, it will do so without its struggling Nigerian fintech business. A Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) directive required the mobile money business to transfer its 25% stake in SmartCash, the vehicle through which Airtel operates its Nigerian fintech business, back to Airtel Networks Limited, its Nigerian telecom subsidiary, according to Airtel Money’s IPO prospectus.
The deal was completed for $3 million. But Airtel Money says it is exploring ways to bring SmartCash back into the group. However, the Nigerian business will not be part of the fintech company investors are buying when it lists on October 14.
“The Group is exploring options to bring Smartcash Nigeria within the Group’s perimeter, consistent with the structure of the Group’s other operations,” Airtel Money said in its IPO prospectus. “There can be no assurance as to the timing or outcome of these, which remain subject to regulatory approvals.”
The prospectus describes the group as a pan-African fintech platform operating in 13 African countries and serving approximately 53 million monthly active users as of June 30, 2026.
Airtel’s situation in Nigeria is part of a broader shift among Africa’s telecom companies increasingly trying to separate their fintech businesses from their core telecom operations. They see mobile money as a business that needs its own capital structures, management focus, growth strategies, and is valued separately from the telecom networks that helped create it.
In April, MTN Nigeria shareholders approved the separation of MoMo Payment Service Bank and Y’ello Digital Financial Services from MTN Nigeria into a new holding structure backed by MTN Group, subject to regulatory approval. MTN Group completed the separation of its mobile money business in Ghana in April.
The Nigerian PSB problem
Since the CBN introduced Payment Service Banks (PSBs) in 2018, telecom-led fintechs have struggled to turn their subscriber scale into financial services dominance because of licence restrictions and their late entry into an already developing market.
PSBs can accept deposits and facilitate payments, but lending is restricted, removing one of the most lucrative ways fintech companies monetise customers.
At the same time, companies such as OPay and PalmPay entered the market with products built around payments, credit and merchant services, and have built large distribution networks of their own.
Large telecom operators have struggled to turn their distribution advantage into fintech scale. MTN and Airtel have a combined 167.62 million subscribers, representing 86.02% of Nigeria’s telecom market, but their mobile money businesses have yet to reach 10 million subscribers combined. OPay, meanwhile, had 39.3 million monthly active users in 2025.
Nigeria’s mobile money market processed ₦20.71 trillion ($13.49 billion) in Q1 2025. By year-end, OPay alone reported a gross transaction value of $358 billion.
In 2025, MTN Nigeria chief executive officer Karl Toriola said the company initially expected MoMo PSB to reach about 20 million monthly active users, but revised those expectations because of competition from OPay and PalmPay, the maturity of cash-in and cash-out networks, and the limitations of the PSB licence.
“The MoMo PSB licence does have its limitations, and we need to look at add-ons to that licence to really evolve in that market to get to where we are,” Toriola said. “So, without a doubt, we are behind our initial excitement about the MoMo PSB, but we are well grounded in reality.”
Airtel has also acknowledged the competitiveness of the Nigerian market. “In Nigeria, it is a well-developed fintech market, compared to many other markets,” Sunil Taldar, Airtel Africa’s CEO, said in 2025.
Both operators are still doubling down on their mobile money businesses. SmartCash is pushing a zero-fee banking model and a 15% annual interest rate on savings deposits. It has also integrated with multiple banks and financial institutions, allowing wallet transfers and interbank transactions across its network as it tries to capture more of the transfer market.
MTN, meanwhile, is investing in more agents and merchants, deeper rural penetration, and expanding its digital payments capacity as it tries to increase transaction volumes.
Smartcash could still return
Airtel Money is about to become one of Africa’s biggest publicly listed fintech businesses. It has priced its London initial public offering at £1.96 ($2.59) per share, valuing the mobile money business at £5.3 billion ($7 billion) ahead of its October 14 debut.
Nigeria is Airtel Africa’s second-largest telecom region by subscribers and one of Africa’s biggest fintech markets. Yet it accounted for only 1.24% of Airtel mobile money’s $404 million quarterly revenue and 6.02% of its customer base as of June 2026.
That makes the Nigerian business a small part of the group being taken public, but a noticeable absence given the potential size of the Nigerian market.
Airtel’s fintech operations in Nigeria are currently conducted through Airtel Networks Limited, reflecting the CBN’s licencing requirements, under which mobile money and payment service bank licences must be held by an entity with the relevant telco licence and local regulatory oversight.
Airtel Networks holds the majority shareholding in SmartCash Nigeria, while a nominee shareholding within the group’s perimeter currently stands at below 0.01%.
“Notwithstanding that it sits outside the Group’s perimeter, the Group’s management team provides limited guidance and support to SmartCash Nigeria in respect of technical expertise and management services, reflecting the Group’s integrated approach to fintech operations across its African footprint,” Airtel Money said of its continued support for SmartCash in its prospectus.
The company said the support is not considered material to the group’s current operations, strategy or resource allocation.
For now, SmartCash remains outside Airtel Money’s group, even as the company explores ways to bring it back. Whether that changes Airtel’s fortunes in Nigeria will depend less on where SmartCash sits and more on whether it can turn its telecom scale into a fintech business capable of competing with the likes of OPay and PalmPay. 
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks.

articles.title: Google analyzed 5 years of Flights data, says buying on a specific weekday won't save you money
articles.text:
In a nutshell: The holiday season is getting closer. For most people that means visiting family and friends, which is (usually) fun, but it often also means air travel, which is anything but fun. Google is taking some of the sting out of the process by analyzing years of Google Flights data to discover the lowest fares for Thanksgiving and Christmas flights in the US.
Google's Trends and tips for 2026 holiday travel highlights how many travelers are faced with the dilemma of buying plane tickets straight away or waiting to see if the price drops.
By aggregating five years of data from Google Flights, Google found that the lowest prices for domestic flights occur 39 days before departure, with a low price range of 21 to 57 days beforehand.
For international flights, the lowest prices hit 89 days before departure. There is a price drop between 50 and 133 days out, but it's insignificant.
Google also highlights the best booking times for specific holidays. Those going away for Thanksgiving should book 34 days before departure for the lowest prices, while the low range is 21 to 57 days beforehand.
The ever-popular Christmas travel period requires booking further ahead to secure a cheap flight: 56 days before departure, while the low range is 33 to 67 days.
So, according to Google, the best time to book a money-saving flight for Thanksgiving is around October 21-23. If you're going away for Christmas, somewhere around October 27-29 could get you the best deal.
Other breaks that Google looked at include trips to Mexico or the Caribbean – book these 43 days before departure (low price range is 24 – 69 days).
Going to Europe? Similar to general international travel, prices reach are there lowest 90 days out. The low-price range is 49 days or more before departure.
Finally, flights for spring break are cheapest 50 days before departure (low price range is 29 – 64 days) for trips in March or April. Prices for summer vacations hit their lowest point 21 days before departure (low price range is 20 – 47 days) for trips in July or August.
Google also writes that rumors you can get cheaper flights by purchasing them on specific days of the week are a myth, though Sunday is the most expensive day by a small margin.
However, the days and times you fly do matter. Flying out on Monday and returning on Tuesday or Wednesday can save you around 14% compared with weekend travel. For domestic trips, savings can reach 20% compared with departing and returning on Sundays. Choosing a connecting flight can also cut costs, as nonstop tickets cost 20% more on average.

articles.title: German unicorn Personio acquires spend management platform Circula | EU-Startups
articles.text:
HRTech unicorn Personio today announced it has acquired Circula, a German spend management platform, to reportedly become the first European platform to unite HR, payroll, and spend management.
This follows Circula’s €15 million Series A in 2025 – as covered by EU-Startups.
“Spend management is one of the capabilities our customers ask us for most, and it’s complex to get right in Europe. Just as with payroll rules change at every border. Over the past 9 years Circula has already solved that complexity in an intuitive and powerful way,” says Hanno Renner, CEO and co-founder of Personio. “With Circula joining Personio, everything a company spends on its people–payroll, expenses and benefits–comes together under one roof. That’s a first in Europe, and a big step towards Personio being the system European businesses run their entire workforce on.”
Today’s acquisition comes amid sustained investment in European HR, workforce-management and adjacent spend-management software during 2026.
EU-Startups has reported almost €500 million across a selection of relevant rounds this year, including €200 million for French frontline workforce platform Skello, €129 million for Barcelona-based HRTech company Factorial, €37 million for Amsterdam-based workforce compliance platform WorkFlex and €30 million for Berlin-based spend-management company Moss.
The latter provides a particularly close German comparison to Circula, combining corporate cards, invoices and reimbursements for SMEs while expanding into AI-powered finance tools.
“Circula has solved syncing employee data between spend management and HR platform and hundreds of joint customers already use that integration. The unsolved part is that the tax logic on the expense side and on the payroll side has always been built by two different companies,” says Nikolai Skatchkov, CEO and co-founder of Circula. “Joining forces with Personio today changes that. For our customers, DATEV stays, the existing integration stays, and expertise that Circula built stays. What changes is that HR, spend, and now payroll are designed to be one.”
Founded in Munich in 2015, Personio is an HR and payroll platform, used by more than 16,000 companies employing 1.6 million people. Today’s acquisition marks a new phase for the company as it shifts into spend management.
The two companies have already worked closely together for several years, serving many of Personio’s 16,000 European customers together.
The idea is for expenses to flow into payroll through both payroll integrations and Personio’s native payroll engine. Each company has built compliance and tax expertise in its own domain, Personio in payroll and Circula in expenses and benefits.
More than 3,000 European mid-market businesses already trust Circula with their expenses, corporate cards, accounts payable and tax-optimised benefits.
Beyond their joint customer-base and focus on small and mid-sized organisations, Circula and Personio are also united in their commitment to making the lives of tax advisors easier. Both companies have built up a community of hundreds of tax advisors and have built features that facilitate the collaboration of tax advisors with their clients.
One part of that strategy has been deep DATEV integrations which transfer data into DATEV’s payroll and accounting systems.They will continue to be further developed and will over time seamlessly integrate into a single solution.
Together, Personio and Circula aim to run all business spend – salary, benefits, expenses and corporate cards – in one integrated platform.
Circula will operate as Circula by Personio from October 6 and the team will join Personio. For joint customers the integration will deepen into a fully connected experience. For Circula customers that do not use Personio, the product will continue to be available and further developed as a standalone product.

articles.title: Valve Confirms Steam for Linux Isn't Officially Supported on Arm Chips
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 6th 2026
Valve Confirms Steam for Linux Isn't Officially Supported on Arm Chips
Valve has confirmed that its Steam Client for Linux-based operating systems on Arm chips is not officially supported. This follows a user's report on GitHub claiming issues with Steam for Linux on ARM64 systems. Despite detailing the problem, a Valve developer responded that "Steam for Linux is not currently supported on Arm-based hardware," a stance that has been consistent for years. While Steam has expanded on Linux-based machines, official support is currently limited to systems running x86-64 processors from AMD and Intel. On Arm-based devices, Valve would likely need to make significant optimizations to get Steam for Linux working properly, but the potential user base is so small that the effort may not be justified.
This is surprising given that Valve's VR headset, the Steam Frame, runs on Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 mobile platform. Valve specifically optimized its SteamOS for this chipset and ported its compatibility layer, Proton 11.0, to Arm. This version of Proton allows a full range of games designed for x86 to run on Arm hardware, but the Steam Client itself, which is crucial for game delivery, is not officially supported.Valve's SteamOS port for the Arm (ARM64) architecture has already inspired creativity in the modding community. They are actively transforming Android-based gaming handhelds into miniature versions of the Steam Deck console. As mobile SoCs like Qualcomm's Snapdragon and MediaTek's Dimensity become more competitive in terms of integrated GPU and CPU capabilities, running a true desktop OS on these SoCs is unlocking new gaming experiences, as demonstrated by the modding community. For devices from makers like Ayaneo, Ayn, Retroid, and Konkr, community projects like Armada enable Arm-based devices that previously ran Android to utilize SteamOS. However, when issues arise, don't expect Valve to resolve them.
Sources:

articles.title: Votou no 1º turno e o sistema diz que você faltou? TSE explica
articles.text:
Eleitores que consultaram a situação no serviço de Justificativa Eleitoral do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) nesta terça-feira (6) encontraram a indicação “FALTOU” referente ao primeiro turno das Eleições Gerais de 2026. A mensagem gerou reclamações nas redes sociais de pessoas que afirmam ter comparecido às urnas e possuem o comprovante de votação.
O TSE esclareceu que a indicação não significa que o eleitor deixou de votar. Segundo o tribunal, os dados de comparecimento, ausência e justificativa do primeiro turno ainda estão em processamento e, portanto, a informação exibida anteriormente não representava uma situação definitiva.
Mensagem já foi alterada
Para evitar interpretações equivocadas, o TSE informou que a mensagem exibida no serviço de justificativa eleitoral já foi alterada para indicar que os dados estão “em processamento”.
O tribunal também esclareceu que os arquivos necessários para atualizar o Cadastro Eleitoral ainda estão sendo processados. Quem compareceu à votação e viu a indicação anterior de “FALTOU” não precisa tomar nenhuma providência neste momento.
A orientação é aguardar a conclusão do processamento, prevista para 11 de outubro.
Quando os dados serão atualizados?
O cronograma operacional do Cadastro Eleitoral, previsto na Resolução TSE nº 23.750/2026, determina que o processamento dos arquivos do primeiro turno comece em 4 de outubro e seja concluído até 11 de outubro.
O procedimento inclui informações sobre comparecimento, ausências, justificativas e presença de mesárias e mesários. Até que o processamento seja concluído, os dados exibidos nas consultas podem ser atualizados.
A norma também prevê a suspensão da emissão da certidão de quitação eleitoral pela internet e pelo e-Título a partir de 5 de outubro. O serviço deve ser retomado até 12 de outubro. Quem precisar do documento antes disso poderá solicitá-lo em um cartório eleitoral.
Abstenção passou de 21%
A situação ocorre dois dias após o primeiro turno das eleições. De acordo com o TSE, 33,4 milhões de eleitores não compareceram às urnas, o equivalente a 21,08% do eleitorado apto a votar.
O índice foi o maior registrado desde 1998. Em 2022, a abstenção havia sido de 20,93%, correspondente a 32,7 milhões de eleitores.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Big Oil asks Supreme Court to kill climate lawsuits before trial
articles.text:
The US Supreme Court heard arguments from oil companies on Monday that could help decide the fate of more than two dozen lawsuits accusing the industry of deceiving the public about climate change. The claims seek potentially billions of dollars in damages to help pay the costs imposed by climate-related extreme weather.
Yet the questions before the court did not focus on the merits of these claims but instead on technical legal matters over whether they should proceed at all.
The case being argued was brought in 2018 by the city and county of Boulder against ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy in Colorado state court. While the case and dozens like it have survived multiple appeals in state and federal courts, the oil companies are asking the Supreme Court to declare that federal law preempts state and local governments from bringing such claims.
“This case represents an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct,” said Kannon Shanmugam, arguing for Exxon and Suncor. In effect, Shanmugam said, Boulder is attempting to use state law to regulate oil company activity around the world. “If Boulder’s claims are allowed to go forward, some 90,000 municipalities across the country would have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil fuel producers.”
But Boulder and dozens of other plaintiffs have argued their claims do not attempt to impose any limits on oil companies at all—the Boulder case seeks damages, not an injunction on any activity.
“This case is not about emissions,” said Kevin Russell, who argued the case for Boulder. “It’s about deception.”

articles.title: Microsoft Exchange flaw allows hackers to read mailboxes across an organization, so patch now
articles.text:
Microsoft Exchange flaw allows hackers to read mailboxes across an organization, so patch now
Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 affected
- Microsoft issues fix for CVE-2026-96940, a high-severity Exchange privilege-escalation flaw
- Attackers with compromised user credentials could access other employees’ mailboxes and emails
- No active exploitation reported, but Microsoft labeled the vulnerability “exploitation more likely"
Microsoft has pushed an urgent update for Exchange Server which fixes a high-severity flaw that could wreak some serious havoc among email users.
The company patched CVE-2026-96940, a “weak authorization in Microsoft Exchange Server [that] allows an authenticated attacker to elevate privileges over a network,” as per the National Vulnerability Database (NVD).
According to Microsoft’s advisory the bug, which was given a severity rating of 8.8/10 (high), can be abused to gain unauthorized access to people’s inboxes within the same organization.
In theory, threat actors who obtained credentials of a low-privileged Exchange user could exploit CVE-2026-96940 to escalate their privileges within Exchange, and then read confidential emails and attachments belonging to other people working for the same organization.
The bug cannot be exploited for cross-tenant access, though.
Establishing a foothold
To exploit the vulnerability, the threat actor needs to have authenticated access beforehand. This, however, is not a major obstacle for the attackers, since they can easily purchase login credentials from the dark web, or use phishing to deploy an infostealer capable of extracting these secrets.
Therefore, even an email account of an “ordinary” employee can be enough to establish a foothold, escalate privileges, and access inboxes belonging to higher echelons within an organization.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
At that point, the vulnerability becomes highly valuable. Corporate email accounts can contain confidential documents, contracts, invoices, internal discussions, and other sensitive information, which the attackers can then use for follow-up attacks such as Business Email Compromise (BEC).
It is worth stressing that CVE-2026-96940 is not known to grant administrator or SYSTEM-level privileges on the underlying Windows server. Instead, Microsoft’s disclosed attack scenario focuses on escalating privileges within Exchange and gaining unauthorized access to other users’ mailboxes
Users of Exchange Online are already secured, Microsoft further explained, since it deployed a related “service-side” fix. However, those using on-prem Microsoft Exchange Server products should upgrade to the latest version to avoid being targeted.
Here is a list of the affected versions:
- Microsoft Exchange Server Subscription Edition RTM
- Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 Cumulative Update 23
- Microsoft Exchange Server 2019 Cumulative Update 15
- Microsoft Exchange Server 2019 Cumulative Update 14
Microsoft says there is no evidence of the flaw being abused in the wild, and at press time, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) does not have it listed in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. However, the Windows maker labeled the bug as “exploitation more likely” suggesting that cybercriminals might try to exploit it, and warning users to apply the provided fix as soon as possible.
It is also worth mentioning that both Exchange Server 2016 and Exchange Server 2019 reached their end of support last year. Microsoft said that these latest security updates are only available to organizations enrolled in its Period 2 Extended Security Update (ESU) program.
The program gives eligible Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 customers access to security updates released between May and the end of October 2026. Organizations that have not enrolled are being urged to migrate to Exchange Server Subscription Edition (SE) if they want to continue receiving the latest security fixes.
Unusual release
Microsoft issued the patch on October 2, as part of its September 2026 V2 Exchange Server Security Updates. The original September updates were pushed on September 8, and the software giant added that the main difference between these two versions is the fix for CVE-2026-96940.
As it was releasing the patch, it confirmed it was pushing it “ahead of its intended schedule”, without elaborating further. Perhaps labeling it as “exploitation more likely” is elaborating enough, especially since the company urged customers to review its deployment guidance and apply the update as soon as possible.
fter installing the update, administrators are also advised to run Microsoft’s Exchange Server Health Checker. The tool can verify whether the security update was installed successfully and determine whether any additional action is required.

articles.title: The best robot vacuum and mop deals during October Prime Day
articles.text:
Spending too much time constantly sweeping and mopping? If you have the money to delegate those chores to a robot cleaner, you could save a lot of personal time. Thankfully, it’s cheaper than usual to buy a robot vacuum / mop hybrid during Amazon’s Prime Big Deal Days, and some of our favorite models are discounted. The deals aren’t just for Amazon Prime members either, with other retailers like Best Buy and manufacturers getting in on the action, as well.
The best robot vacuum and mop deals during October Prime Day
We spotted deals on some of our favorite robot vacuums and mops from brands like Roborock, Qrevo, and Dreame.
That being said, if your floors are already squeaky clean, make sure to check out our roundup of over 100 deals from Amazon’s October sale.
Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow
Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design.
Roborock Saros 20
Roborock’s Saros 20 stands out for its ability to climb tall thresholds, avoid obstacles with impressive accuracy, and clean under low furniture thanks to its slim design. It also combines powerful 36,000Pa suction with great spinning mop pads, which is why we recommend it for homes with multiple floor types and tricky transitions between rooms.
Narwal Flow 2
Our pick for the best robot vacuum-mop if you have all hardwood floors is the Narwal Flow 2. A superb mop with a wide flat roller pad and an excellent vacuum, the Flow 2 also has top-notch navigation and obstacle detection. Its sleek base station is also less of an eyesore than most.
Dreame X60 Ultra
The Dreame X60 Ultra leverages a pair of AI-assisted cameras to help it navigate obstacles and ensure a thorough, consistent cleaning. It’s only 3.13 inches tall, so it can sneak under low surfaces that some other robot vacuums can’t.
Eufy Omni C28
The Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors.
Dreame L40 Ultra
Dreame’s budget-friendly L40s Ultra has storage for up to 100 days of dust, and can clean its own mop pads. The auxiliary climbing wheels help it navigate thresholds and rug edges with ease.
Roborock Q10 S5 Plus
A budget robot vacuum and mop without a multifunction dock. It has AI-powered obstacle avoidance, sonic mopping, auto mop lifting, and an auto-empty dock.
Best overall: Deebot X8 Pro Omni
The Deebot X8 Pro Omni is an excellent roller mopping bot that extends to clean along backboards and furniture. It’s also a powerful vacuum with great obstacle avoidance, a small dock, and a convenient self-cleaning brush system.
Switchbot K11 Plus
The Matter-compatible SwitchBot K11 Plus is ideal for small apartments, bedrooms, and home offices. It can easily navigate around chair and desk legs and into tight spaces that most other bots miss. It also features a commendable 6,000Pa of suction power — which is great for this price point — and works well on both hardwood and carpet.

articles.title: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers
articles.text:
Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers
Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly found the popular medicines reduce molecular markers of age.
Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. They might also melt away the years.
Drug giants Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their drugs age less quickly, according to readouts from molecular “aging clocks.”
Such clocks assess a person’s biological age by looking at changes to DNA that accumulate with time, or, in newer versions, by tracking levels of key proteins.
Both companies found that overweight or diabetic patients taking the drugs, called GLP-1s, had reduced biological age compared to those taking a placebo, although the difference varied widely, depending on which type of clock was used, and what organ was tested.
Overall, the difference was around “two to three years,” according to Nikolaj Roed, a global project leader at Novo, who says the company has been seeing “improved biological age in our patients across trials and across different tissues.”
The findings add to wide speculation among scientists that GLP-1 drugs, as they are known, are acting on basic causes of aging and might be a true longevity treatment.
“Two years is a pretty strong effect, in my book,” says Steve Horvath, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who’s credited with inventing aging clocks. Horvath says the emerging data could provide “evidence that these GLP-1 drugs are actually what is known as geroprotectors, medications that slow or possibly even reverse biologic aging.”
The companies shared their findings over the weekend during Aging Research & Drug Discovery, a conference devoted to seeking scientific remedies for old age. While that quest has not yet produced any clear-cut success, some scientists now think Novo’s drug semaglutide (sold under the names Ozempic and Wegovy) is coming close.
“In an unhealthy population, I do think it’s an anti-aging drug,” says Vadim Gladyshev, a Harvard biologist who assisted Novo with its molecular measurements. “But in a healthy population, no one knows.”
The drugs cause weight loss by stimulating a receptor, GLP-1, that tells your brain you’re not hungry. Yet real-world studies have shown much wider benefit. The drugs improve kidney function, reduce blood pressure, and even sharply cut the overall chance of death.
“If the question is,‘Can semaglutide reach several diseases relevant to health span and aging?’ we know we can say the answer is yes,” said Alejandro Aguayo-Orozco, a senior scientific director at Novo, the Danish drug giant, during the meeting.
The next question to answer, he said, is whether such effects are accompanied by changes to molecular measures of biological aging: “When you intervene with semaglutide, does it actually move the clocks in any direction? And the answer is yes.”
The company found that, over time, the drugs cause a wide slowdown in aging clocks—as much as 4 years in the case of a clock that looks at heart proteins. “I think it’s pretty clear that the organ age is shifting,” said Aguayo-Orozco.
The studies are also a huge boost for the science of aging clocks. Although these measures reflect a person’s age, it’s been uncertain if they are useful as true biomarkers. Now clock makers have evidence that their readouts show a drop in age when people take drugs with broad, well-demonstrated benefits.
“The clock people have been pushing for a decade to get this kind of study done,” says Yuge Ji, a biologist who previously worked in the field and now runs a startup, Reflector Bio. “It’s huge for them.”
As part of its study, Novo took blood draws from 10,052 people, half on the drug and half on a placebo. Their blood, collected at the start of the study as well as months later, was then measured with “proteomic clocks,” which use levels of key proteins to predict a person’s age and risk of dying.
Scientists at Eli Lilly performed similar research on their GLP-1 drug, tirzepatide, using so-called “epigenetic” clocks that assess age by counting accumulated changes to DNA. Lilly’s study was smaller, but also found that for the most part, molecular time moved more slowly for people on the drug.
“All the clocks are telling a consistent story that we’re seeing a reduction in age,” Kevin Duffin, vice president for aging research at Lilly, said during the conference. “It’s not like we’re going to reverse age by 30 years or something, but it’s a significant reduction.”
The molecules have become the best selling drugs in the world,, with Lilly’s tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro for diabetes and Zepbound for obesity, topping the list with more than $36 billion in revenue to the company last year. Novo’s semaglutide, also sold under more than one name, was a close second.
Alex Zhavoronkov, the founder of Insilico Medicine, and the organizer of the Boston meeting, says that extending lives by even one year across the world’s population would be equal to tens of millions of lifetimes.
Last month Zhavoronkov showed that one of his company’s drugs, for a lung disease, also reversed the signals from aging clocks. That drug is experimental, but Zhavoronkov has sought to promote the idea that humanity is entering a new era of longevity medicines. He also disclosed during the event that he has been “microdosing” the available weight-loss drugs, even though he is not overweight.
“I am on tirzepatide and I am an equal-opportunity injector of semaglutide as well,” Zhavoronkov said.
It was part of an effort to directly raise the question of whether the first mass-market anti-aging remedy is already here.
“Do you think a reasonable person should start taking semaglutide?” he asked Aguayo-Orozco, the Novo scientist, in front of a crowded audience.
“I am not a physician. I cannot answer that question,” Aguayo-Orozco replied.
Several people cautioned that GLP-1 drugs do have side effects, including muscle loss. That is one reason they might not help most people, says Horvath, who says he isn’t ready to take the drugs himself, although he’s thought about it.
“Clearly, the drugs have many benefits in obese people, but I did not yet see sufficient evidence that they will benefit skinny people,” he said. “I guess we will have to wait.”
Answers could start to emerge in a year or two. This past January, a US agency, ARPA-H, put $38 million toward a study in Texas that will attempt to determine whether semaglutide has anti-aging effects in healthy people over 60. That research will look at changes in cognition, mobility, and acuity of the senses.
That project also seeks to help define a regulatory pathway for anti-aging drugs and to “build a new therapeutic industry” around longevity.

articles.title: Anthropic is giving startups a free year of Claude Team and $1,000 in credits | TechCrunch
articles.text:
On Tuesday, Anthropic announced an expansion of its Claude for Startups program, offering subsidized access to its AI models and a variety of other benefits to qualifying companies.
The new version of the program, which launched as part of Anthropic’s SF Tech Week event, provides a free year of Claude Team, Anthropic’s paid plan for groups, with up to five premium seats, as well as $1,000 in API credits for building with Claude. Companies will also get access to Claude Marketplace, which lets them build plug-ins for the service. Companies can also book virtual office hours with Anthropic’s Applied AI team.
“We created this program because we believe the benefits of AI will reach most people through the companies that build on top of models, rather than through the models alone,” Anthropic said in an announcement. “That makes partnering closely with founders and developers central to our mission.”
Companies are eligible if they were founded in the last five years or received funding in the last two years. Interested companies can apply through the Claude for Startups program page.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
10 climate tech companies to watch
Each year, MIT Technology Review puts together a list of the most promising climate tech companies in the world. This year, the stakes feel higher than ever. The world is on track for one of its hottest years on record, climate-fueled disasters are taking lives and costing billions, while political shifts and international conflict have stalled progress.
We urgently need to cut emissions and avoid climate change’s most harmful effects, and that’s where our 10 companies come in.
They’re working on everything from mobile flood barriers and semi-solid-state batteries to compressed-CO₂ energy storage and next-generation nuclear reactors. They also reflect the biggest shifts in climate tech—including the surging energy demands of AI data centers.

articles.title: 12 African companies from AT50 take part in Egyptian Exchange event - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Twelve companies represented in the AT50 Index (Africa Tech 50) took part in the AT50 Cairo Market Open at the Egyptian Exchange (EGX) on September 22, bringing together founders, regulators, institutional investors, banks and capital markets leaders from Egypt and across Africa.
The Cairo event marked AT50’s third major exchange engagement following its global launch at the London Stock Exchange in January 2026, and its first African exchange activation at the Johannesburg Stock Exchange in July.
The 12 AT50 companies represented in Cairo included nine Egyptian companies – MNT-Halan, Nawy, Paymob, Bosta, MaxAB, Vezeeta, MoneyFellows, Breadfast and Yodawy – alongside Chari from Morocco, and Flutterwave and Paga from Nigeria.
“Fintech stands as one of the most critical drivers poised to fundamentally reshape the capital markets landscape in the coming period. As companies scale and mature, their engagement with capital markets must not be deferred until the decision to go public is finalised; rather, this connection should be forged much earlier. Exchanges play a pivotal role in cultivating that familiarity and bridging ties between innovators, investors, and the broader financial ecosystem. Hosting the AT50 Index Market Open in Cairo presents an exceptional opportunity to deepen this vision and anchor institutional partnerships both in Egypt and across the continent,” said Omar Radwan, chairman of the Egyptian Exchange.

articles.title: EB Games Canada to get Nintendo's first store-within-a-store in North America
articles.text:
EB Games Canada will become the home of Nintendo’s first-ever store-within-a-store in North America.
The 1,500 sq. ft. space will open at EB Games’ flagship location at 267 Yonge Street in Toronto. The permanent store will feature Nintendo Switch 2 hardware and software, playable demos, merchandise and photo opportunities. The space will also sell Nintendo’s line of My Mario products for young children, some of which will be exclusive to EB Games in Canada.
EB Games’ Nintendo space will officially open on Sat., Oct. 17 following a ribbon-cutting ceremony at 10 a.m. It should be noted that while this is Nintendo’s first “store-within-a-store” in North America, the U.S. has two dedicated Nintendo Stores in New York City and San Francisco.
The Nintendo store partnership comes just over a year after EB Games Canada was bought from GameStop by French-Canadian entrepreneur Stephan Tetrault, the co-owner of McFarlane Toys. Under the new Canadian ownership, the retailer returned to the EB Games Canada branding and promised to “return to its roots with a fresh identity that merges classic elements with modern retail experiences.” Naturally, the Nintendo store is part of that.
The new Nintendo space also comes right on time for the holiday season. Outside of already released 2026 games like Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, Mario Tennis Fever, Pokémon Pokopia and the Star Fox remake, Nintendo still has two more Switch exclusives on the way: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort (Oct. 22) and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake (Nov. 5). A Zelda-themed special edition Switch 2 console is also releasing on Oct. 29, but naturally, that’s been in hot demand and has already been selling out pre-orders.

articles.title: The next chapter for India’s insurtech is about reach, trust, and retention
articles.text:
The next chapter for India’s insurtech is about reach, trust, and retention
India’s insurtech sector is shifting from growth at all costs to sustainable scale, as investors demand clearer paths to profitability. The next phase will favour businesses that combine technology with trust, strong servicing and disciplined distribution.
During calendar year (CY) 2025, Insurtech IPOs and acquisitions hit multi-year highs, even as fresh venture funding into the category grew at a slower rate. Investors are showing more interest in insurance technology but also asking harder questions from companies showing commercial traction.
Insurtech, the sector that uses modern technology to make traditional insurance products and processes faster, cheaper, and more personal, is on a rally. India’s insurtech sector is one of the largest in the world, and its choices will shape the next decade of insurance distribution here.
According to an October 2025 report by BCG and India InsurTech Association (IIA), India’s insurtech ecosystem has over 150 active players, with cumulative valuations crossing $15.8 billion and revenue reaching $0.9 billion in 2024, a tenfold increase since 2019.
The sector has two unicorns, eight players between $100 million and $1 billion and over 45 players with over $1 million.
India’s insurtech sector mirrored the global trends, signalling a shift in investor focus to backing businesses with clear paths to profitability and scale, according to the report.
Health Insurtech ventures in India accounted for four of the five largest deals and more than 70% of the funding, reflecting their role in driving access, efficiency, and innovation.
For much of the past decade, the sector was aiming for scale. This got global capital excited about a market where insurance penetration has been stuck near 3.7% of GDP for years, roughly half the world average.
However, the excitement about India’s large addressable market is also a tale of caution, as many insurance distribution companies have had to raise funds regularly to survive.
Insurance is difficult to scale responsibly, and the reasons have less to do with technology than with the product itself. For instance, a ride-hailing trip or a food-ordering app proves out its unit economics within days. However, an insurance policy plays out over a year, or five years, or sometimes a lifetime. So, insurtech start-ups cannot simply borrow growth playbooks built for other consumer internet businesses.
The sheer cost of distribution in a country where insurance, outside a few urban pockets, is underpenetrated and where regulation is focused more on solvency, claim settlement and disclosure than growth rates, requires an approach that rewards patience over speed.
The question, therefore, is what sustainable insurtech looks like amid the challenges the sector faces.
To be sure, for years, presence across a large share of India's pincodes was the metric most insurance firms were chasing. It mattered far less whether that customer later bought a different product from the same platform. However, the mindset is slowly changing, with renewal rates and cross-selling turning customer acquisition costs into investments.
For instance, an insurance advisor in a small town might spend a Tuesday following up on a claim filed three months earlier, and walking a family through why a certain hospital expense was covered and another was not. That conversation, far more than any app notification or online offers, is what brings the family back when the renewal falls due, and it is often what brings a neighbour or an extended family member to the same advisor looking for a policy of their own.
A second shift is toward hybrid distribution, human advisors backed by digital tools, rather than the app-only acquisition approach. The advisor becomes both the acquisition engine and the retention engine, when trust is built through conversation rather than online.
That same advisor also chases down missing documents, explaining a rejected claim, or simply answering a call when a policyholder does not know who else to ask. It is this servicing layer, built one interaction at a time, that turns a policy sold into a relationship kept, adding service as its own point, next to Trust and Access, the key pillars of the business.
A third, still-emerging shift is that across India's broader insurance sector, from large life insurers to smaller distribution platforms, growth is increasingly being built organically by addressing the expanding population.
However, some companies are also expanding inorganically, especially through mergers, acquisitions and foreign investments in order to scale quickly to meet the growing demand.
In its early 2026 report on the Indian insurance market, Swiss Re Ltd, a Swiss reinsurance company, predicted the country’s mid-term annual premium growth at 6.9% annually between 2026 and 2030, making India the strongest growing major insurance market globally.
Even for the insurtech sector, acquiring an existing agent network or customer base can help in scaling up quickly to tap the market. Perhaps this is the reason why the central government had once considered merging the loss-making state-owned insurers. The centre has since then asked these companies to focus on profitability, with the government monitoring their performance for a possible decision in the future.
To be sure, even policy has started nudging the sector towards consolidation. The opening of 100% foreign direct investment into insurance, the recent rationalisation of GST on individual life and health premiums, and the regulator's own emphasis on capital efficiency and faster claim settlements point towards a sector that wants to be judged on outcomes for policyholders and not headlines about funding raised.
However, none of this means growth stops mattering, as India remains badly under-insured, and closing that gap needs both existing and new players to push harder.
Domestic rating agency, ICRA Ltd., in its April 2026 report on the Indian insurance sector, said it expects the individual New Business Premium (NBP) to rise by 9.4-9.9% to Rs 2.02-2.03 trillion in FY 2027, driven by private insurers.
NBP is the total money collected from newly sold insurance policies industry wide.
The rating agency expects overall NBP to rise by 7.8-8.2% to Rs 4.95-4.97 trillion in FY2027 from Rs 4.60 trillion in FY 2026 and Rs 3.97 trillion in FY 2025. Having spent close to a decade building an insurance distribution business from a handful of towns into a nationwide network, we believe the insurtech companies that matter five years from now will be the ones that create real value for this growing ecosystem, while also treating every funding round as a fuel for growing the business.

articles.title: Pour entraîner Claude, Anthropic veut votre voix
articles.text:
Claude s’est mis à parler en mai 2025, et son mode vocal s’est depuis ouvert à toutes les offres, de la formule gratuite aux abonnements professionnels. Ce week-end, des captures d’écran venues de l’application ont dévoilé une fenêtre inédite au lancement de ces conversations. Le message : « Autorisez-nous à utiliser vos données vocales pour améliorer nos modèles d’IA », avec deux boutons, « Autoriser » et « Pas maintenant ». La collecte serait désactivée par défaut, pilotée par un interrupteur dédié dans les réglages de confidentialité, distinct de celui qui gouverne déjà les conversations écrites et le code.
Une promesse écrite noir sur blanc, toujours en ligne
La page d’aide consacrée à la dictée sur mobile, mise à jour le 16 mars 2026, affirme sans détour : « Nous n’utilisons pas votre voix pour entraîner nos modèles ». Le même document précise que l’audio est supprimé sitôt la transcription terminée. La nouvelle invite viserait, elle, les conversations vocales : un périmètre voisin, absent de cette documentation, qui reste en ligne telle quelle.
La politique de confidentialité entrée en vigueur le 10 septembre 2026 ne contient de son côté aucune clause sur la voix. Pour l’Espace économique européen, elle range le consentement parmi les bases légales de l’entraînement, et la fenêtre semble taillée pour ce cadre. Anthropic n’a pour l’instant confirmé ni le déploiement, ni son calendrier, ni la durée de conservation des enregistrements, d’où le conditionnel qui s’impose encore.
Après vos conversations et votre code, votre voix
Le 28 août 2025, Anthropic avait déjà retourné ses conditions grand public : conversations et sessions de code des offres Free, Pro et Max versées à l’entraînement, sauf refus de l’utilisateur. Qui acceptait voyait la conservation de ses données portée à cinq ans, et l’échéance du choix, fixée d’abord au 28 septembre, avait fini par glisser au 8 octobre. La fenêtre de l’époque arrivait surtout avec un interrupteur préréglé sur « activé ». Celle d’aujourd’hui ferait le chemin inverse, éteinte tant que l’utilisateur n’a rien touché.
En France, la CNIL décrivait dès 2020, dans son livre blanc consacré aux assistants vocaux, la voix comme « une sorte d’image sonore » de la personne. Le gendarme des données la classe parmi les données biométriques dès qu’elle sert à identifier quelqu’un. Un fichier audio transporte en effet bien plus que des mots : un accent, un état de forme, parfois les bruits du foyer. C’est ce qui en fait un carburant précieux pour des modèles qui apprennent la parole, et une donnée plus délicate à confier que du texte.
Pour l’heure, rien ne part de votre micro sans votre accord : la fenêtre se referme d’un « pas maintenant », et le réglage se vérifie à tout moment dans les paramètres de confidentialité de l’application. Un contrôle qui mérite d’être refait après les grosses mises à jour, le précédent de 2025 l’a montré. L’historique invite tout de même à garder un œil sur ces interrupteurs : entre une promesse de mars et une invite d’octobre, la doctrine maison sur vos données aura tenu six mois.

articles.title: Nigeria’s global hiring push faces a job creation test
articles.text:
Nigeria has spent years training young people for the global economy. But for many, the hardest step comes after the certificate: finding a paying job.
Hire From Nigeria is the latest attempt to close that gap by linking Nigerian professionals, skilled workers, digital specialists, creatives and service providers with employers abroad. Tech4Dev, a non-profit that provides digital-skills training to underserved populations, and Univelcity, a Lagos-based technology and AI institute, are leading the campaign, which aims to turn Nigeria’s skilled workforce into a pipeline for global jobs and contracts.
Nigeria has a large workforce with potential to serve global markets: 79.5% of its working-age population participates in the labour force, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. Digital-skills programmes are also expanding the capabilities of its young, English-speaking population.
The government’s 3 Million Technical Talent (3MTT) programme has enrolled and deployed hundreds of thousands of fellows across Nigeria’s 36 states. Women Techsters has trained more than 100,000 women, while Google Digital Skills for Africa says it has equipped over five million young Nigerians with foundational digital skills.
These programmes expand the talent pipeline, but training alone does not establish export capacity. The economic opportunity depends on matching workers with international employers and turning their skills into reliable, well-paid contracts.
“The task now is to turn this capacity into contracts by organising our talent pipeline, meeting international standards, and consistently delivering quality, reliability and value,” Jumoke Oduwole, Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, said at the campaign’s launch on August 31, 2026.
Hire From Nigeria arrives alongside the National Talent Export Programme (NATEP), which is targeting one million export-linked service jobs and $10 billion in economic value by 2030. It follows years of government-backed efforts to train workers for global markets, from outsourcing roadmaps to digital-skills schemes such as the 3MTT.
The test is whether the campaign can turn training and institutional partnerships into paid work, rather than count trainees, certificates and memoranda of understanding while workers wait for jobs.
“Nigerian firms [and] professionals struggle to identify the specific market, the buyer and the professional requirements that apply to those opportunities,” Olisa Amadi, NATEP’s strategic communications lead, told TechCabal in August.
NATEP is designed to build policy, market, and institutional infrastructure for exporting talent, while programmes such as 3MTT build the talent pool. The risk is that Nigeria adds more layers to the skills pipeline without fixing the final one: employer demand.
Joel Ogunsola, Tech4Dev’s co-founder and president, said Hire From Nigeria is intended to be demand-driven. Instead of training people first and hoping employers show up, the coalition wants to start with the market.
“For us to even be sure of the requirements, we need to engage first with the employers,” Ogunsola told TechCabal in an interview. “We have a pool of young people to place with you. What are you looking for, and at what competence level?”
The meaningful test, then, is whether Hire From Nigeria can point to signed job orders, defined roles, salary ranges and actual placement dates.
Ogunsola said the coalition expects to secure at least 50,000 direct outsourced jobs within its first 12 months, as well as about 8,000 placements through legal migration routes. By 2030, the broader ambition is 150,000 outsourced jobs performed from Nigeria and 50,000 jobs through physical migration, with the rest of the one-million target comprising indirect roles linked to export activity.
Those targets require clear accounting. A direct customer-support role serving an overseas company is not the same as an indirect job created around an outsourcing hub. Both may have economic value, but combining them can obscure whether the programme is creating the jobs it promises.
Verified direct placements, pay levels, contract duration and retention after six and 12 months provide a clearer picture of the campaign’s employment outcomes than placement totals alone. These measures distinguish short-term hiring from sustained employment and show whether workers continue to earn from export-linked roles.
Ogunsola agrees, arguing that the initiative should not be judged by how many jobs it creates on paper, but by whether those jobs last. The real measure of success will be the number of people placed in jobs and how sustainably those positions are maintained.
Nigeria already has a small outsourcing base. Ogunsola told me that about 20,000 people are employed in international outsourcing and related operations, including customer service, technical support, data labelling, and AI work.
Moving from roughly 20,000 workers to hundreds of thousands of export-linked jobs will require more than training. Nigeria needs an industrial strategy for services that combines talent development with infrastructure, incentives and policies built around international demand.
India built its IT-BPO industry through tax incentives, Software Technology Parks, telecom infrastructure and closer links between universities and industry. The sector now employs more than 5.4 million people and generates over $245 billion in annual revenue.
The Philippines took a similar approach, aligning English-language and healthcare BPO training with labour policy; its outsourcing sector now employs about 1.7 million people and contributes nearly 8% of GDP. Costa Rica also used its investment-promotion agency, CINDE, to build a high-value services industry that now supports more than 100,000 corporate-services jobs.
For Nigeria, training is only the starting point. Turning skills into steady work requires programmes and recognised certifications tailored to specific industries, alongside clear routes to jobs with foreign employers. Stronger digital infrastructure must support those connections, while tax incentives and trade agreements can help businesses compete for international contracts.
But skilled workers still face barriers beyond their control. Unreliable electricity and internet access make work harder and drive up costs. Fragmented public systems, security concerns, and uncertain regulations add further obstacles. No worker can solve these problems alone from a bedroom with a laptop.
Hire From Nigeria’s answer is to lean on business process outsourcing hubs, where operators provide power, connectivity, equipment, security, and management. That gives foreign clients a more controlled environment.
Ogunsola said this is why the campaign is prioritising outsourcing commitments and identifying infrastructure-ready states. “The case of someone being at home and not having a generator is not going to happen,” he said. “You’re going to need to physically go to an office.”
The initiative’s other major task is trust. Turning employer interest into contracts depends on trust: companies need confidence that workers’ identities, qualifications and experience are verifiable, and that customer data and intellectual property will be protected. Without that assurance, Nigeria’s growing talent pool may struggle to translate into sustained international work.
Hire From Nigeria says it plans to build a central platform linking identity verification, security checks, skills validation and worker profiles. The coalition is discussing partnerships with the Ministry of Labour, Ministry of Interior and the Office of the National Security Adviser.
The proposed platform would make Nigerian workers easier for foreign employers to assess, but it would also hold sensitive personal information and influence access to employment. Its role therefore extends beyond verification to deciding which applicants meet the requirements for international work.
That makes accuracy and accountability central to its design. Clear screening criteria, transparent data sources, and procedures for correcting errors and challenging exclusion would give employers confidence in the checks while allowing workers to contest decisions affecting their prospects.
BPO hubs consolidate power, connectivity, equipment, and security, easing some constraints facing individual remote workers. But they require substantial capital and reliable management. Nigeria’s outsourcing industry remains relatively small, employing an estimated 20,000 people across customer support, technology, data, and specialised services, according to Ogunsola.
Grand View Research values the global BPO market at $328.4 billion in 2025 and projects growth to $695.8 billion by 2033, highlighting a sizeable opportunity for Nigerian providers.
Capturing that opportunity requires more than building facilities. Hubs depend on sustained client contracts to cover operating costs and support continuous employment. Announced centres and state commitments indicate planned capacity; signed contracts, occupied workstations and retained workers show whether that capacity is translating into a viable business.
Hire From Nigeria could help connect Nigerian workers to international demand, but its impact will be clearer through outcomes than institutional participation.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: “We want to partner with you,” Canadian military procurer tells startup founders | BetaKit
articles.text:
Shunning a microphone, Sean Naugle used his “military voice” to address a room of bleary-eyed founders this morning during a session on how entrepreneurs can do business with Canada’s defence sector.
Naugle, a 30-year veteran of the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) and a senior contracts officer at CFB Edmonton, was at Edmonton Unlimited on Tuesday to talk about the complexities of the CAF’s procurement system.
“Everybody here is well aware of the global trade landscape that’s changed dramatically over the past several years,” Naugle told the three dozen or so in attendance. “Canada is very vulnerable to that restructuring. That has translated into a lot of changes at the Department of National Defence (DND) … in terms of some of the programs that are available to everyone in the business community.”
“We want to partner with you: we need suppliers, diversity, more options to make procurement faster and better.”
Sean Naugle, CAF
Canada has seen a rash of investment from the federal government into defence and dual-use technologies over the last 18 months, with billions invested into reinvigorating Canada’s defence industrial complex. A big part of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to overhaul defence has involved procurement, with the government introducing a “build, partner, buy” framework into its defence industrial strategy that centres domestic production, supply chains, and dual-use technology as anchor commitments. That, in turn, has led many Canadian tech startups to eye the DND and the armed forces as prospective clients.
“We want to partner with you: we need suppliers, diversity, more options to make procurement faster and better,” Naugle said, before outlining some of the red tape potential vendors must deal with if they want to land military contracts. Those included managing company-wide security clearances in some instances, and the minutiae of the vendor process and applying for contracts that can be hyper-specific.
Legacy systems
Among those in attendance was Connie Stacey. Stacey is the founder of Grengine, an Edmonton company that develops modular, scalable battery energy storage systems that replace diesel generators. Amid Canada’s push for increased military self-reliance, Grengine’s product has attracted significant interest as a dual-use technology, earning the startup entrance into NATO’s Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic. Stacey is also a member of the federal government’s defence industry advisory group.
Stacey said Naugle’s seminar was a worthy resource for startups, noting the challenges that come with navigating Public Services and Procurement Canada (PSPC), which acts as the central purchasing agent for federal ministries.
“One of the things with PSPC, and probably even more with defence, is they’re very segmented,” Stacey said. “You end up with innovation programs where the CAF is saying … ‘we want to buy this,’ but then it will go to procurement.”
During the procurement process, there are mandatory criteria included in federal solicitation contracts, and not meeting those exact specifications can be enough for an application not to be considered. Stacey said that rigidity, alongside siloed government departments, can be a real stumbling block for founders looking to get their foot in the door of a defence contract.
RELATED: Feds say moving defence procurement to Crown corp will make it “more commercial, more fleet-footed”
“You end up with a process that’s kind of like telephone tag. It gets thinner and thinner as you go through the different departments,” Stacey said. “[In some cases] we wouldn’t qualify [for a contract], even if we could actually provide something that the CAF has clearly said: we want this.
“It creates this long, cumbersome process where the actual experts are no longer the purchasers,” she added.
Canada has made efforts at modernizing procurement already, most recently with the creation of the Defence Investment Agency, a carve-out within the PSPC for defence contracts that the federal government is now attempting to turn into a Crown corporation. But Stacey thinks there’s more that can be done, with her experience with NATO serving as inspiration.
“DIANA has this program called the Rapid Adoption Service,” she said. “Under that framework, any of the 32 NATO countries can say ‘we’d like to buy that,’ and they can write a contract through this mechanism.”
The Rapid Adoption Service creates a fast-track pathway between innovators and military end users by allowing member states to bypass competitive bidding rules, effectively treating DIANA’s initial vetting process as having met the legal requirements for a fair and open competition.
“I don’t think it’s an intent problem, but simply old legacy systems we’re dealing with,” Stacey said.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
