articles.title: So viele der Beschäftigten sehen Open Source in Landesverwaltung positiv
articles.text:
So viele der Beschäftigten sehen Open Source in Landesverwaltung positiv
Fast die Hälfte der Beschäftigten in Schleswig-Holsteins Landesverwaltung sieht die Umstellung auf Open-Source-Lösungen positiv. Dies ergab eine Studie im Auftrag der Open-Source-Unternehmen Univention, Nextcloud, Heinlein und Open-Xchange. Insgesamt nahmen demnach 2.700 Beschäftigte an der repräsentativen Online-Befragung teil.
Dabei bewerten 49 Prozent der Befragten die Umstellung als positiv – 41 Prozent sehen sie negativ. Das Kommunikationsunternehmen boy, das die Umfrage durchgeführt hat, teilte mit, dass das Akzeptanzniveau im Vergleich zu früheren Werten in der laufenden Transformation höher liege. Zudem gaben 74 Prozent der Befragten an, sich bereits an die neue Arbeitsumgebung gewöhnt zu haben – rund 64 Prozent der Befragten in den ersten drei Monaten.
Bei Open-Source-Lösungen ist der Quellcode öffentlich und kann den individuellen Bedürfnissen angepasst werden. Die Verwaltung in Schleswig-Holstein wird schrittweise auf Open-Source-Lösungen umgestellt. So begann das nördlichste Bundesland bereits 2024 mit der Einführung von LibreOffice als Standard-Bürosoftware, Anfang Oktober 2025 wurde das Mailsystem der Landesverwaltung vollständig umgestellt.
Für das Gelingen der Transformation ist ein Grund den Angaben nach die kollegiale Unterstützung. So hätten 74 Prozent der Befragten ein Gespräch mit Kolleginnen und Kollegen wahrgenommen. Für 60 Prozent sei zudem kollegiale Unterstützung als bestes Format wahrgenommen worden.
Umstellung der Verwaltung im nördlichsten Bundesland
«Mich hat vor allem überrascht, wie gut eine Verwaltung einen so tiefgreifenden und anspruchsvollen Transformationsprozess bewältigt hat», sagte Peter Ganten, Geschäftsführer von Univetion. «Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass eine solche Veränderung nicht nur technisch machbar ist, sondern
auch von den Beschäftigten angenommen werden kann» Dies sei vor allem für künftige Umstellungen wertvoll und gebe Hinweise darauf, was bereits gut funktioniere.
Nach Angaben der Staatskanzlei vom Januar umfasst die Open Source Strategie des Landes auch weitere Bereiche der Landes-IT. So soll etwa die Software Nextcloud Schritt für Schritt Microsoft SharePoint als zentrale Plattform für Zusammenarbeit ablösen. Diese werde bereits in zahlreichen Verwaltungen genutzt. Auch werde etwa der Einsatz des Betriebssystems Linux als Alternative zu Windows erprobt.
FDP fordert Prüfung der IT-Strukturen der Justiz
Die Justiz wird durch die Umstellung laut FDP beeinträchtigt. Daher haben die Liberalen einen Antrag in die kommende Landtagssitzung eingebracht, worin die Landesregierung aufgefordert werden soll, die IT-Strukturen der Justiz durch einen externen Dienstleister auf ihre Leistungsfähigkeit prüfen zu lassen.
Wie es in dem Antrag heißt, ist die schleswig-holsteinische Justiz zunehmenden Belastungen ausgesetzt. Gründe seien unter anderem steigende Eingangszahlen, eine an vielen Stellen unzureichende personelle Ausstattung und neue Aufgabenbereiche. So dürfe sich nicht auch die Digitalisierung zulasten der Leistungsfähigkeit der Justiz auswirken.

articles.title: Gears of War: E-Day GPU Benchmark: 44 GPUs Tested
articles.text:
Gears of War: E-Day is the latest blockbuster entry in Microsoft's long-running shooter franchise. And if you want to play it but your GPU isn't quite up to the task, or you're wondering what the best upgrade might be, we've tested 44 of them, so that should help you work it out.
Developed by The Coalition, E-Day is a prequel set 14 years before the original Gears of War, following younger versions of Marcus Fenix and Dom Santiago as they experience the Locust invasion on Emergence Day. It's also the studio's first Gears title built from the ground up on Unreal Engine 5 and DirectX 12, with The Coalition describing it as its most technically ambitious Gears game to date.
Gears of War: E-Day has a built-in benchmark which we found to be pretty good, so for ease of testing, and to let you directly compare your results with ours, we're using the benchmark tool. We did have to use separate performance-monitoring software to record 1% lows, as the game doesn't report that data.
We tested the game using the Medium and Ultra presets. We skipped Ludicrous for the bulk of our testing because performance was horrible for what amounts to a minimal visual improvement, though we have included some preset-scaling data that we'll look at first. We also tested the Ultra preset in two configurations: first at native resolution, and then with upscaling enabled, using DLSS on GeForce GPUs and FSR on Radeon and Arc GPUs.
We've applied the maximum amount of upscaling we generally recommend at each resolution: Quality at 1080p, Balanced at 1440p, and Performance at 4K. Our standard Ryzen 7 9800X3D test system was used for all testing, along with the latest available display drivers. With that, let's get into the results.
Test System Specs
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D | 
| Motherboard | MSI MPG X870E Carbon WiFi [BIOS 7E49v1AA7] | 
| Memory | G.Skill Trident Z5 RGB DDR5-6000 32GB CL30 [CL30-38-38-96] | 
| ATX Case | MSI Prospect 700R | 
| Power Supply | Kolink Regulator Gold ATX 3.0 1200W | 
| Storage | TeamGroup T-Force Cardea A440 M.2 PCIe Gen4 NVMe SSD 4TB | 
| Operating System | Windows 11 25H2 | 
| Display Driver | AMD Radeon Adrenalin 26.8.1 Nvidia GeForce Game Ready Driver 617.14 Intel Arc Graphics 32.0.101.9034 | 
Benchmarks
Preset Scaling: Ludicrous Is Not Worth It
Starting with preset scaling at 1440p, comparing the Radeon RX 9070 XT and GeForce RTX 5070 Ti, we see that with the maximum Ludicrous preset enabled, the GeForce GPU takes the lead, coming in 11% faster than the Radeon GPU. However, dropping down to the Ultra preset leaves the two GPUs virtually tied, with the 9070 XT holding a negligible 1% advantage.
More importantly, moving from Ludicrous to Ultra delivers a massive performance improvement. Average frame rates increase by 97% on the 9070 XT and 74% on the RTX 5070 Ti.
Both GPUs see another substantial 22% performance increase when dropping from Ultra to High, where average frame rates remain neck-and-neck. Moving from High to Medium provides a further 11 – 13% boost, with the Radeon GPU beginning to pull slightly ahead with a 3% lead.
Finally, dropping from Medium to Low increases average frame rates by another 21 – 22%, with the 9070 XT extending its lead over the RTX 5070 Ti to just under 5%.
Ultra Preset
1080p
For our first full GPU comparison, we're using the Ultra preset at native resolution, starting with 1080p. The RTX 5090 rendered 139 fps, making it 29% faster than the RTX 4090, which averaged 108 fps. The RTX 5080 followed closely behind at 102 fps.
In another very tight matchup, the RX 9070 XT edged out the RTX 5070 Ti, delivering 98 fps compared with 95 fps for the Nvidia GPU.
The standard RX 9070 and RX 7900 XT both averaged 88 fps, keeping them well ahead of the RTX 5070, which tied the RX 9070 GRE at 76 fps. This means the RTX 5070 Ti maintains a substantial 25% performance advantage over the standard RTX 5070.
Interestingly, at 1080p, VRAM capacity isn't a limiting factor for most 8GB cards. The 16GB and 8GB versions of the RTX 5060 Ti, RX 9060 XT, and RTX 4060 Ti perform identically, delivering 59 fps, 58 fps, and 50 fps, respectively, regardless of memory capacity.
However, the 4GB RX 9050 managed just 21 fps compared with 33 fps for the 8GB version, demonstrating that 4GB is heavily bottlenecked even at 1080p. Well, that and the fact that AMD halved the memory bandwidth on the 4GB OEM model.
Below 30 fps, cards such as the RX 6650 XT and RTX 3050 begin to struggle, suggesting that lower quality settings will be required.
1440p
Stepping up to 1440p significantly increases the strain on the GPUs. Here, the RTX 5090 averaged 111 fps, making it 37% faster than the RTX 4090 at 81 fps.
The RTX 5080 managed 75 fps, trailing the RTX 4090 by a relatively small margin. Meanwhile, the RX 9070 XT and RTX 5070 Ti were again virtually tied, delivering 69 fps and 68 fps, respectively.
Further down the stack, the standard RTX 5070 managed 53 fps, meaning the RTX 5070 Ti extends its lead over its sibling to 28%. The RX 9070 GRE sits just behind the RTX 5070 at 52 fps, while the RTX 3090 isn't far behind at 49 fps.
As at 1080p, an 8GB VRAM capacity doesn't heavily bottleneck these mid-range cards at 1440p. The 16GB and 8GB versions of the RTX 5060 Ti at 40 fps, RX 9060 XT at 39 fps, and RTX 4060 Ti at 33 fps continue to perform identically. Budget options start dropping into the 20s and teens, with the RX 9050 4GB falling to an unplayable 14 fps.
4K
Moving up to 4K, basically nothing can render the game at a high refresh rate using native resolution and the Ultra preset. The RTX 5090 stands alone as the only GPU capable of breaking the 60 fps barrier, averaging 70 fps and making it 40% faster than the RTX 4090, which managed just 50 fps.
The RTX 5080 trails further behind at 42 fps, while the RX 7900 XTX manages 39 fps. The RTX 5070 Ti and RX 9070 XT remain close, averaging 37 fps and 36 fps, respectively, putting them roughly in line with the RTX 4080. The standard RTX 5070 and RTX 3090 both finish deadlocked at a modest 28 fps.
The VRAM situation changes more noticeably at 4K, where 8GB begins to become a problem, though frame rates are already extremely low even with the 16GB models.
The 16GB RTX 5060 Ti managed a meager 21 fps, while its 8GB sibling collapsed to just 13 fps, giving the 16GB model a massive 61% performance advantage. Of course, both are effectively unusable here. Similarly, the 16GB RX 9060 XT delivered 20 fps compared with 16 fps for the 8GB version, giving the higher-capacity model a 25% advantage.
Below this point, it's fair to say we've entered unplayable territory by almost any standard. Even the higher-end GPUs clearly require upscaling with the Ultra preset, especially at 4K, so that's what we'll look at next.
Ultra Preset + Upscaling
1080p: Quality Upscaling
For our 1080p testing, we paired the Ultra preset with Quality upscaling, using DLSS for GeForce GPUs and FSR for Radeon and Arc GPUs. The GeForce RTX 5090 averaged 162 fps, just outpacing the RTX 5080 at 151 fps, while the previous-generation RTX 4090 trailed both at 139 fps.
Moving down the product stack, a fiercely competitive group emerged between the RTX 5070 Ti, Radeon RX 9070 XT, and standard RX 9070. The RTX 5070 Ti edged out the competition at 127 fps, but the RX 9070 XT and RX 9070 were right on its heels at 125 fps and 124 fps, respectively. All three newer GPUs also managed to outperform the previous-generation RTX 4080, which topped out at 120 fps.
Further down the graph, the RTX 5070 averaged 109 fps, effectively tying the RTX 4070 Ti Super while sitting 15 fps behind the standard RX 9070.
As expected, 8GB of VRAM was entirely sufficient under these conditions. The 16GB and 8GB versions of the RTX 5060 Ti performed identically at 87 fps. The same was true for the Radeon RX 9060 XT models, which both delivered 85 fps, and the RTX 4060 Ti variants, which each reached 75 fps.
For around 60 fps, older hardware such as the RX 6800 or RTX 3060 Ti will do the job. Current-generation entry-level products fell a little short, with the RTX 5050 averaging 57 fps and the RX 9050 8GB managing just 44 fps. Near the very bottom of the graph, the 4GB Radeon RX 9050 struggled significantly, averaging just 38 fps with 1% lows of 29 fps.
1440p: Balanced Upscaling
Stepping up to a 1440p output resolution, we used the Ultra preset with Balanced upscaling. As you'd expect, the RTX 5090 maintained its dominant position at the top of the graph, delivering an impressive 152 fps average. In a notable shift from the 1080p results, the older RTX 4090 overtook the RTX 5080, rendering 126 fps compared with 119 fps for the newer GPU.
Then, in the highly contested upper mid-range or high-end segment, depending on what you want to call it these days, the RTX 5070 Ti widened its lead slightly over the AMD competition, averaging 112 fps. The RX 9070 XT followed at 109 fps, while the standard RX 9070 managed 106 fps, putting it in a dead heat with the RTX 4080.
The standard RTX 5070 dropped to 94 fps, placing it slightly behind the RTX 4070 Ti Super and RX 7900 XT. That left the RTX 5070 trailing the 5070 Ti by a substantial 18 fps.
Crucially, 8GB of VRAM remained a non-issue despite the higher 1440p output resolution. Gears of War: E-Day doesn't use a huge amount of VRAM under these settings, and the lower internal render resolution of Balanced upscaling also helps keep memory usage in check. The RTX 5060 Ti 16GB and 8GB models remained perfectly tied at 73 fps. The RX 9060 XT 16GB and 8GB variants also delivered identical performance at 69 fps, while both versions of the RTX 4060 Ti managed 61 fps.
Below the 60 fps threshold, older and budget-oriented hardware begins to struggle. The RTX 3060 and Intel Arc B580, for example, both averaged around 40 fps.
4K: Performance Upscaling
Moving to a 4K output resolution, we used the Ultra preset with Performance upscaling. Even with upscaling doing much of the heavy lifting, the RTX 5090 was the only GPU to break into triple digits, averaging an impressive 125 fps. The RTX 4090 followed at 99 fps, re-establishing a comfortable lead over the newer RTX 5080, which managed 86 fps.
An interesting shift occurred further down the graph, where the Radeon GPUs handled this configuration particularly well. The RX 9070 XT overtook the RTX 5070 Ti, averaging 82 fps compared with 78 fps for the GeForce GPU. The standard RX 9070 also performed exceptionally well, matching the RTX 4080 at 76 fps. Meanwhile, the standard RTX 5070 struggled to keep pace with its immediate competitors, dropping to 62 fps. That placed it just behind the older RX 7900 GRE and the RX 9070 GRE, both of which averaged 63 fps.
One of the more interesting takeaways from the 4K upscaling results is how well the 8GB graphics cards hold up. Unlike native 4K rendering, where limited VRAM caused serious problems for some models, Performance upscaling uses a much lower internal render resolution, which keeps memory demands under control.
As a result, the 16GB and 8GB versions of the RX 9060 XT performed identically at 47 fps. The RTX 5060 Ti 16GB and 8GB models likewise tied at 46 fps, while both RTX 4060 Ti configurations delivered 40 fps.
Heavy upscaling therefore not only eliminates the VRAM-related performance deficits seen at native 4K, but also makes the game reasonably playable on hardware such as the RTX 5060 Ti and RX 9060 XT.
Medium Preset
1080p
Moving on to the Medium preset, we'll again start with the 1080p data. Here, the GeForce RTX 5090 averaged 173 fps while maintaining 1% lows of 103 fps. Behind the flagship, we once again see a tightly contested battle for second place. The RTX 5080 edged out the immediate competition at 136 fps, but the RTX 4090 and RX 9070 XT were right behind it, rendering 135 fps and 134 fps, respectively.
Further down the stack, the RTX 5070 Ti produced 128 fps, narrowly beating both the standard RX 9070 and older RX 7900 XTX, which tied at 126 fps. A significant performance gap emerged between Nvidia's 70-class siblings, as the standard RTX 5070 managed just 107 fps. That left it trailing the RTX 5070 Ti by 21 fps and placed it almost directly alongside the RX 9070 GRE at 106 fps.
Notably, the Medium preset at 1080p is very light on video memory, meaning 8GB graphics cards face no VRAM bottlenecks. The 16GB and 8GB versions of the RX 9060 XT performed identically at 84 fps, while both RTX 5060 Ti models delivered 83 fps. The RTX 4060 Ti variants were also tied at 68 fps.
The only obvious memory-related struggle came at the very bottom of the graph, where the 4GB RX 9050 topped out at 37 fps, falling well behind 8GB budget options such as the Radeon RX 7600 at 49 fps.
1440p
Increasing the resolution to native 1440p adds more GPU load, though the RTX 5090 still managed an average of 143 fps with a rock-solid 1% low of 100 fps. In another shift from the 1080p results, the older RTX 4090 overtook the RTX 5080, delivering 108 fps compared with 101 fps for the newer card.
The Radeon RX 9070 XT maintained a strong position, averaging 95 fps and successfully outpacing the RTX 5070 Ti. Further down, the standard RTX 5070 found itself trading blows with the RX 9070 GRE at 73 fps and RTX 4070 Ti Super at 76 fps.
Once again, VRAM capacity proved irrelevant for the 8GB models under these settings. The RTX 5060 Ti 16GB and 8GB versions were deadlocked at 56 fps, exactly matching both RX 9060 XT variants, which also delivered 56 fps. At the bottom of the stack, budget hardware begins to crumble, with the RTX 3050 8GB falling to 22 fps and the 4GB RX 9050 managing just 24 fps.
4K
Pushing the game to native 4K using the Medium preset severely limits frame rates across the board. As a result, the RTX 5090 remains the only GPU capable of providing what we'd consider a high-refresh-rate experience.
Nvidia's flagship averaged 93 fps, beating the RTX 4090 by 39%. The RTX 5080 fell further behind the 4090, averaging just 58 fps. Below that, the RX 9070 XT and RTX 5070 Ti were effectively tied at 52 fps and 51 fps, respectively. Both also performed similarly to the older RTX 4080 and RX 7900 XTX, which averaged around 50 fps. Further down the graph, the standard RTX 5070 managed just 39 fps, tying the RX 9070 GRE and RTX 3090.
One of the more surprising aspects of the 4K Medium results is the complete absence of the 8GB VRAM bottleneck seen with the Ultra preset. Medium keeps memory usage low enough that the 16GB and 8GB versions of the RTX 5060 Ti perform identically at 29 fps. Likewise, the 16GB and 8GB RX 9060 XT cards both averaged 28 fps, while the two RTX 4060 Ti configurations each delivered 24 fps.
Avoiding a VRAM bottleneck doesn't help much when the GPUs simply lack the raw horsepower for native 4K, however. All of these mid-range models remain below 30 fps, while cards such as the RTX 3050 and RX 9050 fall all the way to a measly 11 fps.
Strong Visuals, Sensible Hardware Requirements
So there you have it. Gears of War: E-Day is a great-looking game that's also relatively easy to run. Our only real criticism is the noticeable amount of ray-tracing noise when using the Ultra preset, though Tim covered a few tweaks that can improve image quality in his separate optimization guide.
For those targeting Ultra settings at 1080p, averaging around 60 fps is possible with GPUs such as the RX 9060 XT and RTX 5060 Ti, as well as older hardware including the RTX 3080, RTX 4070, and RX 7800 XT.
Native 1440p is more demanding, as you'll need something around a Radeon RX 9070, GeForce RTX 4080, or faster to reach 60 fps. That said, if you're comfortable enabling Balanced upscaling, the requirements drop considerably. Even an RTX 4060 Ti 8GB can deliver around 60 fps under those conditions.
The really good news is that the game still looks great using the Medium preset, and achieving 60 fps at native 1080p is relatively easy. Older GPUs such as the RTX 3060 Ti and RX 6750 XT work well here. Even at 1440p, previous-generation mid-range hardware can provide a solid experience, particularly if you're willing to enable upscaling.
Another positive is that VRAM capacity generally isn't a major concern in this title. The 8GB GPUs performed well throughout our testing, with little to no difference between otherwise identical 8GB and 16GB models under most settings. Even the 4GB RX 9050 wasn't always limited primarily by its small VRAM buffer, though its reduced memory bandwidth was clearly a problem. Using the lowest settings we tested, the 8GB model was still 35% faster.
Unfortunately, Intel's Arc GPUs are a different story. They currently perform very poorly in Gears of War: E-Day, with the Arc B580 often falling behind even the Radeon RX 9050. Hopefully that's something Intel can address with a future driver update.
Overall, Gears of War: E-Day strikes a good balance between visual quality and performance. Ultra can be demanding at higher resolutions, particularly without upscaling, but Medium looks surprisingly good and makes the game accessible to a much wider range of GPUs.

articles.title: Responsible AI governance: How AWS positions customers to align with ISO/IEC 42005:2025 | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Responsible AI governance: How AWS positions customers to align with ISO/IEC 42005:2025
With generative AI adoption moving faster than the personal computer or the internet and global AI-related investment in 2025 representing $581.69 billion, organizations must position their workforce to use AI to power their operations while employing it responsibly. Researchers affiliated with the AI Adoption Initiative argue that the workforce relates to AI through an AI Labor Stack comprised of AI innovators, facilitators, and users, and that facilitators are often “the missing middle” in national AI strategies though they are responsible for “translat[ing] AI capability into practical deployment across firms, sectors, and public services.” (Ferrone et al., 2026).
We support this facilitator population in instituting or improving systematic approaches to AI governance within their organization through review of the international standard ISO/IEC 42005:2025, exploring its guidance on how to efficiently integrate AI impact assessments into their broader governance ecosystem.
Standards-based governance frameworks offer a practical path forward — and AWS has invested in making them actionable. At Amazon we have been proponents of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards development projects for AI risk management, both as certifications we have achieved for multiple AI services (Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Q Business, Amazon Transcribe, and Amazon Textract), and as something we advocate for our customers to use for certifying their own services. Amazon Web Services (AWS) offers tools to support governance work aligned with ISO/IEC 42005 and other responsible AI best practices, including our ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI Management Systems (AIMS) implementation guide on AWS and our Well-Architected Framework: Responsible AI Lens that can assist customers in using this standard in their enterprise risk management ecosystems. In this post we explore the AI system impact assessment: what it is, how it improves enterprise-wide risk management, and how ISO/IEC 42005 codifies AI system impact assessment best practices.
AI system impact assessments
An AI system impact assessment is a documented process of AI system risk identification by which organizations developing, providing, or using AI systems consider impacts to the organization, individuals, communities, groups, and societies. An AI system impact assessment process also channels its outputs, such as identification of privacy impacts, discriminatory impacts, or performance impacts, into the organization’s risk management decisions. Using an AI system impact assessment process helps organizations responsibly manage their AI deployments, choosing appropriate guardrails to manage identified risks.
AI impact assessments facilitate enterprise-wide risk management
AI system impact assessments are an integral part of an organization’s overall risk management process. ISO/IEC 42005 provides explicit guidance on how to integrate AI system impact assessments into existing impact assessment processes within an enterprise, which often include different kinds of impact assessments for IT systems (for example, risk, privacy, cybersecurity).
For organizations with a robust impact assessment ecosystem, Annex D of ISO/IEC 42005 provides a process that organizations can use to simplify impact assessments and avoid duplication, helping organizations coordinate the relevant reviews required by an AI system impact assessment (for example, risk, legal, security, privacy, procurement, or architecture).
For organizations that prefer a standalone AI impact assessment, Annex E of ISO/IEC 42005 provides a ready-to-use template for self-contained implementation.
How ISO/IEC 42005 connects you to your AI governance process
ISO/IEC 42005 unlocks a more integrated AI governance process for customers. Specifically, the standard provides guidance on how to develop the content of AI system impact assessments, how to perform AI system impact assessments, when to integrate AI system impact assessments within the stages of the AI lifecycle, and how to document the AI system impact assessment process and its outcomes.
Creating repeatable and scalable AI system impact assessment processes
Customers aiming to develop a structured, consistent approach to performing and documenting AI system impact assessments will find guidance in ISO/IEC 42005. The standard specifically covers the full assessment life cycle (including scoping and execution, analysis and reporting, and ongoing monitoring and review), and it also identifies when an AI system impact assessment should be conducted, how comprehensive it should be, and how to establish reassessment triggers.
When establishing the timing for assessment and reassessment that fit within the broader AI development lifecycle, the standard recommends considering what triggers (evaluating both external and internal factors) might point to the need for a reassessment, for example, applicable legal requirements, contractual obligations, internal policies, customer expectations, changes (to the AI system, its operational environment, or its context) that might necessitate reassessment, and other factors. The standard explains how to conduct a lighter AI system impact assessment triage, a quick classification to identify whether a more comprehensive assessment is needed or not (depending on level of risk), before committing to a full assessment or reassessment.
Designing assessments: The questions your assessment needs to answer
Customers looking for where to start with establishing AI system impact assessments will find ISO/IEC 42005 specifies the specific information that should be documented in an AI system impact assessment via a templated assessment approach, explaining how to also leverage other risk assessments the enterprise may already be conducting to avoid duplication. Documentation should include items such as:
- A description of the AI system and its intended uses
- How it could foreseeably be misused
- The data used to develop the AI system, its underlying components and algorithms
- The environment in which it will be deployed
- The individuals and communities who may be affected by the AI system.
ISO/IEC 42005 provides a methodology for organizations to identify both positive and negative impacts of AI systems by considering how the system can be used and misused. The standard helps you implement your responsible AI principles because it uses a variety of AI objectives that you might choose to prioritize (for example, fairness, reliability, privacy, and security) as the rubric for harm and benefit impact evaluation. The standard also outlines considerations for stakeholder identification and consultation in the AI system impact assessment process, including encouraging solicitation of inputs from diverse communities and integration of these inputs into the assessment.
Supporting ISO/IEC 42001 certification
For organizations pursuing ISO/IEC 42001 certification, ISO/IEC 42005 provides helpful guidance on how to address AI impact assessment as a key control of ISO/IEC 42001. Annex A specifically details how ISO/IEC 42005 supports ISO/IEC 42001 requirements.
At AWS, we offer ISO/IEC 42001 accredited certification for AI services, covering: Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Q Business, Amazon Textract, and Amazon Transcribe. Based on our experience, we have developed AWS best practices, including how AI impact assessment can support organizations on their Responsible AI journey.
AWS responsible AI tools to support your responsible AI journey
The AWS Well-Architected Responsible AI Lens assists builder teams in responsibly building and operating AI solutions for specific use cases. The AWS Responsible AI Lens aligns closely with the ISO/IEC 42005 standard:
- Benefits and harms identification: Both guide builders to identify expected benefits and potential harms.
- Risk management integration: Both prioritize the integration of the outcomes of risk identification and analysis into risk treatment decisions and mitigations.
- Lifecycle integration: Both position impact assessments as integral to the AI development lifecycle, not as a one-time compliance exercise.
AWS additionally shared in May 2026 our latest compliance guide, ISO/IEC 42001 implementation on AWS, which guides organizations designing and operating AIMS using AWS services.
Conclusion
International standards like ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO/IEC 42005 support trust, interoperability, and accountability, which drive AI innovation and deployment across varied global environments. Our commitment to building tools to support alignment with these standards gives our customers independent validation of AWS commitment to responsible AI development and deployment, and models for customers how AWS AI services can accelerate their compliance journey.
Disclaimer: The risk assessment and impact assessment guidance shared in this blog are intended to provide general direction and practical insight into implementing AI risk management under ISO/IEC 42001, aligning with ISO/IEC 42005, and establishing AI risk management infrastructure. However, organizations are responsible for conducting their own context-specific risk assessments, as mandated by the standard and by regulators. This blog should not be interpreted as an exhaustive approach to or guarantee of compliance with any risk management standards or laws.

articles.title: Hamburg’s Procuros raises €20 million Series A to build AI-native infrastructure for autonomous B2B trade | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Procuros, a Hamburg-based supply chain connectivity platform, has raised a €20 million Series A funding round.
The round was led by XAnge, a European venture capital firm based in Paris and Berlin with around €600 million in assets under management and part of the Siparex Group. W23, a global venture capital fund backed by five leading grocery retailers, joined as a new investor, with existing backers Point Nine, Creandum, and b2venture following on, alongside several angel investors. The Series A funding round comes after the company had raised €1 million pre-Seed in 2021 and €8.3 million Seed in 2022.
“Procuros is showing that AI agents can make autonomous B2B trade a reality today. The team has built the infrastructure AI agents need to work across entire trading networks and proven the model at scale in DACH. What excites us is the opportunity ahead: to take this beyond its home market and establish an entirely new category for global B2B trade,” said Valerie Bures-Bönström, Partner and Managing Director DACH at XAnge.
Founded in 2021 by Patrick Thelen and Benjamin Bradford, Procuros serves suppliers and retailers with a connectivity platform that acts as the agentic data layer for B2B trade. It is built on a simple premise: businesses connect to Procuros once and can immediately exchange data with any trading partner, regardless of what systems, formats, or technical setups those partners use. The platform is designed to validate data on both sides of a transaction, eliminating the need for complex point-to-point integrations.
For suppliers, Procuros automates the flow of orders, shipping notices, invoices, and logistics workflows directly into ERP systems, eliminating manual data entry. For retailers, it delivers a fully digital supplier connectivity platform covering EDI connections, e-invoicing, and automated invoice reconciliation. The company claims its platform has 99%+ data accuracy and up to 95% less manual processing.
From purchase orders and dispatch advice to invoices, the global supply chain handles millions of documents every day, but the infrastructure behind it is old, and many transactions still arrive in the form of PDFs, spreadsheets, or even fax. Procuros believes AI can change that, and its platform is the connectivity layer.
“AI is advancing at incredible speed, while supply chains still run on infrastructure built decades ago. Operations teams are forced to bridge these gaps between systems that simply don’t communicate. We built Procuros to change that. Our infrastructure gives retailers, suppliers and AI agents the connectivity and trusted data they need to automate trade and make autonomous supply chains possible. Because ultimately, AI agents are only as good as the infrastructure they run on,” said Thelen, CEO and co-founder of Procuros.
Procuros already has more than 300 customers across DACH and the UK, including Breuninger, Chefs Culinar, KoRo, flaconi, The Quality Group (ESN), and Hitschler. The company says it has more than €3 billion in annualised order volume flowing through the platform.
The Series A funding will be used across three main areas: scaling Procuros’ go-to-market operations, further developing its AI-native supply chain infrastructure, and driving international expansion beyond its home markets in DACH and the UK into the rest of Europe and the United States.

articles.title: Feds say moving defence procurement to Crown corp will make it “more commercial, more fleet-footed” | BetaKit
articles.text:
The federal government is looking to overhaul its defence procurement processes yet again, this time by making the fledgling Defence Investment Agency (DIA) into a Crown corporation.
Procurement minister Joël Lightbound introduced Bill C-40, also known as the Canadian Corporation for Defence Investment Act, into the House of Commons on Tuesday morning. The bill would create the Canadian Corporation for Defence Investment, the legal name for what will continue to operate as the DIA.
“With the introduction of this legislation, we are making clear that large-scale, agile defence production and procurement is here to stay,” Lightbound said in a statement. “Procurement and investment must live together, by connecting the capabilities our armed forces need with the investments that will deliver them and the industrial capacity that will sustain them.”
“Gone are the days where a government takes three bids, takes the lowest bidder, and we move on with our lives.”
The federal government created the DIA almost exactly one year ago to overhaul military procurement processes that the defence industry said were plagued by inefficiencies. At the moment, the DIA is housed within Public Services and Procurement Canada and directly led by CEO Doug Guzman, a former RBC deputy chair and Goldman Sachs managing director, and overseen by defence procurement secretary of state Stephen Fuhr.
This new version of the DIA will have more independence and authority to negotiate and manage defence production, contracts, and investment under criteria established by the Department of National Defence (DND) and the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF), according to the draft legislation.
“Gone are the days where a government takes three bids, takes the lowest bidder, and we move on with our lives,” Fuhr said at a Tuesday afternoon press conference.
Under C-40, the DIA will operate at arm’s length, with its own CEO, an executive chairperson, and board of directors. In addition to the CEO and chairperson, the board will contain a deputy minister and up to two other directors. The DIA will be housed under the DND portfolio and report to a new Associate Minister of National Defence for Procurement.
Notably, Crown corporations do not fall under the procurement Ombudsman’s mandate, meaning the new DIA won’t be subjected to its oversight. When asked at the press conference if the federal government would expand the procurement Ombudsman’s mandate, Fuhr said he didn’t have an answer, and that the DIA’s oversight would be ministerial.
Earlier, in his own remarks, defence minister David McGuinty said the new DIA will be “more efficient, more professional, more commercial, [and] more fleet-footed” in acquiring goods the CAF requires with the money it’s delegated.
RELATED: Evaluating Canada’s Defence Industrial Strategy
“It’s important to remember that National Defence will still be subject to Treasury Board submissions,” McGuinty said. “We will be subject to the scrutiny of committees. We will be subject to the power of Finance and Treasury Board and the Privy Council Office asking their important and probative questions, so this is not a question of delegating all of this authority to a Crown.”
The DIA positions that bringing procurement, production, and investment functions together under a single organization allows it to make decisions more quickly, reduce fragmentation, and “provide greater continuity and predictability across defence acquisitions.” In a technical briefing, senior government officials said the new structure would make it easier for the DIA to retain experts on certain procurements, or draw from expertise on its board of directors. At the press conference, Fuhr and McGuinty also waved attracting talent outside of the public service as a benefit. McGuinty just made his own outside recruitment, appointing longtime Council of Canadian Innovators chief strategy officer Dana O’Born as his chief of staff this week.
Canada has been pushing to fortify its sovereign and military capabilities, earmarking nearly $82 billion in last year’s budget to help “rebuild, rearm, and reinvest” in the Canadian Armed Forces. This included almost $7 billion to build Canada’s defence industrial base under the Defence Industrial Strategy, which is supported by the DIA.
Feature image courtesy Mark Carney via LinkedIn.

articles.title: Qualcomm Licenses Huawei's LogicFolding, 5G, and Other Technologies
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 6th 2026
Qualcomm Licenses Huawei's LogicFolding, 5G, and Other Technologies
Qualcomm announced today that it is officially licensing technology from Chinese technology giant Huawei. In a deal estimated to be worth $6.9 billion upon completion, Qualcomm will license various technologies from Huawei to integrate across its product portfolio. According to official releases, these technologies include computing, AI, networking, and more. Bloomberg reports that the deal also covers Huawei's latest LogicFolding silicon design. This is a significant win for Huawei, whose R&D teams have spent years designing a way to bypass sanctions and overcome manufacturing technology limits. By stacking silicon vertically across two sheets, LogicFolding dramatically reduces the distance between compute elements, increases efficiency, and significantly improves transistor density. The result is a 55% increase in transistor density and a 41% boost in power efficiency.
Update, 06:30 UTC, October 6: Qualcomm issued a statement that dismantles rumors that the company is licensing LogicFolding technology.
QualcommQualcomm and Huawei entered into a multi-year, broad patent license agreement that includes cross-licenses across a range of technology fields. The terms are confidential, but reports characterizing Qualcomm as a net payor on the license agreement are incorrect. In addition, assertions that the agreement is related to LogicFold are not accurate. Separately, Qualcomm has agreed to purchase certain Huawei non-cellular U.S. patents across multiple technology areas.
Since Huawei lacks access to manufacturing its silicon using EUV lithography, it uses DUV machines with LogicFolding to work around this limitation. Even so, the company claims that LogicFolding on its domestic node production will achieve a transistor density equivalent to a 1.4 nm node by 2031. For Qualcomm, whose access to advanced lithography is unrestricted, this means the company can potentially surpass Moore's Law by stacking multiple sheets of cutting-edge silicon, achieving massive boosts in transistor density and power efficiency.
This agreement will be completed after regulatory approvals are secured. Huawei sees it as a way to collaborate with the industry and share its technology under fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) principles. For other technologies, Huawei's development and contributions to 4G and 5G standards are so advanced that they lead in some areas, such as near-physical-limit signal transmission technology using polar codes. Qualcomm will utilize these technologies in building its own modems and designs, selecting only what best suits its use cases.
Sources:

articles.title: Paramount e Warner Bros. vão cortar empregos após fusão
articles.text:
A fusão entre Paramount e Warner Bros. Discovery criou oficialmente nesta terça-feira (6) a Skydance, um dos maiores conglomerados de entretenimento de Hollywood. Mas o primeiro dia da nova empresa também veio acompanhado de uma notícia ruim para os funcionários: a integração das duas companhias deverá provocar demissões.
Em um memorando enviado aos funcionários e intitulado “Day 1”, o presidente e CEO da Skydance, David Ellison, e o co-CEO Ynon Kreiz reconheceram que a união das duas empresas envolverá “decisões difíceis” que terão impacto sobre os trabalhadores.
A companhia ainda não divulgou quantas pessoas serão demitidas. Um relatório do condado de Los Angeles (EUA), citado pela Variety, porém, estima que a fusão poderá resultar na perda de cerca de 4,5 mil empregos nos setores de cinema e televisão da região ao longo de três anos.
A expectativa é de que a primeira onda de cortes aconteça antes do fim de 2026, enquanto novas rodadas podem ocorrer posteriormente.
Meta é economizar bilhões
- Os cortes estão diretamente relacionados ao esforço da nova companhia para reduzir custos. A Paramount estabeleceu uma meta de alcançar mais de US$ 6 bilhões (cerca de R$ 32 bilhões) em economia anual ao longo de três anos;
- Parte dessa redução deverá vir justamente das demissões;
- No memorando, Ellison e Kreiz afirmaram que a integração pretende reunir os recursos, marcas e talentos de Paramount e Warner Bros. Discovery para criar uma empresa de mídia e entretenimento com maior escala;
- A proposta, segundo os executivos, não é simplesmente somar as estruturas das duas companhias, mas integrá-las para formar uma organização única;
- A mensagem marca o início oficial das operações da Skydance após a conclusão da fusão.
Uma gigante de Hollywood
A nova empresa reúne dois grandes estúdios de cinema, dezenas de canais de televisão, serviços de streaming e operações de notícias que pertenciam aos dois conglomerados.
A Skydance passa a controlar, portanto, um enorme conjunto de marcas e propriedades de entretenimento.
A companhia será comandada por David Ellison e Ynon Kreiz, que assumirão, respectivamente, os cargos de CEO e co-CEO.
A fusão foi concluída nesta terça-feira, depois de uma longa trajetória marcada por disputas e obstáculos legais. Agora, um dos principais desafios da administração será justamente integrar as duas estruturas sem perder a capacidade de produção e, ao mesmo tempo, atingir as metas financeiras estabelecidas para o novo conglomerado.
A própria liderança reconheceu no memorando que ainda há um processo de integração pela frente.
Leia mais:
- IA do McDonald’s gera polêmica e caso vai parar na Justiça dos EUA
- Como o ‘Pix colombiano’ superou o crescimento do modelo do Brasil
- OpenAI pede desculpas e admite falha na resposta a ataque de agentes de IA
Por que haverá demissões?
A sobreposição entre as estruturas de Paramount e Warner Bros. Discovery é um dos principais motivos para os cortes previstos.
Com duas empresas passando a funcionar como uma só, determinadas áreas e funções precisarão ser reorganizadas. A redução da força de trabalho aparece, nesse contexto, como uma das ferramentas para diminuir os custos da companhia.
Segundo a Variety, fontes do setor esperam que os cortes continuem em novas rodadas depois da primeira onda, avançando também para 2027.
A estimativa de 4,5 mil postos eliminados, porém, refere-se especificamente à região de Los Angeles e foi apresentada em um relatório do condado. O número total de demissões da Skydance ainda não foi anunciado.
Novo capítulo para Paramount e Warner
Apesar do impacto sobre os funcionários, Ellison e Kreiz apresentaram a fusão como uma oportunidade para construir uma empresa maior e mais competitiva.
No memorando, os executivos afirmaram que a intenção é combinar as estruturas das duas companhias para ampliar a escala e a capacidade de atuação da nova organização.
A mudança representa o início de uma nova fase para marcas históricas de Hollywood. Ao mesmo tempo, para milhares de funcionários, o primeiro capítulo da Skydance começa com a incerteza sobre quem permanecerá na empresa depois da integração.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Licensing costs driving 90 percent of VMware users to explore options: Survey
articles.text:
VMware customers face multiple obstacles as they rethink their virtualization strategy to reduce dependence on VMware.
Today, Rimini Street published its “2026 IT Virtualization Survey – What’s Next for VMware Users.” The survey examined 300 organizations worldwide that use VMware.
Notably, Rimini sells third-party support for VMware and other software, including Oracle and SAP. That means there’s an incentive for Rimini to portray VMware users as experiencing obstacles. However, the survey was also conducted by a third-party research company, Unisphere Research, and the results align with other recent reports about VMware customers.
For example, 90 percent of participants in Rimini’s survey said they’re exploring VMware alternatives due to VMware’s higher licensing costs, while 54 percent pointed to Broadcom killing support for perpetual license holders.
Since Broadcom took over VMware, customers have said that their VMware costs increased by as much as 1,000 percent, with many more pointing to more modest price hikes of around 100 to 300 percent. In Rimini’s survey, 73 percent of participants pointed to cost savings as a top priority in their virtualization roadmap decisions.
“Significant barriers”
In today’s announcement, Rimini pointed to “significant barriers to progress” for organizations exploring virtualization options, with the most cited barriers being operational complexity (named by 40 percent of respondents), multi-vendor management challenges (38 percent), securing the increased attack surface (37 percent), and team skills requirements (37 percent).
“These findings suggest that while organizations are actively pursuing change, they are also looking for ways to reduce risk and avoid unnecessary disruption,” Rimini’s announcement said.
Broadcom’s takeover has spotlighted the challenges of being overly reliant on a single vendor.

Every single Google Pixel 11 phone is on sale right now — here's how to choose between them, and which model I recommend

Every single Pixel 11 model — along with the Google Pixel 10a, which you can currently get from Amazon for $524 / £399 (was $599 / £499) — is on sale now. So between that mid-range option and the higher-end Google Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold, there should be something for just about everyone.
But with so many options, which should you choose? We’ve got you covered there — scroll down for a look at their key differences. But first, here are Amazon’s current Pixel 11 series deals:

How to choose which model to buy
So, which Pixel is right for you? Well, that depends both on your budget and what features you need.
The Google Pixel 10a is the cheapest of these discounted models, but despite not having ‘11’ in the name, it still launched this year — though its Tensor G4 chipset is two generations old, so it’s not exactly a powerhouse.
Still, it runs the same slick Android operating system as other Pixels and comes with the promise of seven major Android version updates. In our Google Pixel 10a review, we also praised its 6.3-inch screen, dual-lens camera (with a 48MP wide sensor and a 13MP ultra-wide), and long-lasting 5,100mAh battery.
So, if you don’t need a big screen or top-end power, this is a strong choice. It’s perfect if you mostly just use your phone for social media, web browsing, and communication.
If you’re fine with a small screen but do want more power — or more capable specs elsewhere — then the Google Pixel 11 might be the phone for you.
This device also has a 6.3-inch display, but it has a new Tensor G6 chipset, 12GB of RAM, and a triple-lens camera, with a 48MP wide one, a 13MP ultra-wide, and a 10.8MP telephoto offering 5x optical zoom.
The Pixel 11 largely has the same strengths and weaknesses as the Pixel 10a while also being better in almost every way — but of course, it also costs more. It’s a better choice if you take a lot of photos, want a telephoto camera, or like to play mobile games.
Next up, there’s the Google Pixel 11 Pro, which again has a 6.3-inch screen, but it can reach a brighter 3,600 nits, and the top (1TB) model of this also comes with more RAM than the Pixel 11, at 16GB. The triple-lens camera is higher spec too, with two 48MP sensors and a 50MP one, all of which combine to make this Google’s best — and priciest — compact phone.
So, buy the 11 Pro if you want a true flagship phone with a smaller display that's capable of running high-end games and the most advanced AI, and can take fantastic photos. It's a strong all-rounder.
If you want a bigger screen than the 11 Pro offers, then you should take a look at the Google Pixel 11 Pro XL — this is largely the same phone as the Pixel 11 Pro but with a bigger 6.8-inch screen and a higher-capacity 5,115mAh battery (up from 4,850mAh in the Pixel 11 Pro).
It has all the same advantages of the Pixel 11 Pro, but it trades a compact design for a screen that’s ideal for watching videos and playing games, and a battery that lasts all day and beyond.
Finally, there’s the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which is the priciest model, but then you are getting two screens — an 8.0-inch foldable one and a 6.5-inch cover screen. So this is the model to buy if you think you might want a phone and tablet all in one.
That said, its camera specs are slightly worse than on the Pro models, so consider whether you really need a phone with two screens — and if you do, then whether buying a separate tablet might not be a better idea.

articles.title: El iPhone 17 vuelve a ser una opción interesante: subió de precio y ahora ha vuelto a bajar
articles.text:
Hace un mes, Apple subió el precio del iPhone 17 por culpa de la crisis de la memoria RAM. Pasó de 959 a 1.109 euros sin actualizarse ni traer mejoras, simplemente aprovecharon el lanzamiento de los nuevos modelos para imponer la nueva cifra. Hoy hay buenas noticias de nuevo: Amazon acaba de rebajarlo otra vez por las ofertas del Prime Day. El precio no es tan atractivo como lo fue en su lanzamiento, pero es posible ahorrar algo de dinero si estabas buscando este móvil concreto.
¿Es el precio más bajo del iPhone 17? No. Ahora bien, si estabas esperando tras la subida de Apple, es la mejor oportunidad que se va a presentar en los próximos meses. El modelo base de 256 GB está disponible en estos momentos por 1.049 euros, lo que supone un descuento de 60 euros. No es muchísimo, pero teniendo en cuenta que Apple nunca lanza ofertas en sus móviles, es mejor que nada.
Además, lo vende y envía la propia Amazon, por lo que cuentas con 3 años de garantía, soporte oficial, envío al día siguiente y el mejor servicio posventa de todo Internet. Y, aunque está disponible en todos los colores, no todos tienen el mismo precio: si quieres ahorrar el máximo, tienes que ir a por el verde.
El resto de colores del iPhone 17, como el negro o el azul, han bajado un poco menos: están disponibles por 1.075 euros. Sigue siendo menos que el precio a pagar en la Apple Store, por lo que si el verde no te convence, seguirás pagando menos que el PVPr.
¿Sigue siendo buena opción el iPhone 17?
Sin duda. Apple no renovó el dispositivo en septiembre como ha hecho todos los años anteriores, por lo que es el iPhone base más actual que puedes comprar. Cuenta con pantalla a 120 Hz, una buena cámara, un diseño compacto, una batería bastante decente y la posibilidad de actualizar a iOS 27 con todas las novedades.
Además, no se espera que el iPhone 18 base llegue con demasiadas novedades en marzo del año que viene, por lo que el iPhone 17 seguirá siendo una buena compra incluso cuando se haya renovado. Sobre todo, por el hecho de poder tenerlo ya sin esperar y ahorrar algo de dinero con esta oferta de Amazon.

articles.title: Here’s how our climate team picked 10 promising companies to watch
articles.text:
Here’s how our climate team picked 10 promising companies to watch
Our reporters and editors evaluated dozens of climate tech companies from around the world for potential impact, scalability, and signs of commercial progress.
As the team at MIT Technology Review set out to choose companies for this year’s edition of our annual list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch, the challenge felt more daunting than any year since we started compiling the list in 2023.
This year is shaping up to be one of the hottest ever recorded. The world must begin to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions to address the climate crisis, which is already affecting communities around the globe. Wildfires, floods, and other climate-fueled disasters are killing thousands and costing billions of dollars. At the same time, political shifts and international conflict have stalled progress, particularly in the US.
Technology alone can’t solve climate change. But we believe innovations can help us make real changes and improve lives around the world as we try to address one of the most pressing challenges of our time.
In this project, we look for companies developing technologies that can help us face the climate crisis. Some are driving down the greenhouse-gas emissions fueling climate change; others are working to reduce the dangers that communities face from extreme heat, drought, or other shifts brought on by a warming planet. We focus on companies that have established a track record, whether through research findings, capital raised, or deployments.
When we set out to build our list, we start by soliciting nominations from our team of reporters and editors. We ask experts for suggestions and reach out to academics, researchers, investors, and analysts. Once we have a pool of nominees, we then consider each one, digging through literature, reports, and patents to vet both the technology and the business.
We judge each company not only on its own merits, but also on how it might fit into our list overall. We want the final slate of companies to represent a range of industries and include firms based around the globe that are at different stages of development. We also aim to strike a balance between highlighting companies previously included and introducing new names. Finally, we consider some of the most important trends and events of the year and look for nominees that reflect those developments.
The dismembering of US federal regulations and cuts to financial government incentives for innovation means that the country is no longer a leader in climate tech. Like last year, the 2026 list is largely composed of companies that are based outside the US. China is an obvious hotspot for technological innovation across energy and climate. This year’s list includes two Chinese companies: WeLion is building semi-solid-state batteries for electric vehicles, and Envision Energy is installing huge amounts of wind power and energy storage in China and around the world.
Several sectors stood out this year as being of particular importance. One of the biggest stories of the year is the rising demand for electricity, driven in part by AI data centers.
Energy storage is a key piece of that puzzle because it can smooth out variations in the electricity supply as grids incorporate more renewable power. We’ve included several energy storage companies on this year’s list. Energy Dome is building long-duration energy storage systems on the grid that rely on compressed carbon dioxide. Moment Energy is a Canadian company working to repurpose EV batteries for grid-scale storage. And Form Energy, which we also included in the 2024 edition of this list, is producing iron-based batteries that can store energy for multiple days.
A wide range of technologies is represented here: everything from mobile flood barriers to next-generation nuclear reactors. Some of the awardees might be familiar from our past coverage; others are just emerging and may be less well known.
We believe we’ve put together a list filled with businesses that are rising to the challenge of this moment. Political will has weakened even as the damages wrought by climate change continue to mount. By helping us make progress on tackling the climate crisis in such difficult times, these companies point to a better way forward.

articles.title: Vinod Khosla believes ex-DeepMind engineer's Wajo will win agent market on trust | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The personal-agent space has become closely competitive in recent weeks, with Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dot, and Instinct taking the lead and more competitors being launched each week. But Vinod Khosla is betting on former Google and DeepMind engineer Shivani Poddar’s Wajo for one simple reason: trust.
“I think the most important thing in an agent, because it’s acting for you, is trust. You have to have trust in the agent, and I think compared to either Muse or Instinct, Wajo is the most trustworthy because it is architected to focus on trust and safety first, and some of the others are not,” Khosla told TechCrunch over a call.
“I mean, who wants to give all their data to Facebook [Meta]? I don’t. And if I give my data to Facebook, I’m the product, not the product I am buying, because they are in the ad business. So trust is important, and most people don’t trust a large company like Facebook,” he added.
In broad strokes, Wajo’s Fo agent works very much like Muse or Instinct. The agent can work across iMessage and WhatsApp, and has a web interface with cards of potential tasks. Errands are organized into categories like “scheduling,” “gifting,” and “life admin.” Its agent can also call businesses or other people on your behalf, booking or canceling services as needed.
In a few early tests, I asked it to call an airline to check for upgrades, and it successfully did so. However, when I asked it to call my partner and remind her to feed the cats, the call didn’t go smoothly, and disclosures were less clear. As rivals like Instinct and Muse are also rolling out calling ability slowly, we might see more discussions around how an AI calling on someone’s behalf should disclose itself. One of the unique things about the tool is that it can hire a human to complete a task when needed.
Apart from this, Fo can create a virtual credit card and pay on your behalf without disclosing your details. The agent also has its own email and can converse with people and businesses. When websites or services block AI agents, Fo can inform the user to take action or create a group with the user and the business for verification.
The startup has also secured backing from Jeff Dean and Gokul Rajaram, but didn’t specify the money raised. Wajo didn’t provide any numbers around users but said that it’s being used in 107 countries and has grown 10x since its launch in late September.
Founder story
Prior to founding Wajo, Poddar worked in various engineering roles at Meta, Google, and DeepMind and was invovled in making the first Facebook assistant. She said that she wanted to build products that were useful to people.
“The whole journey of bringing Gemini to the world and building safety for it made me realize the technological depth that you need to do this. Google is so good in technology that sometimes it can be left behind in product. I thought I needed to do something that is both technology and product at the same time. It has to be something different, which is very grounded in what the user needs,” Poddar told TechCrunch over a call.
The former Google engineering lead mirrored Khosla’s thoughts around trust, and emphasized that it was one of the core principles for Wajo.
“Trust is something you have to build from the get-go because one of the technological things that has not been solved yet is teaching agents to unlearn. If they get access to your personal data on day zero, they will always have it for the future. I think trust needs to be built from day zero, not only in your architecture, but in product choices,” she said.
The company is doing work in a few areas in relation to trust and safety. It has applied for a patent for its virtual card system that hides users’ information from sites. For calls, the company said it will include a “trusted contact” list for users whose agents can call them. When you get a call, you can also tell the agent not to call you again, and Wajo records that preference.
The startup’s challenge is not to raise privacy concerns like other agents, especially as it is marketing safety as a core value. It also claims that despite tools like Muse being blocked by Amazon, its architecture follows the e-commerce service’s terms of service.
Wajo said that in the coming months it will explore how its Fo agent will work in social settings across multiple users, with the core idea of keeping privacy intact.

articles.title: Sebastian Maniscalco’s SiriusXM channel is hurting up-and-coming talent, comics say
articles.text:
Comedian Sebastian Maniscalco is facing backlash from fellow comics who claim his takeover of SiriusXM’s Raw Comedy channel is harming up-and-coming talent, as reported earlier by Deadline. Many established comics, including Patton Oswalt and Margaret Cho, have posted videos online calling on Maniscalco to carry on Raw Comedy’s legacy by highlighting newer comedians on his channel, instead of mostly focusing on well-known ones.
Sebastian Maniscalco’s SiriusXM channel is hurting up-and-coming talent, comics say
Maniscalco’s channel replaced SiriusXM’s Raw Comedy, which highlighted a wider pool of more than 800 comics.
SiriusXM launched Sebastian Maniscalco’s Comedy Radio in April, which is “curated and headlined by Sebastian himself,” according to the satellite radio provider. The move replaced SiriusXM’s long-running Raw Comedy channel featuring uncensored stand-up comedy shows from a range of talent. Now, the channel airs Maniscalco’s own show, alongside a stream of stand-up content that comedian Dan Soder says features “very famous comics who are dead or who don’t necessarily need the money.”
The widespread criticism comes as Stand Up for Standup, a nonprofit organization that provides resources for comedians in need, published a report about the channel’s shift away from emerging talent, who rely not only on the visibility they receive from appearing on the station, but also on the royalties they earn from SiriusXM. The organization says that since March, the spins on Maniscalco’s channels have decreased from a wider net of more than 800 comics to a much narrower pool of 275 artists, largely skewed toward celebrities.
“We believe this shift, both in the overall quantity of artists enjoying plays on Channel 102, and the change in distribution across all spin-getters favoring the top few, is bad for comedians, and bad for the future of comedy,” Stand Up for Standup says.
“There’s a lot of up-and-coming comedians who are depending on the money and the checks that they get from Sirius,” Oswalt says in an Instagram video. “But 500 of them have been booted off of Sirius… You can easily reverse this decision. Get those young comedians back on the Sirius channel. Let them get those checks.” Many other comedians, including Liz Miele, Kyle Kinane, and Michelle Wolf, have called out Maniscalco as well.
In a statement to Deadline, SiriusXM says Maniscalco’s channel “introduced a new creative direction and a regularly evolving programming mix for the channel,” adding that “SiriusXM continues to invest in comedians more than any other audio platform.” Neither SiriusXM nor representatives for Maniscalco immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment.

articles.title: Programmable Memory Controller Eases Adoption of New DRAM Techniques (ETH Zürich, CISPA, NYU)
articles.text:
Researchers at ETH Zürich, CISPA, and New York University published a technical paper titled “Terracotta: Enabling the Adoption of New DRAM Techniques via a Flexible DRAM Interface and Memory Controller.”
Abstract Excerpt:
“DRAM continues to limit the performance, energy efficiency, and robustness of modern systems. Many prior works propose DRAM techniques that support in-DRAM computation, improve memory access latency and parallelism, and enhance DRAM maintenance and reliability. However, adopting each new technique requires repeated modifications to the rigid DRAM interface and memory controller, hindering its deployment. Our goal is to reduce these repeated modifications. We observe that the DRAM commands and memory controller structures of many DRAM techniques are similar. Our key idea is to use these similarities to compose a set of primitives for implementing diverse DRAM techniques. We propose Terracotta, a new framework with two flexible components: (i) custom command extensions that let DRAM vendors define new commands within a single, standardized interface, and (ii) a programmable memory controller that system designers can program to support new DRAM techniques post-silicon. Together, these enable deployment by configuring the memory controller instead of modifying the interface and controller. ”
Find the technical paper here. October 2026.
Songara, Harsh, Konstantinos Kanellopoulos, F. Nisa Bostancı, Konstantinos Marios Sgouras, Ataberk Olgun, İsmail Emir Yüksel, Andreas Kosmas Kakolyris, A. Giray Yağlıkçı, and Onur Mutlu. “Terracotta: Enabling the Adoption of New DRAM Techniques via a Flexible DRAM Interface and Memory Controller.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.06475 (October 2026). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.06475

articles.title: Strom über die Reifen: Dieses Ladesystem macht Elektrobusse unabhängig vom Kabel
articles.text:
Strom über die Reifen: Dieses Ladesystem macht Elektrobusse unabhängig vom Kabel
Das Schweizer Unternehmen Winduction, ein Spin-off der Eidgenössisch-Technischen Hochschule Zürich (ETH), hat ein kabelloses Ladesystem für E-Busse entwickelt, das die Batterie über die Räder auflädt. Das System heißt „Wheel-based Induction“. Damit umgeht es laut der Firma das zentrale Problem bisheriger Induktionstechnik im Straßenverkehr: den großen Abstand zwischen Ladeplatte und Fahrzeug.
Warum Abstand beim induktiven Laden stört
Induktives Laden überträgt Energie drahtlos über ein Magnetfeld. Bei Smartphones, Smartwatches oder elektrischen Zahnbürsten funktioniert das gut, weil das Gerät direkt auf dem Ladepad liegt und die Spulen dicht beieinander sitzen. Je größer der Abstand zwischen den Spulen, desto mehr Energie geht verloren und desto geringer fällt die Ladeleistung aus. Zudem wird es wärmer. Genau das ist bei Bussen das Problem: Zwischen einer im Boden eingelassenen Ladeplatte und Spulen im Fahrzeugboden liegt viel Luft. Die drei Gründer von Winduction verlegen die Spulen deshalb in die Räder – also dorthin, wo der Bus ohnehin den Boden berührt.
Das Grundprinzip bleibt gleich: In einer Bodenplatte, die im Straßenbelag steckt, erzeugen mehrere Spulen ein Magnetfeld. Die Gegenstücke sitzen in besagten Busrädern, nehmen den Strom auf und laden die Batterie, während der Bus steht. Nach Angaben von Winduction erreicht das System eine Effizienz von mehr als 90 Prozent. Weniger als zehn Prozent der eingespeisten Energie gehen verloren. Allerdings sind dafür eben auch neue Räder notwendig.
Das Problem mit dem Stahl im Reifen
Der grundlegende Vorteil der Idee: Auch kurze Stopps reichen, um Energie nachzuladen. Busse könnten so auch an Haltestellen unterwegsn Strom tanken, nicht nur zu Fahrtbeginn und Fahrtende per Kabel oder Stromabnehmer. Die Batterie muss deshalb nicht den ganzen Tag durchhalten und kann kleiner ausfallen. Kleinere Batterien senken die Anschaffungskosten. Ein Hindernis gibt es: Normale Reifen enthalten Stahlgürtel, die ihnen Stabilität geben. Stahl stört aber das Magnetfeld: Ein großer Teil des Stroms würde dann in Wärme umgewandelt, statt in die Batterie zu fließen. Winduction arbeitet deshalb mit Partnern an einem stahlfreien Reifen.
Der wäre zwar teurer. Doch Berechnungen des Unternehmens zufolge fällt das kaum ins Gewicht, weil an anderer Stelle gespart wird, etwa bei Anschaffung und Betrieb. Die Gesamtkosten eines Elektrobusses samt passender Ladeinfrastruktur sollen spürbar sinken. Wie stark, hängt von der Route ab, etwa davon, wie viele Ladeplatten nötig sind. Das Laden selbst soll günstiger ausfallen als beim nächtlichen Kabelladen, das rund fünf Stunden am Stück dauert. Für die Strecke zwischen Zürich Flughafen und Zürich Oerlikon haben die Entwickler gerechnet: Mit zwei Ladeplatten auf 24 Stationen braucht der Bus bei 16 Stunden Betriebszeit weniger Strom und nur zusammengerechnet drei Stunden Ladezeit.

articles.title: VC funding dips in September despite big deals; More voices join the lineup at TechSparks 2026
articles.text:
VC funding dips in September despite big deals; More voices join the lineup at TechSparks 2026
Venture capital funding into Indian startups saw an 8.3% year-on-year dip in September, despite four $100 million deals. However, there were some positives. Meanwhile, here's a look at the speaker lineup for TechSparks 2026.
Dear Reader,
PhysicsWallah will no longer lend to students directly.
The edtech company’s wholly-owned subsidiary FinZ Finance has agreed to sell a Rs 95.79 crore loan portfolio to Auxilo Finserve, an RBI-registered NBFC focused on education finance. This is part of PhysicsWallah’s strategic move to focus on its core business and reduce balance-sheet and credit risks associated with lending. Going forward, lending will be facilitated through regulated third-party NBFCs.
In other news, TVS Automobile Solutions has raised Rs 425 crore in a Series D round of funding led by CE-Invests, the investment arm of UAE-based Crescent Enterprises. The funding will be used to expand the company’s myTVS aftermarket brand in overseas markets, starting with MENA.
Meanwhile, ecommerce marketplace Flipkart has picked up a minority stake in global B2B travel tech startup TravClan to strengthen international holiday offerings across Cleartrip and Flipkart Travel and expand access to global suppliers and destination support.
Moving on, AceVector, the parent company of Snapdeal, made a weak stock market debut on Monday, with its stock listing at Rs 28.32 on the NSE and Rs 28.30 on the BSE, down 11.5% from its issue price of Rs 32. This caught some investors off guard, especially as grey market trading had earlier indicated a 3% listing gain.
In global news, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman has said we must accept some of the risks associated with AI for the greater good. The benefits outweigh the risks, he argued.
“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency," Altman said in an interview with Politico's tech-centric newsletter Decoded.
In today’s newsletter:
- VC funding dips in September despite big deals
- More voices join the lineup at TechSparks 2026
Here’s your trivia for today: What did the letter ‘Q’ originally stand for in NASDAQ? (Scroll down for the answer)
Funding
VC inflow dips again, but there are some positives
Venture capital funding into Indian startups saw an 8.3% year-on-year dip in September, despite four $100 million deals. However, VC funding rose 15.5% compared to August, revealing the divergent trends in capital inflow into the startup ecosystem.
The total VC funding for September this year was $1.139 billion, compared to $1.242 billion in the same month last year, according to YourStory Research. The VC funding in August 2026 was $986 million.
Key takeaways
- There were some positives in September. The month marked the third time that VC funding crossed $1 billion this year. Also, four deals crossed the $100 million mark.
- The fintech segment raised the highest amount of funding in September at $251 million followed by electric vehicles at $222 million.
- Current trends indicate that 2026 may show a marginal improvement over 2025 in terms of overall funding. However, it will be challenging given that the last three months of the year are generally a period of slower activity.
TechSparks
More voices join the lineup at TechSparks 2026
At TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship startup and technology summit, founders, investors, technology leaders, and policymakers will come together to discuss and deliberate on ‘The New Tech Order’.
The three-day summit will take place in Bengaluru from October 13 to 15. Karnataka ministers Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, and Krishna Byre Gowda, Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, will join the conversations, alongside Pratyaya Amrit, Chief Secretary, Government of Bihar, and others.
Key takeaways
- With founders, investors, technology leaders and policymakers coming together, TechSparks 2026 will look at how technology is changing businesses, industries and the wider ecosystem.
- Here are some of the speakers joining TechSparks 2026: Ananth Narayanan, Founder and CEO of BRND.ME; Mohit Bhatnagar is Managing Director at Peak XV; Kalavathi G V is Executive Director and Head of the Global Development Center at Siemens Healthineers; and Rahul Chari is Founder and CPTO at PhonePe.
- The TechSparks 2026 lineup also features Nupur Goenka, Executive Director, Tally Solutions; Ankit Bagaria, Co-founder and CEO, Loopworm; Vikas Brahmavar, Founder and Director, Boson Whitewater; Chetan Maini, Chairman and Co-founder, SUN Mobility; Angad Daryani, Founder and CEO, Praan; Nikhil Rajpal, Founder, Qubo; Akshay Shekhar, CEO and Co-founder, Kazam; and Sharat Chandra, Founder, EmpowerEdge Ventures.
News & updates
- Debt financing: Quantum computing and artificial intelligence company QpiAI has secured Rs 50 crore in debt financing from InnoVen Capital India Fund II, with the Bengaluru startup allotting 5,000 Series B non-convertible debentures to the fund, per RoC filings.
- Rights issue: Ola Electric founder Bhavish Aggarwal has backed the company’s upcoming Rs 1,000 crore rights issue, pledging a 4.32% stake in the EV maker to fund his participation. This comes days after Ola Electric’s board okayed the plan to raise fresh capital through partly paid-up shares and appointed Deepa Bansal as its new compliance chief to boost governance.
- Beating forecasts: Taiwan’s Foxconn, the world's largest contract electronics maker, has reported a 47% jump in third-quarter revenue year-on-year that beat market estimates, fuelled by strong AI-related demand.
