articles.title: Deux NAS UGREEN en promo : puissance ou simplicité, à vous de choisir
articles.text:
Le téléphone affiche stockage plein après les vacances ? Les fichiers pro et perso se baladent sur des disques durs, voire des clés USB oubliées au fond d’un tiroir ? Un NAS permet de tout centraliser, sauvegarder et partager. Justement, les UGREEN DXP4800 Plus et DH2300 sont en promotion pour le Prime Day, un vrai bon plan Prime Day !
Ah, cette irrépressible envie de faire du tri dans ses photos et ses fichiers… On est nombreux à la ressentir, surtout après avoir fait le plein de souvenirs pendant les vacances.
L’idéal, c’est d’avoir un espace perso pour tout organiser comme on le souhaite, puis de partager ses images, vidéos et autres documents avec les personnes de son choix, famille comme amis, tout en gardant le contrôle. Un NAS apporte cette maîtrise, c’est un peu comme avoir un cloud perso hébergé chez soi.
Reste la question du budget…
Pas d’abonnement mensuel, et un tarif avantageux le temps de Prime Day du 6 au 7 octobre :
- UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus : 549,99 € au lieu de 729,99 € (-25 %)
- UGREEN NASync DH2300 : 189,99 € au lieu de 246,99 € (-23 %)
UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus : le choix de la performance (-25 %)
Si le NAS UGREEN DXP4800 Plus est aussi populaire, ce n’est pas un hasard… Polyvalence, fonctionnalités et excellent rapport qualité-prix… Alors, lorsque le Prime Day lui offre en plus une jolie ristourne, on a du mal à regarder ailleurs. Reste à savoir s’il est fait pour vous.
Conception : un NAS qui coche toutes les cases
Le DXP4800 Plus est très bien construit, et on parle non seulement de qualité de fabrication, mais aussi des équipements présents.
En façade, son lecteur SD et ses ports USB-C et USB-A permettent de transférer des fichiers depuis un appareil photo, un ordinateur ou un stockage externe. À l’arrière se retrouvent des ports USB 3.2 et USB 2.0, ainsi qu’une sortie HDMI pour relier directement le NAS à un téléviseur.
Côté réseau, il propose des ports 2,5 GbE et 10 GbE, un véritable atout pour celles et ceux qui manipulent régulièrement de gros volumes : sauvegardes, fichiers vidéo, photos haute résolution ou médiathèques volumineuses. Avec une infrastructure compatible, des transferts de plusieurs gigaoctets se règlent en quelques secondes.
Sous le châssis, une trappe donne accès à des emplacements M.2 pour ajouter des SSD NVMe, notamment afin d’accélérer certains usages. Le stockage principal repose toutefois sur quatre baies SATA, compatibles avec les disques de 3,5 et 2,5 pouces.
Ainsi, avec une capacité pouvant atteindre 144 To, le DXP4800 Plus s’adresse aussi bien aux particuliers qui désirent un espace centralisé pour leurs sauvegardes qu’aux utilisateurs professionnels ayant des besoins plus exigeants.
Qui plus est, la force d’un NAS est de pouvoir évoluer selon les besoins. Il est donc possible de commencer avec une certaine configuration, puis de compléter le stockage au fil du temps.
Une configuration solide pour multiplier les usages
Le DXP4800 Plus embarque un processeur Intel de 12e génération, accompagné de 8 Go de mémoire vive DDR5, une base confortable pour le quotidien.
Concrètement, cela signifie la possibilité de lire des contenus en 4K, l’accès simultané de plusieurs utilisateurs et des sauvegardes rapides, le tout avec une consommation d’énergie contenue. Au passage, la mémoire vive est extensible jusqu’à 64 Go, histoire de répondre aux usages les plus gourmands.
Du côté de l’interface, c’est ergonomique, facile à prendre en main et surtout, compatible avec la plupart des plateformes : Windows, macOS, iOS, Android.
À vous d’en faire ce que vous voulez : centre multimédia pour vos films et séries, outil de sauvegarde sécurisé, serveur de partage pour toute la famille ou pour votre équipe.
UGREEN NASync DH2300 : la solution simple et accessible pour le quotidien (-23 %)
Tout le monde n’a pas besoin de 144 To ni d’un port 10 GbE… Si vous voulez simplement mettre vos souvenirs et vos documents à l’abri, le DH2300 est une porte d’entrée parfaite dans l’univers du NAS, surtout à moins de 200 € pendant le Prime Day.
Deux baies et jusqu’à 64 To de stockage
Avec ses deux baies de stockage, le DH2300 adopte un format plus compact et donc plus discret, tout en conservant une capacité généreuse pouvant atteindre 64 To selon la configuration choisie. De quoi disposer d’un espace confortable pour centraliser photos, vidéos, documents et autres fichiers.
Ses deux baies permettent également de mettre en place une configuration en miroir, par exemple avec deux disques configurés en RAID 1. Dans ce cas, les données sont répliquées sur les deux disques : si l’un d’eux tombe en panne, une copie reste disponible sur l’autre.
Sans abonnement et avec une IA pour trier vos photos
Comme son grand frère, il fonctionne sans abonnement et s’appuie sur une interface ergonomique, facile à prendre en main. Mention spéciale pour les fonctionnalités IA qui facilitent le tri et l’organisation des fichiers. Vous pouvez ainsi transférer des milliers de photos et laisser le système les analyser pour vous aider à les classer rapidement.
À ce propos, le DH2300 peut se synchroniser avec vos services cloud existants afin de rapatrier vos données et de les centraliser au même endroit. Il prend également en charge la sauvegarde automatique de vos appareils et, une fois connecté à un téléviseur compatible, peut aussi servir de lecteur multimédia.
Bref, le DH2300 ne se contente pas de faire office d’espace de stockage ou de solution de sauvegarde. Il propose tout un ensemble de fonctions pratiques pour simplifier la gestion de ses fichiers et, surtout, pour profiter pleinement de ses contenus plutôt que de les laisser dormir au fond d’un disque dur externe.

articles.title: Prime Deal Days: Viele Fritzboxen sind jetzt auf Amazon günstiger – aber wie gut sind die Angebote wirklich?
articles.text:
Prime Deal Days: Amazon hat viele Fritz-Geräte reduziert – aber nicht alle Rabatte sind so hoch, wie angegeben
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Eine Fritzbox kann deutlich mehr als ein herkömmlicher Router und verfügt über zahlreiche Zusatzfunktionen. Alle Geräte sind Mesh-fähig: In Kombination mit weiteren Fritz-Geräten bilden sie ein Netzwerk mit nur einem Signal. So erreicht das WLAN auch Räume mit dicken Wänden und das Homeoffice im Keller. Smartphones, Tablets und Laptops wechseln zwischen den Zugangspunkten, ohne die Verbindung zu unterbrechen.
Für alle, die eine besonders leistungsstarke Abdeckung für das ganze Haus oder eine zentrale Smart-Home-Steuerung suchen, kann sich die Anschaffung einer Fritzbox also durchaus lohnen. Im Rahmen der aktuell stattfindenden Prime Deal Days hat Amazon zahlreiche Geräte des Berliner Herstellers reduziert. Wir haben die Preise verglichen und verraten dir, welche Angebote sich jetzt am meisten lohnen.
Fritz-SIM-Router für unterwegs
Die Fritzbox 6850 5G ist ein WLAN-Router, der den Internetzugang vollständig über eine eingelegte SIM-Karte herstellt. Er eignet sich vor allem als Festnetzersatz bei schlechtem DSL, für Ferienwohnungen oder temporäre Standorte. Das integrierte 5G-Modem ermöglicht WLAN-Übertragungsraten von bis zu 1,2 Gigabit pro Sekunde. Ohne 5G-Netz greift der Router auf 4G oder 3G zurück. Wie andere Modelle bietet er alle Fritz-Zusatzfunktionen, etwa als DECT-Basis für Schnurlostelefone. Der Hersteller verkauft die Fritzbox 6850 5G für 349 Euro. Bei Amazon kostet sie aktuell 264,99 Euro. Du sparst somit rund 24 Prozent. Laut Vergleichsportalen ist das der günstigste Preis seit Mitte August.
Auch die Fritzbox 6820 LTE International stellt das Internet über eine SIM-Karte her. Sie ist deutlich kompakter und eignet sich für den gelegentlichen mobilen Einsatz, etwa im Wohnmobil. Im Ausland lässt sie sich ebenfalls nutzen. Weil dort aber teilweise andere Frequenzbänder verwendet werden, muss laut Hersteller gegebenenfalls die Option „Roaming gestatten“ aktiviert werden. Über das 4G- und 3G-Netz bietet das Modell WLAN mit bis zu 450 Megabit pro Sekunde. 5G wird nicht unterstützt. Im Fritz-Shop kostet das Gerät 99,99 Euro. Bei den Amazon Prime Deal Days zahlst du derzeit 30 Euro weniger – also 69,99 Euro. Laut Vergleich war sie zuletzt im April zu einem ähnlichen Preis verfügbar.
Fritzboxen für Glasfaser, Kabel und DSL
Auch klassische Router sind jetzt günstiger. Die Fritzbox 7690 ist das Flaggschiff der DSL-Serie und richtet sich an Haushalte mit vielen gleichzeitig genutzten Endgeräten. Sie ist mit Wi-Fi 7 ausgestattet. Der Standard gilt als besonders störungsresistent, da er mehrere Frequenzbänder gleichzeitig verwendet. Mit einer WLAN-Geschwindigkeit von bis zu 7,1 Gigabit pro Sekunde eignet sich der Router auch für schnelle Downloads, Streaming und Gaming. Für das Smarthome unterstützt er neben DECT auch Zigbee, auf das Hersteller wie Bosch und Philips setzen. Bei Amazon kostet die Fritzbox 7690 249,99 Euro, beim Hersteller 279,99 Euro. Die tatsächliche Ersparnis fällt damit kleiner aus als von Amazon angegeben.
Ähnliches gilt für die Fritzbox 5690 für Haushalte mit Glasfaseranschluss. Sie unterstützt ebenfalls Wi-Fi 7 und erreicht dank Dualband-WLAN-Übertragungsraten von bis zu 6,4 Gigabit pro Sekunde. Der Amazon-Preis liegt mit 249,99 Euro nur 30 Euro unter dem Herstellerpreis. Deutlich größer ist die Ersparnis bei der Fritzbox 6690 Pro, dem neuen Kabel-Flaggschiff des Herstellers. Sie bietet High-End-WLAN mit bis zu 12,2 Gigabit pro Sekunde. Ein Triband-WLAN-Mesh sorgt für eine starke Verbindung bis in den letzten Winkel. Zudem ist die Fritzbox Zigbee-kompatibel. Bei Fritz kostet das Gerät 429 Euro, bei Amazon 365,99 Euro. Laut Vergleichsportalen ist das der niedrigste Preis seit Einführung des Geräts.
Fritz-Gadgets für WLAN im ganzen Haus
Für große Haushalte oder Wohnungen mit dicken Wänden können sich auch Zusatzgeräte lohnen. Reicht beispielsweise der Router allein nicht für eine stabile WLAN-Verbindung im gesamten Zuhause aus, kann ein Repeater Abhilfe schaffen. Je nach Modell wird dieser in die Steckdose gesteckt: Er empfängt das Signal des Heimnetzwerks, verstärkt es und sendet es erneut aus. Herkömmliche WLAN-Verstärker hingegen erstellen ein separates Netzwerk mit eigener Kennung, sodass beim Wechsel die Verbindung kurz abbrechen kann. Fritz-Repeater sind Mesh-fähig und bilden ein gemeinsames Netzwerk mit einem Signal für eine stabile, lückenlose Abdeckung. Der Fritz-Repeater 1200 AX ist bei Amazon aktuell für 69,99 Euro erhältlich, also zehn Euro günstiger als im Hersteller-Shop.
Mit Powerline wird das Internet über die Stromleitung auch in entlegene Räume gebracht. Dafür brauchst du mindestens zwei Adapter: Den ersten steckst du in eine Steckdose nahe dem Router und verbindest ihn per LAN-Kabel. Den zweiten installierst du im Zielraum, also zum Beispiel in deinem Arbeitszimmer. Powerline-Geräte mit WLAN lohnen sich, wenn du in diesem Raum auch mobile Geräte nutzt. Laut Angaben des Herstellers funktioniert Powerline oft zuverlässiger als ein WLAN-Repeater. Das Mesh- und WLAN-fähige Set Fritz-Powerline 1260 kostet 129,99 Euro und ist damit 20 Euro günstiger als im Fritz-Shop. Laut Vergleichsportalen ist das der niedrigste Preis seit Juli.

articles.title: Sam Altman acusó a Elon Musk de ser un “abusón” y pidió no ceder ante sus ataques
articles.text:
El director ejecutivo de OpenAI, Sam Altman, acusó a Elon Musk de ser un “abusón” y defendió responder con firmeza a sus ataques públicos.
La declaración, publicada recientemente en una entrevista con Vanity Fair, reaviva la disputa entre dos antiguos socios que ahora encabezan empresas rivales en el mercado de la inteligencia artificial.
Qué dijo Sam Altman sobre Elon Musk
El responsable de OpenAI fue consultado por el enfrentamiento que mantiene con el propietario de Tesla y de la red social X. Altman dijo que no le gustan los abusones y situó a Musk dentro de esa categoría. “Pienso que de vez en cuando hay que devolverles el golpe con un puñetazo”, afirmó durante la entrevista. La frase describió su postura frente a las descalificaciones públicas.
El ejecutivo añadió que Musk, como muchos abusones, solo respeta a quienes responden de la misma manera. Con esa idea, Altman sostuvo que una reacción contundente busca marcar límites y no impedir una futura cooperación. Según explicó, contestar a los ataques no supone renunciar a trabajar con su antiguo socio cuando haya intereses comunes.
La rivalidad se remonta a la fundación de OpenAI en 2015
Altman y Musk formaron parte del grupo fundador de OpenAI en 2015. Con los años, la relación se deterioró por diferencias sobre el rumbo de la organización y el desarrollo de la inteligencia artificial. Musk criticó la evolución comercial de la firma, mientras Altman quedó al frente de una empresa que ganó visibilidad mundial con el lanzamiento de ChatGPT.
La distancia aumentó con la creación de xAI, la empresa de inteligencia artificial de Musk. Esa compañía compite con OpenAI en un sector marcado por nuevos productos, inversiones y discusiones sobre seguridad. La disputa también llegó a los tribunales, con cuestionamientos de Musk a las decisiones corporativas de la empresa que ayudó a fundar.
Altman reclamó una regulación con participación pública
Más allá del enfrentamiento personal, Altman afirmó que las decisiones sobre inteligencia artificial no deben quedar solo en manos privadas. “Necesitamos que nuestros gobiernos den un paso al frente”, señaló. A su juicio, la voluntad de la población debe reflejarse en algunas de las decisiones cruciales que la sociedad tendrá que adoptar ante la expansión de estos sistemas.
El director ejecutivo defendió que los beneficios potenciales de la tecnología superan sus riesgos y rechazó frenar su desarrollo. Entre los usos que mencionó figura la posibilidad de ayudar a encontrar una cura para el cáncer y el Alzheimer. Su posición apuesta por avanzar con controles, sin detener la innovación.
El choque importa hoy porque combina rivalidad empresarial, un conflicto legal y el debate sobre quién debe fijar los límites de una tecnología que gana presencia en la economía y la vida cotidiana. Altman dirige la firma creadora de ChatGPT, mientras Musk cuestiona su rumbo comercial y desarrolla su propia competidora, xAI.
La presión financiera coincide con el poder económico de Musk
Altman también abordó las presiones de los inversores ante una posible salida a bolsa de OpenAI. Aseguró que tomará decisiones beneficiosas para la humanidad aunque impliquen costes financieros y una eventual caída en el precio de las acciones. Esa definición coloca el futuro corporativo de la compañía dentro de la discusión sobre cómo se financia la carrera tecnológica de la inteligencia artificial y sus infraestructuras globales.
Como complemento, Musk volvió a superar el billón de dólares de patrimonio el 6 de octubre, impulsado por las acciones de SpaceX y Tesla. Su fortuna supera en más de USD 378.000 millones la suma de los patrimonios de Jeff Bezos y Mark Zuckerberg. Ese peso económico añade contexto a un pulso que une competencia empresarial, influencia pública y visiones enfrentadas sobre la inteligencia artificial actual.

articles.title: ASOS confirms data breach after “HACKED” in-app notifications
articles.text:
UK fashion retailer ASOS confirmed a data breach Tuesday after hackers sent unauthorized push notifications through its mobile app while claiming to have stolen customer data from the company's Snowflake environment.
ASOS is a large UK-based online fashion retailer that sells clothing, footwear, accessories, and beauty products to customers worldwide, including in the United States.
ASOS has confirmed that third-party platforms used to communicate with customers were accessed without authorization and says basic personal information, including names and contact details, may have been exposed.
The company is now displaying an in-app notice telling customers to disregard the unauthorized push alert and not to click or engage with the external third-party link it contained.
However, the company has not confirmed the threat actor's claim that its Snowflake environment was compromised or disclosed how many customers may be affected.
ASOS says it does not believe payment-card information or account passwords were impacted.
If you have any information regarding this incident or other undisclosed attacks, you can contact us confidentially via Signal at 646-961-3731 or at tips@bleepingcomputer.com.
Hackers abuse ASOS mobile app
The notifications began appearing at approximately 5:00 a.m. ET on Tuesday, with multiple BleepingComputer readers contacting us after receiving the alerts on their phones.
"ASOS HACKED," reads the notification seen by BleepingComputer.
"Dear Asos DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it."
Numerous other ASOS customers also reported receiving the same notification on Reddit, indicating that the message reached many, if not all, mobile app users.
The notification directs ASOS to a Telegram channel operated by a threat actor calling itself the "Xuanye group."
In messages posted to the channel Tuesday morning, the threat actor claimed the breach did not affect payment information.
However, the attackers later published a "FINAL STATEMENT," claiming that they stole customer information in the attack.
"The affected organisation's app is safe to use. The incident involves customer information, it is safe on our server, and it will not be touched for a designated period," reads the group's message.
"Considering the current situation regarding incident disclosure in the cyber security landscape, you can thank us for our generous clarity regarding this incident."
The group did not disclose what customer information was allegedly stolen, how many customers were impacted, or provide evidence showing that it had compromised ASOS's Snowflake environment.
BleepingComputer attempted to contact the threat actors about the breach, but the only contact point required payment. We did not continue as it is against our editorial guidelines to pay for information.

articles.title: Cybersecurity M&A Roundup: 39 Deals Announced in September 2026
articles.text:
Thirty-nine cybersecurity-related merger and acquisition (M&A) deals were announced in September 2026.
For a detailed view of the more than 420 acquisitions announced in 2025, check out SecurityWeek’s annual M&A report.
Here are some of the most important cybersecurity M&A deals announced in September 2026:
A-LIGN acquires AssurePoint and Pathfynder
Cybersecurity compliance firm A-LIGN has acquired Sydney-based AssurePoint, a cloud security assessment company. The deal adds IRAP assessments to A-LIGN’s portfolio and marks its entry into Australia. A-LIGN also acquired Pathfynder, a firm providing penetration testing, red teaming, and incident response services. Pathfynder will operate as Pathfynder by A-LIGN.
Aiuken Cybersecurity acquires 4Elitech
Spanish managed security provider Aiuken Cybersecurity, part of the Allurity group, has acquired 4Elitech, a Spanish specialist in industrial and critical infrastructure cybersecurity. The deal adds OT threat detection and industrial incident response capabilities to Aiuken’s offering.
Dragos acquires NetRise and runZero
Dragos has completed its acquisitions of NetRise and runZero as part of Accenture’s $4.1 billion OT cybersecurity push announced in June. NetRise contributes firmware-level insight into device exposure and software supply chain visibility, while runZero adds asset discovery, exposure assessment and attack surface intelligence. Dragos said the acquisitions add exposure management and software supply chain security to its platform alongside existing OT asset visibility and threat detection.
IBM has acquired UK-based Logiq Consulting, a cybersecurity consultancy serving the UK defense, government, and critical infrastructure sectors. The deal expands IBM’s secure digital transformation and sovereign technology capabilities in the UK.
Kiteworks has announced the acquisition of AI data security company Bonfy.AI, a move aimed at extending real-time policy enforcement over sensitive data exchanged by both human users and AI agents. Bonfy technology will extend Kiteworks’ policy enforcement across agent and human data exchange and usage.
NetSPI and Synack have agreed to merge, creating an offensive security company with more than $200 million in revenue. The KKR-backed combined company will pair expert penetration testers with agentic AI for continuous security testing.
Palo Alto Networks acquires Console
Palo Alto Networks has acquired Console, an AI-native platform for building agentic workflows using natural language, reportedly for $500 million in cash and stock. Console’s technology will deepen agentic capabilities in the Cortex platform, letting security teams automate investigation and remediation.
Oslo-based human risk management company Pistachio has acquired the intellectual property of Norwegian cyber-risk management platform Hugin.io. Pistachio plans to use the technology to launch a compliance management product in 2027.
Quantum eMotion to acquire Plurilock
Quantum security firm Quantum eMotion (QeM) has agreed to acquire Plurilock Security for roughly C$33.8 million ($23.6 million) in cash and stock. Both companies are based in Canada. The deal gives QeM an established cybersecurity revenue base, customer relationships, and public-sector procurement channels.
Quorum Cyber to acquire Ontinue
Edinburgh-based Quorum Cyber has agreed to acquire Ontinue, a managed extended detection and response (MXDR) provider headquartered in Redwood City, California, and Zurich. The deal will combine AI-powered MXDR, cyber resilience and human expertise to create a Microsoft-first agentic SOC.
Cloud security firm Upwind has acquired Israeli AI security startup Aegis in an all-equity deal reportedly valued at $30 million. Aegis’ co-founders will lead the newly launched Upwind AI Security Labs, which will research and build defenses against AI-driven attacks.
Other cybersecurity M&A deals announced in September 2026:
Act Security acquires Cloud Copilot
CBTS acquires Recovery Point Systems
CloudFirst acquires Forvis Mazars’ IT and cyber managed services practice
Concentrix acquires CastleHill Managed Risk Solutions
InfraVia acquires a majority stake in Nexis
IT Solutions acquires STACK Cybersecurity
ITC Federal acquires Apriva ISS
Malam Team acquires Foretech Software
Project Eleven acquires Riva Labs
Risk X Group acquires Wolfpack Information Risk
S&P Global to acquire OpenZeppelin
SGS acquires majority stake in NetSentries
Surfshark acquires majority stake in Optery
ThreatBook acquires CyberStrikeAI

articles.title: Xiaomi 18 Pro : nos 5 fonctions préférées sur l'écran arrière — Frandroid
articles.text:
Nous avons acheté un modèle chinois du Xiaomi 18 Pro. Le nouveau smartphone suscite un certain engouement notamment depuis qu’on s’attend à ce qu’il arrive en France (ce serait le premier modèle Pro de la marque vendue chez nous depuis le Xiaomi 13 Pro). Le téléphone dispose d’un petit écran de 2,7 pouces à l’arrière, près de ses capteurs photo (l’écran principal mesure 6,4 pouces).
Voici cinq fonctions de l’écran arrière du Xiaomi 18 Pro qui nous ont marqués (et une sixième qui nous fait envie). N’hésitez pas non plus à lire :
Retour écran pour prendre des photos
C’est sans doute la première chose qui vient en tête quand on parle de l’écran arrière du Xiaomi 18 Pro : celui-ci permet d’avoir un aperçu de la photo que vous vous apprêtez à prendre.
Vous pouvez ainsi prendre des selfies avec la meilleure caméra du Xiaomi 18 Pro. Un glissement du bord gauche vers le centre du petit écran permet de lancer l’interface de l’appareil photo. Vous accédez ainsi à tous les boutons classiques (mode de prise de vue, réglages…), mais l’écran de 2,7 pouces laisse peu de place pour les manipuler.
Vous pouvez aussi faire en sorte que la personne que vous photographiez puisse voir à quoi elle ressemble. Pour cela, en ouvrant l’appareil photo depuis le grand écran principal du Xiaomi 18 Pro, vous devez utiliser le petit bouton tout en haut à gauche de l’interface. Il sert à activer le retour caméra (exactement à la manière de ce qu’on voit déjà sur les smartphones pliables).
Répondre à un appel sans retourner le téléphone
L’écran arrière du Xiaomi 18 Pro permet de consulter certaines informations sans retourner le téléphone. On peut notamment y répondre à un appel.
L’écran arrière affiche l’appel entrant. Il suffit de tapoter dessus pour afficher le numéro ou le nom de l’appelant. Il ne vous reste plus qu’à refuser la communication ou décrocher (en haut-parleur par défaut).
Vous pouvez aussi afficher les notifications entrantes sur l’écran arrière, mais il faudra d’abord faire un tour dans les paramètres pour donner l’autorisation aux applications de votre choix d’afficher une notification sur l’écran verrouillé.
Générer une application par IA
Le Xiaomi 18 Pro permet de créer votre propre application dédiée à l’écran arrière. Il suffit d’un prompt pour décrire votre idée auprès de l’intelligence artificielle. L’IA met ensuite environ 5 minutes à générer l’application.
La fonctionnalité, accessible depuis les paramètres de l’écran arrière, est encore en phase bêta. Toutefois, elle fonctionne déjà assez bien. Par dictée vocale, j’ai, par exemple, pu générer un simulateur de d20 (dé à 20 faces) pour Donjons et Dragons.
    À lire aussi : 
Xiaomi 18 Pro : j’ai créé ma propre application pour l’écran arrière, ça m’a pris 5 minutes
Météo, compteur de pas, lecteur de musique, Xiaomi Home
Depuis les paramètres, vous pouvez choisir le fond de l’écran arrière. Certains sont basiques, d’autres affichent des animaux mignons. Deux, cependant, ont retenu notre attention : la météo et le compteur de pas. Deux informations pratiques à avoir à portée de main, sans même retourner le téléphone.
L’utilisateur décide aussi des applications qui peuvent s’afficher sur l’écran arrière du Xiaomi 18 Pro (à partir d’une liste prédéfinie). On trouve ainsi le lecteur de musique, l’agenda ou un centre de contrôle pour vos appareils connectés Xiaomi Home.
Xiaomi Home propose aussi un flux vidéo de votre caméra de sécurité connectée.
Gestion du minuteur
C’est tou bête, mais si vous lancez un minuteur sur le Xiaomi 18 Pro, vous pouvez garder un œil sur le décompte depuis l’écran arrière. C’est un détail en soi, mais ça nous a plu.
Ce qu’il reste à découvrir ou améliorer
Dans la liste des applications pouvant s’afficher sur l’écran arrière, on trouve notamment DiDi et AMap. Ces deux applications chinoises sont des équivalents d’Uber et de Google Maps, mais fonctionnent mal en France. Il semble toutefois possible d’afficher la progression en direct de votre chauffeur de VTC ou de consulter les instructions de navigation pendant un itinéraire. Nous n’avons pas pu tester, mais il sera intéressant de surveiller ce genre d’options sur le modèle français du Xiaomi 18 Pro.
La présence de DiDi et AMap s’explique par les partenariats que Xiaomi a noués avec plusieurs marques chinoises pour proposer des cartes d’applications sur l’écran arrière des 18 Pro.
Les paramètres de l’écran arrière restent par ailleurs assez fouillis. On s’y perd vite entre la gestion des fonds d’écran, des applications qu’on peut afficher et des éléments de personnalisation. Gageons que le firmware français saura s’adapter (en plus d’être mieux traduit).

articles.title: The Civic-Tech Platform Democratising Nigeria’s Mining Data
articles.text:
Across rural Nigeria, host communities watch heavy machinery dig up their land daily. But ask locals who hold the operational licence, what minerals are being extracted, or what community benefits they are legally owed—and the room goes silent. To fight this “information opacity,” Anthony Adejuwon and his team at Urban Alert spent nine months building Minetrix AI. By ingesting over 37,000 public records, land registries, and environmental audits into a multilingual conversational engine (available in English, Hausa, Igbo, and Yoruba), the platform gives communities the exact data they need to negotiate Community Development Agreements from a position of knowledge. In this feature, JOHN ADOYI explores how retrieval-first AI is turning paper archives into public power, and why civic tech might just rewrite the rules of Africa’s extractive sector.
For over six years, Anthony Adejuwan has worked alongside Nigerian communities impacted by solid mineral extraction. Across dozens of rural settlements, he repeatedly observed the same predicament: residents knew active mining was taking place on their land, yet could not ascertain who held the operational licences, what minerals were being extracted, or what statutory rights they possessed as host communities.
“The problem is that people can only ask questions from what they know,” Adejuwon told TechCabal. Without access to the right information, he said, communities, journalists, and researchers struggle to ask the questions they need to understand what is happening in the sector.
That systemic opacity prompted Adejuwan and his team at Urban Alert—a Nigerian civic-tech organisation focused on extractive transparency—to spend nine months building Minetrix AI. The conversational platform enables users to query Nigeria’s solid minerals sector in English, Hausa, Igbo, and Yoruba. To establish factual context, the team ingested and indexed more than 37,000 documents sourced from government registries, research bodies, and civil society organisations.
The information gap
The information barrier facing these communities is rarely a matter of non-existent data; rather, it is a problem of accessibility and comprehension. Adejuwan characterises this as an “information opacity” crisis within Nigeria’s solid minerals industry.
“Data is often buried behind fragmented government portals, locked on physical office shelves, or presented in technical formats and languages that ordinary citizens cannot digest,” he explains.
Public repositories do exist. The Mining Cadastre Office (MCO) maintains a central register of mining titles, while the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (NEITI) publishes data on licences, production volumes, corporate entities, and royalty payments. However, administrative disclosure does not automatically translate into community usability.
A May 2026 investigation by Premium Times in Shiroro, Niger State, illustrated this divide. Residents affected by gold mining struggled to identify the commercial entities operating four sites across Farin Doki and Ajata Aboki, or verify whether they possessed valid permits. While two sites were known to be worked by local artisanal miners, the corporate entities backing the remaining sites remained completely anonymous to the community. Poor internet connectivity, low digital literacy, and limited smartphone access further compound these barriers.
NEITI’s 2023 Solid Minerals Industry Audit Report says Community Development Agreements (CDAs) between mining companies and host communities were being kept in hard copy by the Mining Environmental Compliance Department. The documents could be accessed by the public through a formal request, while the ministry was working to digitise them. The audit also noted the absence of specific government policies on the public disclosure of CDAs.
The agreements are important because they set out the social and economic benefits expected to flow to host communities. Yet, a community may still have to make a formal request to see the document that spells out what its mining operator is expected to provide.
For someone living next to a mining operation, basic questions around mine ownership, mining history, what the miners are allowed to do, and benefits the community is obligated to receive, ultimately require navigating different institutions, databases, and documents.
Adejuwon said this was a pattern Urban Alert had encountered across the communities where it has worked, including in Kaduna, Plateau, Osun, Ogun, Ekiti, and Ebonyi.
“People can only ask questions from what they know,” he said. Without access to information, communities may not know who to approach or even which questions to ask.
For Urban Alert, closing that gap became the starting point for Minetrix AI.
How Minetrix AI works
Building Minetrix AI required Urban Alert to aggregate and standardise disparate datasets, collaborating closely with software engineers, geospatial analysts, mining engineers, and geologists.
“It’s quite difficult because they are in different formats from different sources,” Adejuwon said. “The first thing is to first ensure the kind of information available from each sector within the sector … and convert the format in which they have their publications into formats readable by Minetrix.”
Minetrix is currently a web-based platform. After signing up with an email address, users are taken to a conversational interface where they can type questions about minerals and mining in Nigeria. They can ask questions in English, Hausa, Igbo, or Yoruba, and the platform responds within seconds.
Adejuwon said AI was important because of the amount of information the system has to synthesise and the need to respond across multiple languages.
Minetrix AI uses a “retrieval-first” design. When a user asks a question, the system first retrieves relevant information from the documents in its database before generating a response.
“It’s not trained in a way that it’s just going to go and search for responses online, which may or may not really be trustworthy,” Adejuwan said.
The platform also provides citations for the information used in its responses. A question about a mining title, for example, would draw from documents released by the government agency responsible for issuing titles, while questions about mining laws would draw from relevant laws, regulations, and other legal documents.
Users can keep track of their previous questions and responses through an audit log. Adejuwan said this allows them to return to earlier conversations rather than starting again each time they use the platform.
The system is also designed to continue working around interruptions in internet access. Adejuwan said that when a user’s connection drops, Minetrix AI can switch to a format that allows them to continue developing their understanding of the sector, then return to their previous conversation when the connection is restored.
For now, the platform remains web-based, although Adejuwan said Urban Alert plans to develop an app as it tries to reach young users. The organisation also plans to add audio functionality and other accessibility features for people with disabilities.
Adejuwan said the mining data and records on Minetrix AI are periodically updated as new information becomes available. The team adds relevant material from government agencies and other stakeholders so that users are not relying on outdated records.
The result is intended to feel less like searching through a collection of documents and more like having a conversation with the information contained in them.
The real test
Minetrix AI is undergoing active pilot testing across Nigeria, and early user engagement has upended Urban Alert’s initial projections.
The team originally cautioned that a niche civic-tech product focused on mining governance might struggle to gain traction in an ecosystem dominated by commercial fintech. “A major lesson for us was never to underestimate public demand for civic accountability,” Adejuwan reflects. “Citizens actively seek out tools that demystify public interest data.”
Encouraged by this uptake, Urban Alert is evaluating expansion into Ghana and other West African mining jurisdictions. Scaling the platform, however, presents distinct operational headwinds—chief among them being the retention of specialised cross-disciplinary talent.
“We are not merely building a software product; we are building a domain-specific solution for the extractive industry,” Adejuwan explains. “That requires professionals who possess deep geological and legal expertise alongside software development capabilities—a talent pool that is difficult to retain against commercial market competition.”
Sustainable funding remains an equal hurdle within a venture landscape that heavily favours revenue-generating commercial software over public-interest technology.
Over the coming year, Urban Alert aims to achieve compliance with Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) by integrating text-to-speech audio responses tailored for visually impaired users and low-literacy communities.
Ultimately, Adejuwan views technology as a catalyst for community empowerment. “Our ultimate goal is to cultivate informed host communities capable of negotiating Community Development Agreements from a position of knowledge,” he concludes. “We want to ensure that mineral wealth yields tangible local development, rather than environmental degradation and silent extraction.”
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: À 10 000 €, elle va tout casser : Citroën ressuscite la mythique 2CV en version électrique
articles.text:
L’une des voitures françaises les plus célèbres au monde s’apprête à faire un retour en fanfare. La Citroën 2CV revient en effet au XXIème siècle sous une forme électrique qui entend une nouvelle fois révolutionner le marché. Le constructeur vise en effet un prix ultra bas qui pourrait tutoyer les 10 000 € aides comprises, ce qui ferait de l’auto la voiture électrique la moins chère d’Europe, tout simplement.
En attendant une présentation officielle le 11 octobre, Citroën fait monter la température avec les premières images de ce concept car prometteur. On y remarque par exemple un feu semi-circulaire mordu sur deux côtés. L’ensemble évasé rappelle bien entendu les optiques rondes de la 2CV originale plantés sur les ailes. L’histoire se répète sur le capot bombé orné de stries comme sur l’ancêtre. Une signature que l’on pourrait retrouver en série.
Des clins d’œil rétro qui font mouche
Ce qui a également toutes ses chances de passer en production sont les jantes au look éminemment rétro. Pleines avec quatre écrous au lieu de trois, elles se voient chaussées de pneus Michelin arborant la police d’écriture des années 1950. Un sympathique clin d’œil, qui s’accompagne de flancs bas garnis de chevrons indiquant le sens de rotation du pneumatique. On remarquera aussi des passages de roues noirs brillants.
Dépourvu de vitre, le montant C montre pour sa part un feu de position orange tiré droit de la première 2CV. Pivotantes, les poignées de portes devraient loger sur des portières avant à charnières inversées comme sur le modèle original. Peu de chance en revanche qu’un tel système soit repris sur la version de série en raison des coûts de développement supérieurs. Car là est toute la philosophie de cette réinterprétation.
Le pari fou du low-cost : comment Citroën casse les prix
L’auto devra être extrêmement compétitive à l’instar de son ancêtre en contenant sévèrement ses prix. Citroën vise un tarif de 15 000 € sans aides, ce qui est bien en deçà de la ë-C3. Avec la Prime Coup de Pouce maximale, la facture devrait alors atteindre les 10 000 €, ce qui serait tout bonnement imbattable sur le marché, toutes catégories confondues. Alléchant, même s’il faudra forcément faire quelques compromis.
L’autonomie devrait être limitée par une batterie des plus compactes. Le pack de 30 kWh de la ë-C3 en version Autonomie Urbaine sera le candidat pressenti. Le rayon d’action tournera alors autour des 200 km sur le cycle WLTP. La puissance sera aussi bien modeste en passant sous les 100 ch, alors que la recharge rapide figurera en option. Rendez-vous la semaine prochaine pour tout savoir sur ce concept qui entrera en production en 2028 !

articles.title: Ce mini-four à 350 € veut aussi remplacer votre airfryer
articles.text:
Our Place Wonder Oven Pro : un mini-four de 30 l qui joue aussi les airfryers
Petit four, grande carte
Our Place lance en France le Wonder Oven Pro, un four de comptoir doté de huit modes de cuisson et d'un apport d'humidité. Proposé à 350 €, il vise les gratins, les frites et le pain maison.
Avec sa porte vitrée et ses grilles, le Wonder Oven Pro reprend le format du mini-four. Ses 30 l permettent, selon Our Place, d'accueillir une pizza de 30 cm ou plusieurs plats. Avec environ 42,5 × 33 × 33,7 cm, il faudra tout de même lui réserver une place sur le plan de travail.
D'une puissance de 1700 W, il se règle de 30 à 230 °C grâce à des commandes numériques. Huit modes sont proposés : airfryer, cuisson, rôtissage, gril, gratin, réchauffage, levée de pâte et déshydratation. Le pain maison entre donc aussi au menu.
Un peu de vapeur
Des résistances en quartz et en acier inoxydable sont associées à un ventilateur à convection. Un système ajoute également de l'humidité pendant la cuisson ou le réchauffage pour, selon la marque, préserver le moelleux tout en faisant dorer la surface.
Our Place annonce un préchauffage jusqu'à 60 % plus rapide et une cuisson jusqu'à 40 % plus rapide qu'un four traditionnel. Ces chiffres reposent sur des essais à 190 °C en mode cuisson, notamment avec de la volaille. La polyvalence annoncée peut intéresser les petites cuisines.
Le Wonder Oven Pro est annoncé disponible dès ce 6 octobre en bleu, charbon et crème. Panier airfryer, plaque de cuisson, grilles et bac ramasse-miettes sont fournis.

articles.title: Cybersecurity startup Hadrian raises €35.68 million to scale its agentic AI offensive security platform | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Hadrian, a London-Amsterdam-based agentic AI offensive security platform, today announced a €35.68 million ($40 million) funding round to fund expansion across EMEA and the U.S. and deepen investment in its engineering and research teams.
The round was co-led by Forgepoint Capital International and SmartFin, with participation from existing investors HV Capital, Motive Partners, Picus Capital and Oetker Ventures. The backing brings the company’s total funding to nearly €58 million ($65 million).
Rogier Fischer, CEO of Hadrian, said, “Everyone can see that AI is changing the threat landscape. It might also hold the answer, but most people are focused on automating the wrong bits. We have been working with LLMs since before they went mainstream, and we know that AI can work much faster than any human offensive security team. So we built a platform that emulates hackers’ attack paths, helping our customers to understand their key risks and prioritise their security resources appropriately.”
Founded in 2021 in Amsterdam by Fischer, Olivier Beg and Maurice Clin, Hadrian offers an offensive security platform that helps enterprise security teams identify, verify and close security gaps before attackers can exploit them.
The company says its agentic engine delivers always-on discovery, validation, and mobilisation of an organisation’s most critical cyber risks. It adapts to each organisation’s environment to probe, discover and validate the risks attackers can actually exploit. Coupled with a proprietary predictive discovery agent, Hadrian autonomously verifies remediation, delivering an end-to-end solution.
The cybersecurity startup highlighted how AI has upended the offensive security landscape and cited recent reports of AI agents escaping test environments and hacking company systems without human direction. It also referenced Anthropic’s disclosure that criminals and state-linked groups had used its models to automate entire attack chains and write zero-day exploits.
According to the company, while attackers now move at machine speed, many security teams are years behind and still run manual pentests. It also noted that the volume of irrelevant signals distracts teams, making it difficult to determine which exposures are exploitable.
Hadrian argues there is a real market need for a solution that can identify genuine threats and cut through the noise. It claims to let businesses see security through a hacker’s eyes, map the digital footprint, discover risks, and prioritise remediation so security teams can harden their external attack surfaces.
It states that humans set the mission and make the decisions that matter, while AI does the work in between, providing the coverage, repetition and speed that no team can sustain around the clock.
To achieve this, Hadrian combines continuous exposure management and agentic penetration testing in one platform and claims to be the only vendor offering this approach. Its product Atlas continuously maps an organisation’s external attack surface and uses purpose-built AI agents to validate which exposures are actually exploitable. Nora, its other product, provides agentic pentesting on demand at a human pentest level and beyond.
Together, the company reports that these products deliver 10x greater visibility into critical exposures, 80% faster time to resolution, and 5x ROI compared to manual pentesting.
Damien Henault, Managing Director and Partner at Forgepoint Capital International, said, “There are too many vulnerabilities and noise out there for teams to manage, so they need tools that can help them see clearly and think like AI-armed hackers. Hadrian’s AI native always-on solution delivers both depth and breadth and helps its customers to focus on genuine issues and risks, and the companies using its platform are testament to both its innovative approach and the strength of its team, both aspects which make them a natural choice for us to back.”
Hadrian works with companies in the US and Europe, including Fortune 500 leaders and industry disruptors such as McKesson, NBCUniversal, Francisco Partners, Total Energies, Amadeus, Leroy Merlin, and Damen Shipyard.

articles.title: Manage Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Spaces directly from SageMaker Studio | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Manage Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Spaces directly from SageMaker Studio
We recently introduced the ability to create and manage Amazon SageMaker Spaces on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS clusters directly from the Amazon SageMaker Studio UI. Data scientists and machine learning (ML) engineers can now launch JupyterLab and Code Editor environments on HyperPod clusters without leaving their browser or using command-line tools, reducing the time from cluster access to productive development to a few clicks.
Background
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod provides purpose-built infrastructure for foundation model (FM) training and inference at scale. With Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) orchestration, teams can run distributed training jobs across hundreds of accelerators with built-in resiliency and automatic fault recovery. In addition to training, HyperPod extends this EKS orchestrated infrastructure to serve low-latency, scalable inference for multi-billion-parameter foundation models.
Earlier this year, we launched Amazon SageMaker Spaces for HyperPod, an add-on ML developers can use to create interactive development environments directly on HyperPod EKS clusters. Organizations could then maximize their GPU investments by running interactive workloads alongside training jobs and model deployment on the same infrastructure, with support for fractional GPU allocations.
Previously, creating and managing Spaces relied primarily on the HyperPod CLI or kubectl commands. While this approach provides powerful, granular control for infrastructure administrators, data scientists who prefer a visual interface can now use this new SageMaker Studio capability to bypass command-line tools and focus entirely on model development.
What’s new
With this new capability, data scientists can now create, configure, start, stop, and open Spaces directly from SageMaker Studio. The new IDE and Notebooks tab on the HyperPod cluster detail page provides a complete user interface for Space management, eliminating the need for CLI tools for day-to-day Space operations.
Key capabilities available through Studio include:
- Create Spaces with configurable compute, namespaces, storage, HyperPod Task Governance for compute quota management and image settings through a guided form.
- View all Spaces in a searchable table showing name, application type, status, access type, storage, GPU, and vCPU allocations.
- Start and stop Spaces with a single selection to clear up compute resources when Spaces aren’t used.
- Open Spaces directly in the browser (JupyterLab or Code Editor) or connect through a remote IDE of your choice (for example, VS Code).
Getting started
Setup involves two roles: administrators prepare the cluster, and data scientists create and open Spaces. The following sections cover each.
For administrators
Administrators install the SageMaker Spaces add-on on their HyperPod EKS cluster using either the Quick install (one-click with optimized defaults) or Custom install option (required to set up web UI access) from their SageMaker HyperPod EKS cluster’s IDE and Notebooks tab. After it’s installed, the administrator can configure namespaces, create Space templates, and manage access through EKS access entries.
The following is a one-time setup that administrators must do:
- Install the Spaces add-on: From the Amazon SageMaker AI console, open your HyperPod cluster, go to the IDE and Notebooks tab, and choose either Quick install or Custom install (Custom install is required to enable web browser access). See the AWS documentation for full instructions.
- Configure EKS access entries: Attach the three managed policies AmazonSagemakerHyperpodSpacePolicy, AmazonSagemakerHyperpodUserClusterPolicy, and AmazonSagemakerHyperpodSpaceTemplatePolicy to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles used by your data scientists.
- Enable per-user identity propagation on the Studio domain: If your Studio domain was created before the SageMaker Studio and HyperPod Spaces integration was rolled out, you must enable per-user identity propagation to the HyperPod EKS cluster. This ensures each Studio user’s actions on the cluster (create, stop or delete Space) are attributed to their user profile in EKS access entries and AWS CloudTrail. Furthermore, this identity mapping enforces strict Space ownership. It tracks which user created the environment and determines whether the Space is private or shared across the SageMaker Studio domain.
        Run the following command once per Studio domain:
After updating the domain, verify that the following command returns “USER_IDENTITY”:
Existing running apps are unaffected. Users pick up the new setting on their next sign-in.
- Optionally turn on additional capabilities: Enable any of the capabilities from the following Optional capabilities table.
For data scientists
After the add-on is installed and access is configured, data scientists navigate to their HyperPod cluster in SageMaker Studio under Compute → HyperPod and select the IDE and Notebooks tab to see the Spaces management interface (see Figure 1). Learn more about creating and managing Spaces: Create and manage Spaces on HyperPod.
After the Space status shows Running (typically a few minutes on a cold cluster, approximately 30–40 seconds with over-provisioning), choose Open to launch JupyterLab or Code Editor in your browser (Figures 2 and 3), or Open in VS Code to connect from your local editor through SSH-over-SSM (Figure 4).
Working in a JupyterLab Space
After you open a JupyterLab Space, you get a fully configured development environment with access to:
- Python 3 notebooks with ipykernel.
- Glue PySpark and Glue Spark consoles.
- SparkMagic PySpark and Spark kernels.
- Terminal access for running commands.
- File browser with persistent storage.
- Built-in chat and contextual help.
Your work persists on the attached Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume, so you can stop and restart Spaces without losing progress.
Working in a Code Editor Space
For developers who prefer a VS Code-style experience in the browser, Code Editor Spaces provide a lightweight, web-based IDE with:
- Full file editing with syntax highlighting and IntelliSense.
- Integrated terminal for running shell commands, submitting training jobs, or interacting with cluster resources.
- Extension support for language servers, linters, and formatters.
- Git integration for version control workflows.
- Direct access to the cluster file system and mounted Amazon FSx volumes.
Code Editor Spaces are well-suited for writing and debugging training scripts, managing experiment configurations, and working with code repositories, all without leaving the browser.
Remote IDE connection (VS Code)
Choose Open in VS Code from the Spaces table to connect your local Visual Studio Code to the Space running on HyperPod. This uses SSH-over-SSM tunneling internally, providing a secure connection without requiring you to manage SSH keys or expose port 22.
You get the full power of your local VS Code environment, including extensions, themes, and keybindings, while executing code on HyperPod cluster compute.
You can also connect using the AWS Toolkit for Visual Studio Code, which lists your Spaces under SageMaker AI > HyperPod, and you can start, stop, and connect to Spaces directly from the toolkit panel.
Optional capabilities
Every capability that follows is optional and composable. Enable any combination that fits your team’s needs.
| Capability | Description | 
| Web browser access | AWS Application Load Balancer and custom DNS through Amazon Route 53 to route browser traffic to Spaces. Not required for remote IDE (VS Code over SSM) access. | 
| Space templates | Admin-defined templates that pre-configure compute, images, storage, and lifecycle scripts for consistent Space configurations across teams. | 
| Task Governance | Namespace-level compute quotas, queues, and priority-based admission through Kueue for multi-tenant clusters. | 
| Karpenter autoscaling | Dynamic node scale-up/down based on Space demand. | 
| Karpenter over-provisioning | Pre-warmed nodes with pre-pulled images that drop Space startup from 5–7 minutes to approximately 30–40 seconds. See the following Pro tip section. | 
| Persistent volumes (EFS / FSx) | Shared user directories and team datasets that persist across Spaces. | 
| Custom images (ECR) | Team-specific runtimes and libraries baked into container images hosted in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). | 
| Idle shutdown | Auto-terminate inactive Spaces to protect against runaway compute cost. | 
| NVIDIA MIG | Fractional GPU allocation for cost-efficient interactive workloads on A100/H100 hardware. | 
Pro tip: Reduce Space startup time with node over-provisioning
By default, SageMaker Spaces on HyperPod EKS clusters using Karpenter autoscaling incur a cold-start delay of 5–7 minutes the first time a Space is created on a scale-to-zero cluster, dominated by:
- Amazon Elastic Compute cloud (Amazon EC2) instance launch.
- Kubernetes node registration.
- SageMaker Distribution (SMD) image pull.
For latency-sensitive interactive workloads (JupyterLab, Code Editor), you can maintain a pool of pre-warmed, image-cached nodes using the standard Kubernetes over-provisioning pattern. This drops Space startup time from minutes to around 30–40 seconds.
How it works
- A low-priority (-1000) placeholder Deployment keeps one Kubernetes pod on each warm node. These pods request the same CPU/memory a real Space would.
- An initContainer on each placeholder pre-pulls the SageMaker Distribution image onto the node when Karpenter provisions it.
- When a user creates a Space (default priority 0), the Kubernetes scheduler preempts the placeholder (priority -1000). The Space then lands on the already-warm, image-cached node in a couple of seconds, with no image pull and no node launch wait.
- Karpenter provisions a replacement node for the displaced placeholder in the background.
Learn more about Pro tip deployment: Overprovisioning for HyperPod Spaces.
Verified startup latencies on ml.m5.12xlarge (24 vCPU allocatable, 2 vCPU placeholder, 8 GiB placeholder memory) with the sagemaker-distribution:latest-cpu SMD image, which is about 3.5 GB:
| Path | Latency | 
| Space fits alongside placeholder (coexist) | ~14 s | 
| Space preempts placeholder | ~35 s | 
| Cold start (no warm pool) | 5-7 min | 
Note: These numbers are CPU-only. GPU Spaces need their own placeholder Deployment requesting nvidia.com/gpu with the GPU image pre-pulled. Otherwise, GPU nodes stay cold, and at roughly 10 GB the GPU image costs far more to pull than the 3.5 GB CPU image.
Note: Each warm node holds one EC2 instance in the Running state. For on-demand nodes, this is an extra cost of keeping the warm nodes up and running.
For more information about installing the HyperPod Spaces add-on and getting started, see the AWS documentation.
Pricing
Configuring the SageMaker Spaces add-on doesn’t incur additional charges. You pay for the underlying HyperPod cluster compute consumed by your Spaces, and a per-hour charge for the AWS Systems Manager Advanced On-Premises Instance used for SSH-over-SSM remote connectivity. See AWS Systems Manager pricing for details.
If you use the over-provisioning described earlier, note that there’s an added cost for warm nodes. Depending on the instance type and size, these nodes stay in the running state waiting to provision Spaces.
Conclusion
Managing HyperPod Spaces with SageMaker Studio bridges the gap between data scientists and high-performance compute infrastructure. Teams can now go from cluster access to a running JupyterLab or Code Editor environment in minutes, without needing to learn CLI tools or Kubernetes concepts. Combined with features like HyperPod Task Governance, fractional GPU support, and idle shutdown, organizations can provide self-service access to shared clusters while maintaining cost control and resource fairness.
To get started, navigate to your HyperPod EKS cluster in the SageMaker AI console and select the IDE and Notebooks tab. For more information, see the SageMaker HyperPod Spaces documentation.

articles.title: Signal VP reminds lawmakers the secure messaging app won’t comply with Bill C-22 | BetaKit
articles.text:
Secure messaging service Signal is still ready to shut down its Canadian operations if Bill C-22, known as the Lawful Access Act, becomes law and is enforced.
The news: Signal VP of strategy and global affairs Udbhav Tiwari reiterated his non-profit’s stance against Canada’s Bill C-22 at an intimate gathering of senators and lawmakers on Monday evening. The bill, which is currently before the Senate, would compel companies like Signal to keep user data and give law enforcement more power to collect it.
Tiwari said that Signal has three main issues with Bill C-22: how it engages with encryption, how it engages with metadata collection, and its technical access measures. Tiwari explained that Bill C-22 could effectively sidestep Signal’s encryption with an order to share encryption keys with the government, force it to collect more than the bare minimum metadata it already collects and store it for six months, or demand Signal make a targeted change to how its platform works so it collects more information.
From the source: “For us, this is a serious enough issue that it would fundamentally break Signal,” Tiwari said. “If we would have to [choose between] serving the users of Canada with the end-to-end encryption that we provide around the world, or creating a much weaker version of our product that connects all of this metadata, the choice for us, unfortunately, would be starkly clear.”
“We will not make changes to our products … to comply with such demands that place the privacy of not just Canadians but everyone else in the world at risk,” Tiwari added.
The context: Bill C-22 is currently in the Senate, after being rushed through the House of Commons before the chambers broke for the summer. The Canadian Internet Society, which ran the event Tiwari spoke at, said the session was being recorded and would be sent to relevant Senate committees.
The act has been met with vocal opposition from Canadian civil liberties groups, which argue it would give police unprecedented surveillance powers. Canadian and European tech companies also argued in an open letter sent to the ministers of industry and public safety last month that the proposed legislation would “erode trust” in Canada’s tech industry and weaken the competitive landscape.
Final thought: In response to a question from BetaKit, Tiwari explained in a panel discussion that Signal has never deliberately cut off access to any country in the world, but that it has refused to comply with legislative orders from certain countries like Russia, China, or North Korea. Those countries, in turn, order their internet service providers to throttle access to Signal.
If C-22 passes, Tiwari said a similar order of events would have to occur in Canada for the app to become unavailable to Canadians. While it’s possible that would end in some kind of stalemate, he said he thinks the powers granted by C-22 make that outcome very unlikely.
Feature image courtesy Alex Riehl for BetaKit.

articles.title: Form Energy and its iron batteries
articles.text:
Form Energy and its iron batteries
Form’s 100-hour batteries could make clean energy more weather-resilient and help power data centers.
 Form Energy is building iron-based batteries that can store energy for multiple days. The company is ramping up supply at its factory and signing deals for commercial projects.
New solar and wind installations produce electricity more affordably than fossil fuels in most places, but their output varies based on season, time of day, and weather. To compensate, utilities are increasingly investing in battery storage systems, which can charge when power is abundant and discharge when the grid needs a boost.
Lithium-ion batteries are the fastest-growing storage technology. Although light and energy-dense, they require pricey metals and are costly to scale, and few of the large batteries of this type used in industry are designed to store energy for longer than four to six hours.
Form Energy wants to build cheaper long-duration energy storage technology. The company has developed a new type of battery, built with a far more abundant and cheaper metal, iron, that can store energy for 100 hours. It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting.” During discharge, oxygen from the air converts the iron metal to rust, releasing electrons. When charging, current converts the rust back into iron metal.
Over the past two years, Form has gained commercial traction. It began producing batteries at its West Virginia factory for its first commercial deployment, a 150 megawatt-hour system for Minnesota electricity provider Great River Energy, which is set to come online in 2027. And Form has signed several other deals with power providers. The largest is a project with another Minnesota-based utility, Xcel Energy, where wind and solar power, backed by 30 gigawatt-hours of Form’s batteries, will be used to power a new Google data center. That project is expected to come online in phases between 2028 and 2031.
Key indicators
- Industry: Energy storage
- Founded: 2017
- Headquarters: Somerville, Massachusetts, US
- Notable fact: Once complete, Form’s proposed 30 gigawatt-hour energy storage system at a Google data center in Minnesota could be the world’s largest battery project by energy capacity.
Potential for impact
Wind and solar power play a major role in limiting growth in global carbon dioxide emissions. Still, many grid operators depend on fossil fuel plants, especially natural gas ones, to fill gaps caused by periods of low renewable supply or high demand. Form’s batteries are designed to cover multiday supply-demand imbalances, like those that crop up during heat waves, deep freezes, or periods with little sun or wind. The company declined to share the current cost of its battery systems, but says its goal is to reach $20 per kilowatt-hour, which would make them cost-competitive with the natural gas alternative.
The company’s technology could help reduce emissions from the AI data center boom. AI’s thirst for energy has already delayed closure of aging coal plants, led to the building of new natural gas plants, and caused price hikes for consumers. Cheap energy storage could help renewables meet more of this AI-driven growth in electricity demand.
Caveats
The long-duration storage market is still nascent. Form’s iron-air technology faces a crowded field of approaches, including pumped hydropower, compressed gas, fuel cells, gravitational devices, and flow batteries that store energy in liquids. The economics of multiday batteries, which require large capital expenditures yet frequently sit idle, remain tricky.
While funding from data center developers could be a major boost, Form also has to prove it can deliver: Its existing production capacity, 2 gigawatt-hours of battery storage per year, is a fraction of the 80 gigawatt-hours it has promised through commercial agreements. Success will hinge on its ability to scale.
Another remaining question is the technology’s physical footprint. Form’s batteries, which are stacked together in enclosures the size of shipping containers, require an acre for every two to three megawatts. That means its Google installation would take up the equivalent of at least 75 football fields.
Next steps
In addition to finalizing its first commercial project, Form is outfitting its factory with new equipment that will help it scale manufacturing to meet its production backlog. It will do so with the help of new financing, announced in August, that brings its total money raised, in addition to West Virginia state and US federal grants, to more than $2 billion.

articles.title: Google’s power-hungry data centers crave nuclear energy
articles.text:
Google announced a new agreement to update six nuclear power plant sites across the US as the tech giant seeks to generate more electricity for its power-hungry data centers.
Google’s power-hungry data centers crave nuclear energy
Google signed long-term agreements meant to cover the costs of upgrades at nuclear power plants.
Google signed the 20-year deal with Constellation, the leading nuclear power plant operator in the US. The power purchase agreement is meant to guarantee the revenue needed to cover the cost of efficiency upgrades at existing nuclear plants and “represents more than $4.3 billion of new investment by Constellation,” according to the press release.
Over the next five years, the companies expect new equipment at each site to collectively lead to 890 megawatts of additional nuclear capacity. That’s roughly equivalent to the amount of electricity one large new nuclear reactor or three small modular reactors might generate, according to Google and Constellation.
PJM has struggled lately to meet growing demand from AI data centers
They plan to modernize 11 reactors at six sites in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. Each is connected to the PJM Interconnection grid, the largest power grid in the US, which spans 13 states and the District of Columbia — including the nation’s largest hub for data centers in Loudoun County, Virginia.
PJM has struggled lately to meet growing demand from AI data centers. An independent market monitor filed a complaint last year with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) saying that PJM was planning to allow huge data centers to connect to the grid that it could not reliably serve, which could lead to blackouts.
In January, the Trump administration and governors from all of the states where PJM operates issued a joint statement calling on PJM to hold an “emergency” power auction to support the buildout of new power plants through long-term contracts. PJM postponed its auction last week following a directive from FERC to revise its proposal in order to ensure stronger protections to prevent data centers from raising electricity bills for other customers. Electricity rates have skyrocketed in states connected to PJM, including New Jersey, where prices have climbed 54 percent over five years.
Along with the nuclear power deal, Google also inked a separate, much larger 15-year energy supply agreement with Constellation meant to guarantee continued revenue for other existing power plants Constellation operates within PJM, regardless of fuel type. Nuclear energy made up 70 percent of Constellation’s total generating capacity last year, and another 8 percent came from renewables. Gas and oil made up the remaining 22 percent, according to the company’s latest sustainability report. Gas also accounts for the largest chunk of PJM’s fuel mix. At 2,700MW, the second deal is much larger than the nuclear power purchase agreement.
Data centers are driving a surge in new gas infrastructure projects in the US, moving many tech companies further from their sustainability goals. Google’s carbon emissions rose by 18 percent last year along with a jump in electricity demand of 37 percent, according to the company’s latest sustainability report.

articles.title: Emmys will move from broadcast TV to Prime Video in 2027 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Amazon announced on Tuesday that Prime Video will be the new home for the Emmy Awards, marking another major Hollywood awards show’s move from broadcast television to streaming. This will also be the first time that the ceremony has had a dedicated home, as the show rotated across broadcasters like ABC, CBS, Fox, and NBC over the past seven decades.
Prime Video will stream the awards show worldwide for six years for free, starting in 2027, where it will go live in over 240 countries and territories. Non-Amazon Prime subscribers will also be able to watch the awards show on the Prime Video platform.
The terms of the deal were not disclosed.
The move comes as the Emmys face potential viewership declines, as more of its audience moves to streaming services. This year’s ratings for the 78th primetime Emmy Awards on NBC were down nearly 10% from the year prior, after a couple of years of growth, the AP reported. However, the telecast’s 6.87 million viewers this year were higher than its all-time low of 4.3 million in January 2024.
The Emmys aren’t the only major awards show making the shift to streaming. Last year, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a deal giving YouTube the rights to stream the Oscars beginning in 2029, while Netflix has streamed the Screen Actors Guild Awards since 2024.
